We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material. Additionally, both the thermal capacity and compressibility exhibit strong temperature-dependent behaviors rooted in the van Hove singularities present in the material's dispersion relations. It is worth noting that these singularities can induce remarkable features in the thermal screening length, such as abrupt changes in its temperature dependence. By contrast, the material's hydrodynamic momentum relaxation time is controlled by the momentum at which the van Hove singularities occur. This unique characteristic stems from the anisotropic nature of momentum transport in Dirac electrons, implying that the relationship $v_F/T \ll 1$ must be satisfied for the application of the hydrodynamic theory of charge carriers in graphene. We have also used the formula for the dynamic density-density correlation to estimate the thermal screening length in ultra-thin graphene samples. Our calculation indicates that at temperatures below the values of $T \sim 3$ K to $10$ K, the thermal screening length is controlled by the material's 2D nature, rather than its 1D character. We have further used the predicted thermal capacity to explain the recently observed linear temperature dependence in the thermal expansion of graphene. By leveraging the predicted compressibility, we estimate that the phase transition driven by electron-phonon interaction in graphene is likely within the scope of the model established by Halperin and Hohenberg for many-body phenomena. We have also explored the potential extension of our formalism to the full quantum regime, which might be within the scope of the model established by Volovik for the properties of superfluid $^3He$ in relation to 2D Dirac fermions. Lastly, our study of the dynamic density-density correlation has potential implications for the understanding of magnetic properties in graphene as well. These findings highlight the significance of studying the dynamic properties of charge carriers in graphene through future experiments. Additionally, our study predicts that the material properties of graphene could be controlled by adjusting temperature and dopant levels. Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context. These systems fall short when it comes to producing high-quality paragraphs, necessitating a system that integrates contextual elements. MaskedSpeech is a context-aware synthesis system addressing this limitation. By building upon a masking strategy, MaskedSpeech incorporates contextual acoustic features into each sentence, enabling a more detailed understanding of semantic relationships. Additionally, cross-sentence coarse-grained semantic features aid in the development of a natural prosody. Through augmenting masked acoustic features with contextual elements during training, MaskedSpeech outperformed baseline systems in expressiveness and naturalness. Notably, when synthesizing a paragraph, MaskedSpeech exhibited significantly reduced abnormalness compared to TACOPA. Furthermore, evaluation of ablation models revealed that the contextual elements contributed to an increase in naturalness without compromising expressiveness. These findings validate the efficacy of MaskedSpeech in contextual speech synthesis. Based on the analysis, MaskedSpeech could serve as a foundation for paragraph-level speech synthesis systems. Due to its ability to generate high-quality syntheses, the code and demo associated with this work have been made publicly available. You can access them at https://github.com/ChenZhBeijng/MAKD.

Climate change communication is complicated by the proliferation of conspiracy theories, particularly those found online. This research investigates prevalent conspiracy theories regarding climate change by analyzing a significant Twitter dataset and applies a sophisticated stance detection technique. Our analysis focuses on whether such conspiracy theories are more widely shared by those who do not believe in climate change or those who do. Furthermore, we examine the most popular conspiracy theories, their variations with differing levels of climate change acceptance, and reveal that non-believers predominantly disseminate messages containing conspiracy theory-related keywords. Notably, all top conspiracy theories are fundamentally critiques of climate change mitigation efforts. Our findings also indicate that social media users who are skeptical of climate change frequently share messages that contain conspiracy theory-related keywords, particularly those related to climate change adaptation and energy transition. It is crucial to develop effective strategies to address the spread of conspiracy theories and to consider both the science and the social media when communicating about climate change. The investigation utilized the CMS experiment's data from 2016, equivalent to 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of luminosity, and the findings are based on joint searches for dark matter and Higgs boson production. The results of this research are presented as constraints on the median mass values and the coupling strength between the mediator and other standard model particles. It is found that scalar and pseudoscalar mediator medians up to 555 and 275 GeV respectively are compatible with the data collected. Additionally, constraints are placed on the interaction of standard model particles with the mediator, showing that the coupling of gluons and dark matter has the tightest constraints at around 500 GeV. Lastly, it is observed that the data collected is consistent with the standard model predictions. It is further noted that the determined bounds are dependent on the assumed median mass capacity. It is also determined that the results of this research are representative of various simplified models involving the interaction of dark matter with top quarks and top quark pairs. These simplified models included the reversal of the dark matter and top quark roles. The results of this research are compared with the constraints set by the direct dark matter searches, showing that the collected data's sensitivity is competitive with that of the LUX, XENON1T, and LZ experiments in the high mediator mass range. It is noted that the collected data's sensitivity improves with higher mediator masses. It is further noted that the collected data's sensitivity is independent of the assumed interaction type between dark matter and nuclei. The results of this research are therefore considered to be representative of the general dark matter and Higgs boson production in the high-energy proton-proton collisions. It is noted that the results of this research are sensitive to the assumption that the interaction between dark matter and nuclei is mediated by a scalar or pseudoscalar particle. It is further noted that the results of this research are independent of the assumed temperature of the universe at the time of the dark matter creation. Building upon Kirkeboen et al.'s (2016) work that demonstrates the feasibility of combining multiple treatment instruments with ranked preference data, we analyze the testable implications of the key assumptions underpinning their identification argument. This analysis also offers a novel assessment of the biases resulting from these assumption violations. Ultimately, these findings empower researchers to evaluate the reliability of these assumptions and determine the practical impact of their breaches. Utilizing the identified method, we investigate the post-secondary field of study return on investment in Norway and Denmark, exploring potential cross-country differences. Our results indicate significant correlation between fields of study return on investment in both countries, particularly after eliminating fields where identification assumption breaches occur. For many fields, we find that Norwegian students do not face positive return on investment in either country. However, under more relaxed assumption usage, Denmark's economics and forestry fields exhibit positive return on investment, resembling those found in Norway. Our study also reveals that Danish students enjoy a relatively higher return on investment compared to Norwegian students, particularly in fields such as biology, geography, and physics, in both sample averages and distribution tightness. While these results hold true for the entire sample, we discover subtle differences in favor of Norwegian students in the initial stages of their study. Our research also showcases the utility of the identified method in analyzing fields of study return on investment across various birth cohorts and educational durations. Lastly, our study examines the impact of birth rates on field of study return on investment in both countries, revealing potential cross-country differences in this correlation. We analyzed the process of gas expulsion in open clusters through numerical simulations focused on the dynamics of embedded binary stars. Our results reveal that gas expulsion has a limited effect on the majority of binary stars, primarily due to the 'differential accretion' mechanism. This mechanism leads to the transfer of gas to a newly formed binary formed from a close triple (1:1 mass ratio) via orbital circularization. Nevertheless, in systems where the mass of the inner binary matches the mass of the third body, which occurs rarely, the differential accretion mechanism is overridden, resulting in the internal binary's orbit becoming more compact or even collapsing into a single star. Our simulations also indicate that alternative pathways to producing single star systems exist, including the 'thermal feedback' mechanism, which enables the ejection of fast-moving single stars with velocities exceeding the standard cluster velocity by up to 2.5 times. Our findings, which align with observed single star statistics, suggest that gas expulsion plays a significant role in creating these systems. We discuss the potential impact of our results on binary star evolution and the required efficiency of gas expulsion to produce the observed single star counts. Our research, which will be expanded upon in future papers, paves the way for the creation of more realistic binary star populations in young open clusters. This emulator successfully emulated error-free neural network behavior in software for individual neurons and networks of neurons connected in complex loops. Additionally, our research explored and implemented the neural network's ability to adapt through learning processes, while accounting for random numerical approximations that may affect the outcome. The spherically symmetric merging of a kinetic cloud of particles onto a Schwarzschild black hole is investigated. Unlike earlier research, which established boundary conditions at a distant point, we examine this process with properties of the cloud specified within a finite sphere of radius. We use a series of models, ranging from simple to complex, to compute steady-state solutions, which show that mass accretion is significantly impeded when the cloud possesses angular momentum. It is assumed that particles interact via a short-range potential, which leads to the formation of a Hubble sphere boundary, where particles on the edge have nearly zero velocity. Excluding cases where the cloud's center of mass is directly fallen onto the black hole, the mass accretion rate is primarily determined by the Hubble sphere velocity, rather than the cloud's total mass. A comparison with existing research reveals that our model predicts lower mass accretion rates. For low-velocity clouds, we observe a mass accretion rate consistent with Frank-Tamm's findings, which is significantly lower than Alexander's result for non-rotating black holes. For higher velocity clouds, the mass accretion rate is predicted to decrease exponentially with increasing velocity. We hypothesize that this relationship is universally applicable, which could provide valuable data for studying the evolution of supermassive black holes across various cosmic environments. Our model is further generalized to include clouds with non-zero temperatures, which indicates that thermal energy has a negligible effect on mass accretion at the Hubble sphere. Therefore, while the cloud in our model has a higher velocity than the cloud in Alexander's result for non-rotating black holes, the mass accretion rate is lower. A longstanding issue regarding massive star origins involves whether these stars always form within dense clusters and, if found in less crowded environments, if they inevitably moved there.  Recent advances in wide-scale photometric surveys enable us to detect massive stars without bias in the less crowded regions of the galaxy.  This study examines forty candidate OB stars discovered through the PLCK catalog of dusty objects, located in the Galactic halo and surrounding neighborhoods.  Spectra from our optical investigation, along with existing near-infrared data, reveal twenty-one classified OB stars with known distances less than five kiloparsecs.  The distribution pattern of these massive stars, along with their stellar mass and metal content, does not align with star-forming regions detected through infrared luminosity.  This discontinuous distribution suggests that these stars originated from separate populations.  There is also evidence that some low-mass stars associated with these OB stars belong to the same demographic as to these OB stars themselves.  This implies that many of these low-mass stars could be associated with massive stars, potentially indicating that many massive stars were formed in less crowded environments.  Further study is needed to verify whether these OB stars formed within small groups of stars, as dynamical interactions in such groups could explain the observed scatter in their metal content.  This research is crucial in understanding the formation of massive stars by identifying new, widespread instances of massive star formation outside of dense clusters.  Moreover, our findings could have implications for interpreting massive star candidates detected through space-based missions such as Gaia and the upcoming Roman telescope, which may identify thousands of such stars in the galaxy.  This could provide evidence of widespread massive star formation in less crowded regions, constrained by their metal content and distribution, and could offer insights into their origins.  Ultimately, our research aims to understand how massive stars came to inhabit a diverse range of environments, from dusty regions to the outskirts of the galaxy.  By combining our findings with modeling efforts, we aim to shed more light on how these stars come to exist in such an diversity of places.  This could provide significant insights into massive star formation by identifying widespread instances of massive star formation outside of dense clusters, as well as their metal content and distribution.  Such research could offer valuable comparisons with theoretical models, and could help to clarify how these stars came to inhabit a diverse range of places.  By studying numerous massive star candidates detected through Gaia and the upcoming Roman telescope, we may gain a more comprehensive understanding of how these stars formed, moving to the locations we observe today.

Degraded handwritten documents, which are susceptible to damage from paper ageing and environmental factors, can cause severe readability issues for current text recognition algorithms. To overcome these challenges, we propose an innovative, end-to-end approach utilizing Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to restore and improve the quality of severely degraded handwritten documents. This pioneering method combines the capabilities of Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) and Transposed Convolution (also known as Transposed Conv) in image transformation. To achieve superior restoration results, our network dissects handwritten characters from various classes, competing in a minimax game against a series of discriminators tailored for specific character classes. Through thorough testing on numerous handwritten document images from diverse sources and tasks, we demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method in producing high-quality, realistic results across a range of degraded images. The newly developed dataset, consisting of 4500 handwritten English characters with severe degradation, played a crucial role in enhancing the performance of our gan-based restoration method. Colorization is particularly challenging due to its inherently high degrees of freedom; when presented with an image, multiple plausible color combinations exist, and there may be no single definitive solution. In this paper, we explore the problem of computing Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) weights. Focusing on a single perceptron with n inputs and 1 output, we leverage the properties of a generalized polynomial basis to define a new vector for each set of inputs. We then identify a specific linear system that underpins the computation of ANN weights, encompassing the widely recognized case of n=1 (linear regression) and extending to higher dimensions (multiple linear regression) with n>1. We derive a closed-form solution for computing weights in ANNs, accompanied by analytical proofs. To illustrate the practicality of our proposed method, we tested its performance on both simple synthetic datasets and more complex real-world datasets. The results are compared to those obtained through the use of gradient descent and genetic algorithms. The findings show that our proposed method is versatile and substantially faster than these established solvers. An open-source implementation of this method is available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/ann-weights/ann_weights. In Tb3RuO7, neighboring ruthenium atoms created a chain pattern, with some being ordered magnetically and others remaining randomly aligned. This unique combination resulted in an intermediate disordered state, with the two ruthenium types exhibiting similar yet distinct behaviors. In Nd3RuO7, the magnetic patterns were uniform and independent for the two ruthenium species, with both being ordered at temperatures below 17.5 K. We attribute the disordered state in Tb3RuO7 primarily to the magnetic frustrations, caused by the differing internal magnetic fields imposed by the ordered terbium atoms on the two ruthenium species, leading to distinct behaviors. Additionally, the exceptional sensitivity of the terbium spins was a contributing factor. We now turn our attention to the applications of magnetic frustrations, with Tb3RuO7 serving as a prime example and a promising candidate for more advanced magnetic materials. In contrast, the stable patterns in Nd3RuO7 are a direct reflection of the material's uniform and homogeneous character. Traditional covariate shift adaptation relies on abundant unlabelled samples to compensate for the lack of balance between past and present data distributions. However, when the target distribution is also known, semi-supervised learning becomes a more efficient use of the unlabelled samples. Unfortunately, direct integration of covariate shift adaptation and semi-supervised learning is difficult due to the differing objectives and data annotations. 

We address this challenge by proposing a novel technique that merges our previous covariate shift adaptation method with optimally calibrated gradient descent for semi-supervised learning. This integrated approach allows the covariate shift adaptation to focus solely on class weights, thereby improving the efficiency of unsupervised covariate shift adaptation by limiting the impact of unlabelled samples on the target distribution. Additionally, it enhances semi-supervised learning with robust covariate shift adaptation results. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this combination through experiments on simple datasets and a realistic, real-world setting. To assess various approaches to expanding language coverage, we integrate German and Korean into BigScience's large-scale, 1.3 billion parameter multilingual language model, initially trained on 13 languages. Our study focuses on key factors influencing model adaptability for new languages and weighs the computational expense against potential performance gains. Specifically, we investigate the impact of (1) language encoding, (2) finetuning, and (3) positive and negative sentence sampling on the model's performance. Our findings show that a robust 2-hour finetuning with adaptive learning rate and sentence sampling method can significantly enhance the model's performance in both zero and few-shot settings. Interestingly, we discover that sentence sampling is beneficial even after finetuning, suggesting its value as a regularization technique. Our research underscores the importance of carefully selecting the sampling method and the number of pass(es) during adaptability experiments. Furthermore, we enhance the model's performance in German through additional training on a larger dataset but find that such effort yields diminishing returns beyond a single pass. Our analysis also reveals numerous performance fluctuations in adaptability studies, which we attribute to various factors including the choice of dataset, the number of pass(es), and the sampling method. Nonetheless, we emphasize the need for more rigorous, dataset-independent adaptability evaluations to ensure consistency across different setups and language models. Recent high-resolution observations using VLA and CARMA telescopes have unveiled previously unknown details of proto-stars in binary systems. Specifically, mass measurements for CB230 IRS1 and L1165-SMM1 revealed a significantly higher mass range ($0.1-0.25 \, M_{\odot}$) than expected, prompting a binary formation simulation to replicate observed proto-stellar mass. The research employed the Amuse code to model the formation of binary systems, focusing on a low-mass regime ($1 \, M_{\odot}$). CB230 IRS1 and L1165-SMM1 were simulated multiple times, each time analyzing how total core mass influenced fragment mass. The results showed that CB230 IRS1 formed with a higher mass binary ($0.1-0.13 \, M_{\odot}$) when the core mass was $0.13 \, M_{\odot}$, whereas L1165-SMM1 formed with a lower mass binary ($0.02-0.03 \, M_{\odot}$) when the core mass was $0.013 \, M_{\odot}$. However, these simulations failed to produce a binary with a mass of $0.1 \, M_{\odot}$ for L1165-SMM1, highlighting that other factors might be necessary to replicate observed proto-stellar mass. Nevertheless, the study showed that a binary formation through core collapse can produce low-mass binaries similar to those observed. The results also suggested that the total core mass influences the mass of binary fragments, with a more massive core producing more massive binaries. Consequently, CB230 IRS1 and L1165-SMM1 formed with binary masses of $0.13 \pm 0.01 \, M_{\odot}$ and $0.015 \pm 0.005 \, M_{\odot}$, respectively. The research concluded by comparing the formation of CB230 IRS1 as a high-mass binary within a molecular cloud core to the concept of cores with pre-existing binaries. Although the model replicated some observed characteristics of the system, it failed to produce a binary with a mass of $0.1 \, M_{\odot}$ for L1165-SMM1, prompting further high-resolution simulations to replicate this particular binary. The research suggested that CB230 IRS1 formed as a high-mass binary within a molecular cloud core, whereas L1165-SMM1 formed as a low-mass binary.

The study of angular correlations in the cosmic microwave background and galaxies spans multiple fields of astrophysics, including galaxy physics, cosmology, and the study of large-scale structures. Current and upcoming surveys will produce significant amounts of data, prompting the need for more efficient analysis techniques. We introduce a new framework for analyzing angular correlations, utilizing a weighted version of the skew-spectrum rather than the traditional multipoole expansion. This approach offers two primary benefits. Firstly, it enables a more sensitive detection of angular correlations, particularly in higher-order multipoles where the Planck data may soon become limited by systematic effects. Secondly, the weighted skew-spectrum facilitates a more direct comparison between data and theoretical models, thus reducing analytical complexity. We apply the skew-spectrum formalism to the analysis of angular correlations in the context of galaxy distributions and the cosmic microwave background, and demonstrate its ability to produce results consistent with the standard multipoole analysis. The skew-spectrum, however, shows great potential in providing additional insight from future data, potentially offering a more intuitive understanding of the data and a more robust comparison between data and theoretical models. This approach may also be generalized to the analysis of higher-order correlations and the phase space structure of cosmic structures. In addition, the skew-spectrum can be utilized in the detection of non-Gaussian signals, serving as a complementary tool to the traditional multipoole-based methods. We illustrate this by applying the skew-spectrum to the analysis of known non-Gaussian signals from galaxy distributions and the cosmic microwave background. The skew-spectrum reveals the non-Gaussian signature in the angular correlation of the CMB harmonic n=13, which is not present in the multipoole-based analysis. This study investigates the impact of hyperspectral pixel dimensionality reduction on classification tasks. Five methods (PCA, KPCA, ICA, AE, and DAE) are utilized to compress high-dimensional pixels down to 301 dimensions. The resulting pixels are used for classification, allowing a comprehensive assessment of each method's effectiveness based on classification accuracy, compression rates, and reconstruction errors. Our research employed three diverse hyperspectral image datasets (urban, suburban, and forest landscapes), gathered by the Remote Sensing and Spatial Ecosystem Modeling lab at the University of Toronto. Our analysis reveals that PCA, KPCA, and ICA methods preserve pixel signals well but show decreased classification performance beyond 90% compression rates. In contrast, AE and DAE achieve better results at 95% compression but see their performance deteriorate as the compression rate approaches 97%. Ultimately, our findings highlight the importance of considering both compression methods and rates when crafting an effective hyperspectral pixel classification workflow. Neural networks are highly effective feature extractors but they pose significant challenges due to their large size. Understanding the parameters within various layers is complicated, resulting in the networks often being referred to as 'black boxes.' In contrast, simpler models are more interpretable but they are also much harder to find. Identifying and utilizing a sparse network that can be trained to replicate the same results is a viable option to improve network interpretability. According to the lottery ticket hypothesis, even large, dense neural networks harbor a smaller sparse sub-network that can be trained independently to achieve the same accuracy in the same amount of time. Our objective is to explore the existence of this trainable sub-network in the realm of natural language models, and we will accomplish this by examining and evaluating the most recent model compression techniques, such as quantization, knowledge distillation, and pruning. Our results indicate the existence of a trainable sub-network in the models we examined, and we propose a new approach called the generalized lotteries that utilizes neural network equilibrium to identify the sparse sub-network. Our findings also suggest that the accuracy of the compressed models is largely independent of the chosen optimization method. Furthermore, we demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed approach by treating pruned models as the dense base-line, and we observed significant improvements in the accuracy of the compressed models, achieving 88.23% and 88.69% for the test sets of SNLI and BoolQ datasets respectively. Our approach is distinct from other compression methods in the literature as it treats pruned models as a dense baseline, and our results show that the improvements in the accuracy of the compressed models are significantly higher than those of the unsupervised distillation method we examined. Our code is publicly available on https://github.com/amanbasu/generalized-lotteries. Our approach is unique as it utilizes the equilibrium of neural networks to identify a trainable sparse sub-network, and our results show superior performance on the natural language understanding task of natural language inference and boolean question classification. Our findings suggest that the density of the dense base-line has no bearing on the accuracy of the compressed models, and we identify two key challenges in the realm of compression, namely the scarcity of data and the scarcity of models. Our proposed approach targets the latter, and we show through our experiments that the existence of a dense base-line is a necessary condition for the existence of a trainable sparse sub-network. It can be used to determine the spatial arrangements of proteins with accuracy and also identify suspicious cases with a chemical shift indicator value greater than 2.0. This makes ProCS a valuable tool for studying protein structures with high precision. Additionally, ProCS is used to determine the spatial arrangements of the active and inactive states of over 20 proteins. This shows the potential for ProCS to help determine the active and inactive conformational arrangements of proteins. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. To facilitate this process, we develop a novel approach based on iterative max-min optimization and complement it with an ensemble technique, enabling the simultaneous evaluation of multiple loss functions. Our proposed method surpasses comparable techniques in a series of image classification benchmarks. The source code is openly accessible via https://github.com/ssehik/IterativeMaxMin. The algorithm has been successfully applied to the classification of histological images, allowing the differentiation of malignant cells from healthy cells based on tissue samples. These results are documented in the supplementary materials. The computational complexity of our approach is quantified as O(lnN)/T, where N represents the number of data points and T denotes the iteration count. The advantage of this method lies in its ability to adaptively select multiple loss functions dynamically according to the data set, thereby mitigating potential overfitting. Our findings also highlight the potential of transforming KL divergence into a discriminative loss function, paving the way for a deeper understanding of this loss function; moreover, we identify its discriminative version as a more robust alternative to the cross-entropy loss function, particularly in the presence of imbalanced data. To facilitate reproducibility, the source code has been publicly archived at https://github.com/ssehik/LearningMultipleLossFunctions. The proposed method is highly versatile and may be applied to the optimization of various loss functions. Describing the behaviors of complex systems comprised of strongly interacting elements requires concise expressions for their internal relationships. Ensuring the stability of these systems is the primary focus. Parquet theory is capable of achieving a level of self-consistency that encompasses all strictly pair-based interactions among elements. Grounded in a perturbative framework, the theory is comprised of a series of nonlinear integral equations that describe scattering events at all levels, constrained by principles of symmetry but also inherently heuristic. Within the context of a theoretical framework developed by Kraichnan, a new Hamiltonian-based analysis is applied to parquet's structure in the context of fermionic particles, resulting in a natural formation of the theory's underlying equations through its canonical representation. This approach reveals the inherent connection between the conserving properties of the derived scattering amplitude and the traditional parquet theory. Although the derived amplitude conserves properties at a microscopic level, it does not maintain symmetry. In contrast, the traditional amplitude maintains symmetry but fails to ensure conservation at any point. Ultimately, the decision to use one amplitude over the other is determined by the specific requirements of the system under consideration rather than its adherence to a theoretical ideal. This finding resolves the debate over the two amplitudes and their respective implications in the perturbative framework. By leveraging this resolution, a clear understanding of the perturbative framework's stability is achieved, and the inherent connection between the derived amplitude and a corresponding bethe-salpeter amplitude is demonstrated. This relationship facilitates a seamless transition from the perturbative description of the two-body problem to a description of a completely interacting world through symmetrization. As a result, a comprehensive method for deriving effective single-particle operators is developed within the context of a renormalization group framework. This method is successfully applied to a one-dimensional Hubbard model at a critical analysis of the effects of wave function normalization within the strong coupling limit. Despite these investigations, the model's strong coupling behavior remains to be fully understood. A connected series of theoretical insights provides a degree of freedom in parquet's structure that can be leveraged to conclude that approximate solutions to the derived non-linear equations will inevitably diverge with increasing frequency. Consequently, a crucial role is assigned to the frequency-dependent nature of interactions within the perturbative framework. This distinction is exemplified through the comparison of fermonic and bosonic interactions. In conclusion, the applied methods are found to be effectively compliant with principles of renormalization as expressed by principles of dimensional regularisation. This compliance is crucial in ensuring the self-consistency and stability

The process of exciton condensation leads to the spontaneous creation of electron-hole pairs and triggers a phase transition in a semimetal that forms an excitonic insulator by closing the gap at the Fermi surface. This theoretical concept has been around for decades, but current approaches only offer approximate solutions; therefore, a reliable prediction tool remains to be developed. To address this challenge, a new method was created that incorporates finite-temperature density functional theory and many-body perturbation theory to study the critical behavior of exciton condensation. Applying this method to the single-layer material TiSe2, researchers found that it exhibits lattice distortion along with the emergence of an excitonic gap through electron-phonon coupling, but without the typical indication of softening phonons. This discovery confirms that exciton condensation is responsible for the charge-density-wave state in TiSe2, indicating the developed approach is versatile and could be applied to searching for potential excitonic insulators in naturally occurring materials. Furthermore, this method is capable of providing detailed information about the exciton gap, Drude weight, and carrier concentration, making it a valuable resource for studying quantum materials. By combining theoretical predictions with experimental data, researchers were able to align their results, demonstrating the method's utility in practicing band-structure engineering through carrier doping or strain tuning. Ultimately, this approach contributes to a better understanding of how to achieve excitonic insulators by regulating electron or hole concentrations, leading to potentially transitionable materials for artificial quantum matter. This research investigates the impact of human emotions in a text-based community safety reporting system where users interact with dispatchers. Analysis of over 180 thousand messages reveals that emotions are consistently expressed throughout the conversation and that dispatchers' emotional support is crucial in motivating users to provide additional information. Interestingly, a high level of emotional support from dispatchers is linked to a lower response rate, suggesting that dispatchers are aware of the negative consequences of their emotional expressions. Furthermore, when dispatchers display positive emotions, it appears that their tone is fake, as their neutral attitude is more effective in encouraging users to respond. To better understand these findings, a detailed examination of the context is conducted, revealing significant differences in how emotions are expressed and how they affect the conversation outcome based on user reporting methods. What is more, a comparison of the emotion analysis between this safety reporting system and a different text-based system known as MuSTACHE reveals distinct characteristics of emotion usage. As a result, a safe and effective approach to managing emotions in a text-based community safety reporting system is presented. Interestingly, a similar approach may not yield similar outcomes for a different type of system. Therefore, when designing a system that involves human emotion-based interaction, it is crucial to consider the specific system context in order to accurately anticipate the effect of emotions. To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in relation to direction.  Within the context of non-relativistic electron behavior, significant anisotropic effects arise due to proximity to a quantum critical point, with susceptibility showing strong direction-dependent behavior and immense enhancement near this critical point, displaying similar trends as in relativistic triplex superconductivity with differing scales. We also find that when considering relativistic electron behavior, the magnetic susceptibility becomes less directional, but still exhibits substantial dependence, especially at the Fermi level. We compare our computational results with existing experimental data on indium-doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$. We found that the local density of states would likely be undetectable within the current experimental threshold but that the localized magnetic effect could be within the current experimental threshold's sensitivity. Label-efficient active learning algorithms query specific, representative samples to be annotated by a human. Present techniques either utilize a model's uncertainty or rely on diversity measures, such as clustering or reconstruction, to choose unlabeled examples. However, model uncertainty-based methods are susceptible to outliers and diversity-based methods may overlook key information. To address this, we introduce a semi-supervised active learning approach that simultaneously considers both uncertainty and diversity in a minimax framework. Our method incorporates a network that minimizes the difference between its training loss and a test loss, while a discriminator tries to distinguish labeled and unlabeled data. We then use a query strategy based on the least confident sample selected by the discriminator, which we demonstrate to be a hard sample. Experimental results show that our method outperforms other baseline techniques on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. We also introduce a simple semi-supervised learning approach using an ensemble of labeled and unlabeled data, which can serve as a standalone method. A novel category of stochastic processes that incorporate reinforcement involves sequences of random groupings denoted as $\{\mathcal{P}_t\}_{t \ge 1}$. These groupings, or partitions $\mathcal{P}_t$, split a continuously increasing set of items $\{1,2,\dots, Rt\}$. When time progresses to $t$, a fixed number of items $R$ are appended to this set; a fraction of these added items joins existing groups based on probabilities defined across different time intervals, initiating new subgroups separately from the ones that merged with existing groups. The items integrating existing groups make selections according to the group's current size proportionality, acting independently from each other. Theorems concerning the asymptotic quantities within specific groups are proved along with central limit theorems explaining deviations from the identified trends in relation to: individual subgroups' growth, and the subgroups' collective fluctuations in growth. The same set of theorems applies for the subgroups' collective fluctuations in growth when the greatest subgroup's growth in comparison to other subgroups is assessed. Our analysis shows that a single group, given an infinitely extending timeline, holds and maintains dominance through the course of its development; and the fluctuating changes within its growth pattern follow an approximate normal distribution pattern. Similarly, the collective fluctuating changes within the group's growth pattern also approximate a normal distribution pattern. Our analysis also finds that when assessing the fluctuating changes within the group's growth pattern that surpass others, the results conform to a normal distribution pattern as well. Additional related findings are that the probability measures defining the successful integration of newly added items within existing groups decay to zero despite the groups' ongoing growth and that the probability measures also exhibit unbounded spikes in relation to the group's ongoing growth and dissolution patterns particularly in scenarios where multiple groups compete against each other. A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance, even when human labeling time remains constant, across basic Mujoco tasks. We show that a topological space's Smyth powerspace is core-compact if and only if the original space has local compactness. Consequently, this implies the Smyth powerspace does not uniformly preserve core-compact properties. In order to improve the efficiency of two NN models with no parameter regularization except SGD, our simulations indicate the significant drawbacks that arise when AIPW is used. The results show nAIPW and AIPW have similar variance properties under both regulated and unregulated scenarios, with AIPW exhibiting greater bias when L1 regularization is present. The proposed nAIPW and AIPW are used to analyze the effect of smoking on lung cancer. The findings of this study align with those of earlier research and provide stronger evidence for the causal relationship between smoking and lung cancer. The utility of double robust estimators in identifying treatment effects, even in scenarios with limited data, is also underscored by this study. A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter interdependence, making estimation more complicated. We introduce a novel approach to estimating the parameters of the Poisson process in a Bayesian framework, by transforming them using a tuning parameter'm'. This study develops a technique for selecting the optimal'm' value, which nearly orthogonalises the parameters, by minimising the correlation within their asymptotic posterior distributions. By choosing this optimal'm', the parameters converge faster and efficient sampling is possible using Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. Finally, parameter values are then extracted through a straightforward transformation. We present results from simulations involving models of both identical and non-identical extreme rainfall in Cumbria, UK. These simulations compare the efficiency of our'm' method with a method which maximally orthogonalises the parameters by transforming only the frequencies, while keeping the other parameters unchanged. The results show that the'm' method has a faster convergence rate and similar accuracy in parameter estimation. The method is then applied to model daily maxima from a set of rainfall data and demonstrates improved convergence rates in parameter estimation compared to the traditional approach. In the field of offline reinforcement learning, we focus on adversarial robustness, a critical consideration in RL that deals with the challenge of learning a nearly optimal policy when a fraction of data in the training set has been compromised by an adversary. Our study begins by examining a worst-case scenario involving the linear Markov decision process and finding that even with the adversary only modifying the reward in each data tuple, a certain threshold of optimality gap cannot be avoided. Conversely, in contrast to robust supervised learning, which has seen significant breakthroughs with little dimension-related impact and similar lower bounds for the online RL with data corruption. Moreover, we introduce robust variants of Least-Square Value Iteration that are applicable both when data coverage is complete and when it is incomplete. These robust LSVO variants show promising performance, but in instances of data incompleteness, we require prior knowledge of epsilon for the bonus of pessimism to function. Unexpectedly, we discovered that the adaptability to the value of epsilon when its value is not previously known is impossible, which highlights the significance of epsilon in the context of robust offline RL. Our research also shows that in order to achieve robustness when epsilon is 0 (in other words, when no data corruption takes place), we need to rely on a different approach as our current LSVO variants do. This paper marks a first in the field of robust offline RL, and given the prevalence of data corruption in RL, it holds great potential for future contributions. This study demonstrates a logarithmic convexity linked to observability at a specific point in time for a one-dimensional heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions, leading to impulse approximate controllability in similar scenarios with dynamic boundaries. Additionally, we provide a detailed estimate for the cost of impulse control. Our research includes a step-by-step procedure for finding the impulsive control of minimal L^2-norm and supports these findings with numerical tests to verify the efficiency of the developed algorithm. This study expands the results of [C. Castionovo, J. J. Ritto, R. Zimmermann, J. Dyn. Diff. Equations, 2019; 71(2), 269-282]. Our approach to finding the minimum L^2-norm impulsive control draws on the concept of minimizing a cost function with convex constraints, ultimately resulting in a problem amenable to solution by iterative methods and illustrating the feasibility of impedance identification through vibration control in real-world applications. Our numerical results demonstrate the precision of our algorithm in solving this optimization problem, even in cases where the duration of impulsive control is very short. Finally, we explore the application of our algorithm to regular (non-impulsive) control problems, showcasing its efficacy in solving these types of problems as well. This work is inspired by and extends the research in [A. Zamani, M. S. Ahmad, T. K. Singh, J. Math. Phys., 2020; 61(4), 043901]. Our study also incorporates new ideas, including the logical extension of controllability to higher-dimensional heat equations with dynamic boundaries, which could have implications for the control of materials undergoing phase transitions. This work also raises the possibility of encoding information in heat equations through impulsive control, thus representing a new type of computational model that could facilitate the development of artificial neural networks inspired by heat diffusion. This perspective is further reinforced by the remarkable agility of our algorithm, which demonstrates its ability to efficiently solve control problems involving short impulsive signals, even at high spatial resolutions. As a result, this study opens up new avenues for the control of phase transitions in materials and the development of advanced artificial neural networks inspired by heat diffusion. This work also implies the existence of a new type of computational model based on heat diffusion, which could be used for encoding information and developing high-performance artificial neural networks inspired by heat diffusion. This study also highlights the feasibility and efficiency of using impulsive control in vibration control applications, which could have implications for the control of vibrations in fluid dynamics

A consensus has not been established on the definition and optimal detection methods for out-of-distribution examples despite general agreement on their importance. We identified distinct behaviors of two major detection methods - model calibration and density estimation - in response to background and semantic shifts in data, which were found across various language understanding datasets. In our evaluation, density estimation outperformed model calibration in background shift scenarios but struggled with semantic shifts, with both approaches underperforming when confronted with challenge data, underscoring a need for clearer definitions in method comparison. Consequently, we proposed modifying the evaluation protocol to account for test data categorization based on conceptual labels and data source, yielding more accurate assessments and nuanced insights into test data characteristics. This revised approach enables researchers to design more effective methods capable of identifying out-of-distribution examples reliably. Our findings are available in the repository https://github.com/amanbasu/oood-paths.\\
\textit{What are the key insights into out-of-distribution example detection achieved in this research?} The research provides clarity on the performance of model calibration and density estimation in different data shifts and introduces a new classification-based evaluation method to assess model performance. It also demonstrates the limitations of density estimation in handling semantic shifts and the underperformance of model calibration when confronted with challenge data. Moreover, the study reveals that a simpler density estimation method outperforms a more complex calibration approach. These insights offer valuable guidance for future research in out-of-distribution example detection.\\
\textit{What are the benefits of using test data conceptual labels and data source in evaluating model performance?} The labels and data source can differentiate test data concepts and origins effectively, resulting in a more accurate assessment of model performance. This can be particularly useful in data augmentation, where a clear distinction between generated and original data is desired to evaluate the efficacy of augmentation methods. Using conceptual labels and data source also enables researchers to explore the detectability limits of out-of-distribution examples and potentially find more efficient methods.\\
\textit{What role do challenge data play in out-of-distribution example detection, and why is it important to label such data conceptually?} Challenge data offer a natural setting for evaluating out-of-distribution example detection methods. Since these data are often vastly different from training data, they pose significant challenges, but their limited availability means that a random labeling may introduce bias, leading to false positives. By applying conceptual labels, a more accurate assessment is achieved, allowing researchers to explore the detectability limits and potentially find more efficient methods.\\

In this study, we investigate the concept of general convolution by considering the set of all possible $n$-dimensional vectors from a finite domain $D$, where the elements of these vectors can take on values from $D$. A specific operation, denoted as $\oplus_f$, is defined as the application of function $f$ to pairs of elements from $D$ applied element-wise. This enables us to define a new convolution, known as the $f$-Convolution, for two given functions $g$ and $h$, each mapping $n$-dimensional vectors from $D$ to integers between $-M$ and $M$. By applying $\oplus_f$ to pairs of $n$-dimensional vectors, $g \otimes_f h$ is calculated as the sum of the products of the function values of $g$ and $h$ for each possible pair. This framework encompasses multiple other well-known convolutional problems. A naive approach for computing $f$-Convolution would involve exhaustive enumeration, with an estimated time complexity of $\widetilde{O}(|D|^{2n}\log|D|)$ for fixed $n$. This study aims to provide more efficient solutions depending on whether $n$ is fixed or variable, focusing on the latter scenario. Additionally, we introduce the concept of $\lambda$-convolution, where $\lambda$-Convolution is defined as the $f$-Convolution where $f((a, b), (c, d)) = (d - c)^2(a - c)(a - d)$, especially for $D = \{0, 1, \ldots, k\}$ with $k$ being an integer. This new convolution, denoted as $\lambda \cdot g \otimes_f h$, finds its applications in evaluating certain summability related to polynomial properties. By applying the underlying ideas from this case study to the general convolution problem, we are able to provide a more efficient solution, which runs in time complexity of $2^{n+1}$. This new approach suggests that when $n$ is not fixed, the previously proposed brute-force solution is no longer the best possible option. This revised solution further stimulates the exploration of more generalized convolution problems. Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze virus-laden aerosol transport. Our models considered multiple factors such as breathing, coughing, and breathing rates, as well as disparate emission patterns, penetration probabilities, and dispersal patterns. Furthermore, we investigated the impact of various factors on the accumulation of infectious aerosols in the bus. Our simulations revealed that aerosol transport is highly dependent on the interplay of different factors and slight variations in parameter values can result in significantly different conclusions regarding the likelihood of airborne transmission. Double-sided auctions are commonly used in financial markets to facilitate matching of demand and supply. Our work builds on prior research, which mainly focused on handling a single quantity of trade requests. To expand this knowledge, we developed methods to support multiple quantity trade requests and established fully formalized matching algorithms for double-sided auctions. These algorithms come with rigorous correctness proofs. Additionally, we formulated new theorems for verifying the uniqueness of an exchange's output, allowing for automatic detection of potential program errors. To ensure the accuracy of our work, all the mathematical proofs were conducted using the Coq proof assistant, which did not introduce any additional axioms into the system. From these formal proofs, we were able to derive verified and executable OCaml and Haskell code for double-sided auctions. To validate the practical value of our research, we successfully tested the verified code using real market data from an exchange to automatically identify potential program errors at compile time. As a result, our work provides an approach to formally verifying the correctness of double-sided auctions and detecting potential program errors prior to execution. The verified code is freely available online at https://download.starlingsoftware.eu/verified-ocaml-haskell-code.zip for OCaml and https://github.com/stst-rs/verified-rs-code.git for Rust. More information regarding our research can also be found at https://www.starlingsoftware.eu/. All the articles from our research team are also available at https://www.starlingsoftware.eu/index.php/category/publications/ and https://github.com/stst-rs/verified-rs-code.git. A method to derive constants of motion beyond local bounds for ODE-based Lagrangian systems is outlined, including a practical example that illustrates its utility for dissipative mechanical systems and its implications on solution existence and behavior under specific assumptions. The framework is further extended to cover Euler-Lagrange equations with order greater than two, yielding new first integrals for particular models, such as the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator, paving the way for potential applications in Euler-Lagrange partial differential equations in the future. The provided analysis demonstrates that these integrals can provide valuable existence estimates for dissipative Euler-Lagrange equations up to order two. Moreover, the approach offers a connection between integrable ODE-based systems and their Euler-Lagrange partial differential equation counterparts. To demonstrate the feasibility of this approach for higher-order variational problems, a constant of motion for a specific variant of the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator is derived, and its implications on solution behavior are explored. The research reveals that these integrable constants can offer valuable insights into the fundamental nature of dissipative Euler-Lagrange equations, potentially shedding light on essential aspects of their invariant measures under specific assumptions. Furthermore, the integration of Noether symmetries within this extended framework appears promising, as it could lead to a more comprehensive understanding of the integral structures of variational problems, their implications on solution behavior, and the existence of invariant measures, thereby opening up new avenues for research in this area. As this approach primarily focuses on ODE-based Euler-Lagrange equations, its applications to partial differential equations remain subjects for future investigation. Moreover, the integration of external Noether symmetries into this extended framework of dissipative mechanical systems and their implications on solution existence and behavior is another promising research direction. Lastly, the potential application of this methodology to variational problems with external forces remains a subject of future research within this field. Developing free online collections of 3D shapes has driven research in 3D retrieval. Debates surrounding the optimal input method for retrieval and the ultimate application have been ongoing. In this research, we present an alternative approach, focusing on using 3D sketches as input and envisioning a virtual reality (VR) environment for retrieval. We aim to allow users to freely access 3D models through air-drawn sketches in a VR setting. As a first step, our study contributes four aspects: implementing a tool to collect and retrieve 3D sketches in VR, gathering the first dataset of $167$ sketches in two categories from ModelNet, developing a novel approach to generate synthetic human-like sketches, and evaluating the performance of different approaches. We observed that in the context of sketch-based retrieval, volumetric methods outperform traditional approaches. The implemented tool and dataset are accessible through https://lr3dv.github.io. We intend for this work to mark the beginning of a new line of inquiry, providing novel technical contributions and facilitating future research in using sketch inputs for 3D retrieval in VR. A video demonstrating our approach can be found on YouTube at https://youtu.be/1C1YV7zRUYw. From our evaluation, we recommend volumetric methods for sketch-based retrieval, and suggest collecting more data to strengthen our findings. We also propose using the generated synthetic sketches as additional training data for 3D shape reconstruction, achieving improved results. Ultimately, we hope this research will lead to greater efficiency in using air-drawn sketches for 3D retrieval in VR. To achieve this, we recommend collecting more data, combining traditional and sketch-based approaches, and leveraging VR technologies to boost public awareness and engagement. We believe the vr-sbs dataset can foster research in utilizing sketch inputs for 3D retrieval in VR, presenting an untapped opportunity for contributions. We envision the future of this line of inquiry to not only surpass our outcomes but also leverage VR technologies' growing impact to reach a broader, more engaged audience. As VR technology continues to progress, we anticipate increased precision in using air-drawn sketches, paving the way for revolutionary 3D retrieval experiences. We believe our study not only presents unique technical contributions but also shows the potential for using sketch inputs to revolutionize 3D retrieval in VR. High-definition videos and additional information can be found at https://lr3dv.github.io. This method involves integrating a specific divisor of the Einstein equation to obtain the perturbed metric, which is then used to calculate the perturbed energy, angular momentum, and electric charge. Interestingly, our findings suggest that to the extent that extremality corrections are quantifiable, they are constrained by the strong energy condition. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that to the extent that entropy is a physical quantity, it is coupled to the electric charge. Additionally, we have shown that for non-extremal black holes, corrections to the mass are positively related to the charge, and specifically, we have derived an upper limit on corrections to $M_{\rm H}^2$ in terms of $e^2$, for any value of $J_{\rm H}$ and $Q_{\rm H}$. As a concrete example, we have applied our formalism to determine the leading-order corrections to the entropy of Kerr and Kerr-Newman black holes. This approach may also serve as a useful tool for exploring the thermodynamics of more complex black holes such as those found in ${\cal N}=2$ gauged supergravities. Lastly, we have suggested a potential application of our method to the study of the thermodynamics of fundamental particles in quantum field theory. A related work, discussing the potential application of our method to the study of the thermodynamics of fundamental particles in quantum field theory, is also presented in the accompanying document. End-effect models utilize a straightforward statistical representation of policy effects, which serve as a substitute for more computationally intensive predictive models. When combined with a reward structure, they form the foundation of a streamlined variational free energy minimization system. However, the primary challenge is balancing the upkeep of this simplified effect model with the policy's continuous updates. Interestingly, when the target distribution is uniform, our approach facilitates learning an efficient exploratory policy consistent with the principles of intrinsic curiosity. Moreover, when paired with an external reward, our method yields faster training times than traditional off-policy techniques. A key advantage of our method is its exceptional interpretability due to the straightforwardness of its underlying statistical representation. To showcase its various applications, we present a range of experiments, including a pioneering assessment of goal-oriented learning from scratch within a complex environment. Our open-source code is accessible via the link https://github.com/alex-mo/End-Effect-Drive.

Image-based goal navigation is a difficult problem, requiring agents to navigate to visually identified objectives in unfamiliar environments.
Previous methods often employ diverse memory mechanisms to track navigation history but fail to account for the fraction of relevant information in their memories.
We propose the MemoNav, a novel memory-based navigation framework, designed to improve performance in multi-goal scenarios by selectively retaining both short-term and long-term memories.
The short-term memory in MemoNav stores dynamic agent topological maps, updated as navigation progresses. To augment this memory, a graph attention module aggregates past short-term memories to generate long-term memories.
A forgetting module using a Transformer decoder retains only the informative fraction of the short-term memory, ensuring that both the updated short-term memory and the accumulated long-term memory are integrated into the working memory, guiding action generation.
Experimental evaluations of MemoNav on a new dataset demonstrate significantly better performance compared to state-of-the-art approaches using a fraction of the navigation history, with reduced instances of deadlock situations. Project details are available at https://github.com/timillm/MemoNav. Our associated video can be found at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5048247.

In a general setting, we show that the feedback capacity of a finite state channel is characterized by a specific, compact formula when only limited channel state information is available for use in feedback. When no restrictions are placed on the availability of state information, a previously established formula holds, wherein the capacity is defined as the minimum value over all possible state information rates achieved by a specific inequality involving conditional mutual information. Building upon big big O analysis, we now provide a simplified proof that confirms the previously established lower bound. Additionally, we identify a specific condition under which the capacity can be accurately determined. Specifically, when the average information gain in a single use of the channel equals the entropy of the source, we demonstrate that the capacity is solely dependent on the entropy of the channel's state and can be expressed as the minimum value over all possible state information rates achieved by a specific inequality involving conditional mutual information. We further establish that when only limited channel state information is available for use in feedback and the source is ergodic, the capacity can be expressed as the negative of the average information gain in a single use of the channel. Moreover, when both the source and channel states are ergodic and only limited channel state information is available for use in feedback, we derive the feedback capacity and confirm that it is essentially equivalent to the capacity of the ergodic source. We utilize the newly established compact formula for feedback capacity to identify scenarios under which it is solely dependent on the entropy of the channel's state information. Specifically, when only limited channel state information is available for use in feedback, the capacity is solely dependent on the entropy of the channel's state information when one of two conditions is met: either the source and channel states are jointly ergodic or the source's information divergence from the channel's state information is zero. This analysis examines how complex numbers are employed in Quantum Mechanics, with the goal of determining the underlying rationale for their use. It is observed that numerous applications of complex numbers in Quantum mechanics are rooted in the inherent characteristics of the complex number field. Furthermore, the article discusses the potential implications of reformulating Quantum mechanics using real numbers alone. It appears that a widely accepted principle of Quantum mechanics, known as the superposition principle, arises naturally as a consequence of employing complex numbers. However, it is possible to maintain the superposition principle while using real numbers by incorporating a different mathematical structure, namely, an ordered field. If real numbers are substituted with an ordered field, the resulting formulation of Quantum mechanics may still be capable of generating probabilistic outcomes. On the other hand, the possibility of using other mathematical structures, such as a field of numbers based on sine functions, to reformulate Quantum mechanics is also explored. It is demonstrated that such a formulation either fails to reproduce the predictions of standard Quantum mechanics or only produces exact matches for related phenomena. Ultimately, the article concludes with a survey of diverse approaches to Quantum mechanics that differ from one another using different mathematical structures, with the aim of facilitating further discussions on the subject. \\ \\ Published in \\ Int. These notes document my process of reviewing equations governing distant groundwater movement for a paper. By "distant," I'm referring to horizontal distances exceeding the thickness of the aquifer. They're based on assumptions discussed later on. These equations aren't an original contribution but rather a reference guide for those working with simplified numerical models of groundwater flow where the fluid's viscosity and specific weight are constant. As part of this review, I clarified some concepts and examined the continuity equation and Darcy's law from a modern perspective of vector calculus. I also derived the time-dependent groundwater flow equation through the diffusion equation, considering it relevant to quasi-steady scenarios where temporal discontinuities are caused by sudden changes in the surface water table or pressures. These equations are applicable when the aquifer's porosity and hydraulic conductivity can be considered uniform. I did not explore situations involving spatially variable properties, which are essential for modeling local flow patterns. Additionally, I did not delve into the mechanics of fluid flow, assume local steady-state conditions, or analyze cases of flowing fluids where the groundwater flow velocity approaches the rate of flow due to viscosity. As a result, these simplified equations may not be suitable for modeling clogging, fluid chemical reactions, or saltwater intrusion into fresh water. I examined the relevant physical principles governing these processes but did not develop equations for them. I've presented the groundwater flow equations in terms commonly used in Cartesian, cylindrical, and spherical coordinates, aiming for a clear and intuitive understanding. Although the review is comprehensive, it lacks the level of detail found in dedicated hydrology textbooks. Some topics, such as the Slichter integral, are only mentioned briefly. I've omitted topics like non-steady flow statistics and boundary condition modeling, which are important but also complex. I've attempted to organize the content in a logical order, starting from basic principles and equations, then applying them to groundwater flow scenarios. Along the way, I often provided additional context and explanations, aiming to facilitate a more comprehensive understanding. As a result, these notes might be of greater interest to students and researchers who learn by exploring topics in a non-linear fashion. I hope these reviews will still be useful for those following a traditional learning path. I've made no effort to conceal the fact that my reviews were conducted during leisure time, often sparked by the need to understand a particular concept or equation in relation to its application, as exemplified by a recent episode where I sought insight into the thermal conductivity equation to model freezing soils effectively. I've since realized the value of documenting these reviews

This work has investigated the potential of integrating an ozone O3 and ultraviolet (UV) light system for effectively eliminating pollutants in flue gas emissions. A numerical model of a continuous stirred tank reactor (CSTR) was used to simulate and analyze the removal of sulfur dioxide SO2 through gas-phase oxidation. Various UV radiation models were considered, each involving a grid convergence study to determine the optimal number of discrete light sources for maximum performance. Furthermore, the study examined the influence of residence time and reactor size on SO2 removal. Ultimately, under optimized conditions, the results show that an ozone-UV light system can be a suitable solution for sustainable air pollution control applications. The DTW distance is commonly applied in time series analysis across classification, clustering, and similarity search tasks, but its time complexity hinders its scalability. To overcome this, some strategies involve halting DTW early or omitting its computation in advance, tailored to nearest neighbor search scenarios. Nonetheless, PrunedDTW introduced an innovation in DTW's development. Building upon PrunedDTW's capacity to eliminate unproductive alignments, it was later integrated with early abandoning. A new variant of PrunedDTW, known as EAPrunedDTW, was designed with early abandoning incorporated, and it achieves faster abandoning times compared to previous versions. In experiments, we observed a notable improvement in EAPrunedDTW's computation efficiency during similarity searches on the UCR Suite, and it renders pre-calculated upper bounds unnecessary.
