Current educational tools used in testing can either provide coverage insights comparable to professional tools or highlight instructor-defined test cases that a student has overlooked. While this feedback has some value, it can lead students to rely on guesswork rather than structured testing methods. Moreover, this feedback style does not educate students on the shortcomings of their test suites, potentially making them dependent on the tool's advice rather than relying on their own judgment. As a more effective approach, inquiry-based learning has the potential to promote student autonomy by reinforcing key testing concepts through feedback. We aim to improve this aspect by introducing Testing Tutor, a platform that offers various testing pedagogies and a customizable feedback engine. An empirical study comparing the impact of traditional and conceptual feedback on two groups of sophomore students was conducted. By providing students with either code-focused or concept-based feedback using Testing Tutor, our study demonstrated that conceptual feedback led to increased code coverage, fewer redundant test cases, and improved programming grades. Notably, the conceptual feedback group outperformed the code-focused feedback group in terms of coverage and redundancy, highlighting the efficacy of conceptual feedback as a teaching tool. Based on these results, we recommend that the instructional use of Testing Tutor can enhance students' testing skills and promote a deeper understanding of testing concepts, as defined by the FIT framework. You can access a live demonstration of Testing Tutor at <https://tinyurl.com/tt-fpiso2021>. Additionally, the system is freely available for download at <https://github.com/ospllab/Tuning-Testing-Tutor> and can be installed on any Java-enabled server. Key technological components include the utilization of Graphical Modeling Language for defining test feedback logic and the employment of WebSocket connections for real-time interactions between the client and server. We anticipate that Testing Tutor will facilitate the exploration of various conceptual pedagogies within the software testing field. Moreover, the platform may serve as a starting point for designing educational tools specifically for other software engineering subjects. \par Overall, our work indicates that software engineering educational tools can transition from purely supportive to actively instructional roles, shedding light on a promising research direction within software engineering. Moreover, this study's findings can be applied to other research fields within this field.}

In domains requiring reliability or transparency, explainable AI is increasingly becoming essential for handling the unpredictability of black-box machine learning methods, particularly in healthcare and data protection regulations. However, standard visualizations often fall short due to their inability to differentiate between subtle feature variations or accurately represent the interplay between absent and present features. This issue could be addressed by using more advanced symbolic surrogate models but, since these typically demand symbolic inputs not commonly available in computer vision, we instead explore the creation of symbolic images by interpreting deep learning models' computational graphs. We then evaluate the efficacy of these symbolic images in perturbation analysis and explainability, demonstrating improved ability to identify and distinguish feature variations within perturbed images. This approach also enables the reproduction of images through the removal of specific features and the simulation of attribute swaps, highlighting their importance. This contributes to understanding the black-box nature of deep learning models and could potentially lead to the development of more reliable and transparent vision models. The project code is available on GitHub at https://github/symbolic-image-explanation. We have also made the data available at https://doi.org/10.21228/TJZ69D. We present results from our experiments with various models and datasets. We found that the symbolic image approach outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in perturbation analysis and understandability, particularly in the case of resilient models which exhibit improved robustness. We found that the symbolic images are more interpretable than state-of-the-art visualizations and understandability metrics, particularly in high feature-density scenarios. We observed a trade-off between model robustness and interpretability but found that the symbolic images offer substantial gains in interpretability with minimal losses in robustness. We hope this finds applications in reliable and transparent machine learning. We discuss potential future extensions, including the use of symbolic images in perturbation analysis and the development of more reliable vision models. We believe this work marks a significant advancement towards achieving reliable and transparent machine learning with deep learning models. We conclude with suggestions for future work and potential applications of this approach. To summarize, we presented a novel approach to visualizing deep learning models' images, explored its performance in perturbation analysis and understandability, discovered its applications in attribute identification and feature removal, and hopefully contributed to achieving reliable and transparent machine learning with deep learning methods. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods are ideal for this purpose.  Listening to heart sounds with a stethoscope is a common technique used to diagnose and monitor heart conditions.  However, interpreting heart sounds accurately can be challenging for non-experts.  Recent studies have investigated the use of machine learning (ML) to classify heart sounds, with mixed results.  These studies generally used long recordings of heart sounds, but direct classification from short-time recordings is more practical for point-of-care use.  In this study, we classified the fourth heart sound (S4) as present or absent in very short time frames (10 milliseconds) using deep convolutional neural networks. In a 2021 study, we had developed a more accurate calculation for a specific nuclear transition in $^{133}$Cs using relativistic coupled-cluster theory. Recently, Roberts and Ginges raised concerns about a part of this calculation that they disagreed with, but it aligns with earlier calculations. In response, we thoroughly justify our method and highlight that all components were treated equally, whereas other calculations relied on sum-over-states methods. Additionally, we addressed concerns about the approximate treatment of certain corrections that were not the main focus, but rather included for completeness, without changing our overall conclusions, as our results hold even when replaced with a previously estimated correction value. Lastly, we emphasize the significance of accurately calculating nuclear transition amplitudes in atomic physics, particularly for those independent of spin and parity, which are crucial for certain experimental tests. 

Our publication details the calculations and provides a clear explanation of the theoretical methods used, including a relevant example in Section 3, where we discuss the role of relativistic effects, and how to correctly apply approximate corrections, but the core results from our 2021 study are also relevant and important.

A twist is utilized as a localized element in the study of topological K-theory. 
Within the framework of equivariant analysis, a twist can be applied uniformly to a space or a bundle. 
This paper achieves two significant outcomes: 
First, the twists that are equivariant under the action of a group G are systematically categorized, 
with their form being entirely determined by a specific formula derived from the study of germs. 
Second, the article describes a one-to-one correspondence between the twists equivariant under the action of G and the odd cohomology classes of the group, 
with the relationship between these twists and the cohomology classes being preserved under addition. 
This classification extends previous findings by G. Segal, who identified the classification of twists in the context of fixed points, to the context of equivariant analysis. 
Additionally, the article demonstrates that the twists equivariant under the action of a group are isomorphic to the relative K-theory of the group, a finding that builds on the work of D. Kazdan. 
This article represents a completion of work previously initiated by M. Bernardi. 
A few potential applications of the findings are suggested. 
The articles' content can be summarized as follows: 
Section 1 introduces the concept and utilization of twists within the context of equivariant analysis. 
Section 2 summarizes the classification of twists. 
Section 3 outlines the correspondence between twists and cohomology classes, 
and describes the application of the findings to the context of compact manifolds. 
Section 4 discusses localization and the process of change of rings, 
with particular focus on the context of fixed points. 
Section 5 discusses the relationship between the twists and the K-theory of the group. 
Section 6 discusses a few potential applications of the findings. 
Section 7 concludes the articles with a discussion of the potential generalization of the findings to the context of stratified spaces. 
A unique notational system is employed throughout the articles, 
with key concepts and terminology summarized at the close of the articles.

This study offers the first empirical evaluation of the influence of auction format integrity on bidding tactics and outcome profitability. Through a controlled lab experiment where human auction participants earn revenue, we assess whether a credible or uncredible auction environment impacts bidding. We discover that the majority of bids in an uncredible second-price auction occur within the revenue-maximizing range of both a credible second-price auction and a first-price auction. Sellers often deviate from the auction rules, but when participating in an uncredible auction, typically don't prioritize maximizing revenue. We explain the outcomes of our experiment using a theory that combines bidder misperception and a seller's reluctance to break auction rules, as confirmed by a test of actual preferences. Our findings suggest that auction formats can influence bidding tactics and that a credible auction environment typically yields more profitable results. Nonetheless, in cases of low credibility, the outcomes of our experiment mirror the predictions of a game theory model that assumes a low level of importance placed on maintaining auction integrity. This research has significant implications for designing auctions that are both intact and effective. We are one of the first studies to explore actual preferences for maintaining integrity in human auctions, and our results provide new insights for practitioners running auctions. Our research focuses on the promising potential of a new symmetric teleparallel theory of gravity, denoted as $f(Q)$, where the non-metricity scalar $Q$ facilitates gravitational interactions and addresses some longstanding issues. To study the universe's initial phase, we establish a model based on a specific type of spacetime with both rotation and anisotropy and then derive equations governing the model's motion. By analyzing energy density, the relationship between energy and pressure, and spatial geometry characteristics, we find that this theoretical model exhibits spatial anisotropy during the universe's initial phase due to possible anisotropic fluid, which may however gradually diminish and allow the universe to achieve isotropy due to inflation and eventual fluid homogenization. Our findings suggest the possibility of the universe's anisotropic phase in the early stages, which may provide a new perspective on the universe's initial phase. Moreover, the anisotropy of rotation is identified and its influence on rotational anisotropy is examined, showing that it can persist and affect the universe's anisotropic phase, albeit at a lower intensity compared to other anisotropy. By incorporating the effects of acceleration and inhomogeneity, we may gain a deeper understanding of the universe, which could be utilized to investigate various phases of the universe, including inflation, the phase transition from inflation to the radiation era, and the universe's late stages, including the expansion of the dark energy domain and the emergence of matter dominance. Our study paves the way for further research into the universe's diverse phases, which is essential for comprehending the dynamics of the universe. To facilitate the analysis, we provide numerical charts to illustrate how the energy density, pressure, non-metricity scalar, and spatial geometry characteristics evolve over time. Our theoretical model exhibits excellent consistency with the observed data, which is a significant advantage. Our study discovered that the universe contains energy components with properties analogous to dark energy and matter, which is consistent with the observed data. We initiate a study of local defining ideals of Hessenberg varieties, specifically focusing on regular nilpotent Hessenberg varieties of type A, utilizing an affine coordinate chart based on the maximal element of the Weyl group corresponding to GL(n,ℂ). Key findings include the following. Firstly, we prove that the local defining ideal associated to a given Hessenberg function within this specific coordinate system can be decomposed into vertices. Furthermore, combining our result with existing work on generators, we demonstrate that this set of generators constitutes a Gröbner basis for this ideal under a suitable monomial order. Lastly, applying our analysis, we derive an explicit splitting of a key region of Flags(ℂ^n), effectively decomposing its local defining ideals across all indecomposable Hessenberg functions. These outcomes follow from a novel algorithm, which describes a specific subvariety within Flags(ℂ^n) associated with a given permutation, and characterized by a specific set of equations involving the first symmetric power of ℂ^n. This subvariety is distinct from a previously studied variety, which shares a codimension and structure with it, but fails to accommodate certain path symmetries. Our method allows the explicit description of geometric vertices, which are crucial for understanding various complex problems, such as resolving decomposition difficulties in Flags(ℂ^n) and computing local defining ideals of Hessenberg varieties. As a consequence, we are able to provide explicit descriptions of geometric vertices for permutations of the form s_i*, which are a critical component of Flags(ℂ^n). Additionally, our work leads to further mathematical discoveries, including a characterization of a previously studied variety, known as the Schubert variety, as a decomposition of Flags(ℂ^n) into specific subvarieties, known as shape Hessenberg varieties, and the proof of a previously conjectured result by Matherne and Wang. These researchers previously showed that the regular nilpotent Hessenberg varieties of type A exhibit a specific property, known as vertex decomposition, for certain 'high' levels of Hessenberg functions, by utilizing an approach based on combinatorial arguments, which are independent of the underlying field characteristics. Our work presents an alternative, more element-driven description of this decomposition, which is unaffected by field characteristics. As a result, our descriptions of geometric vertices provide a meaningful connection between Hessenberg functions and the underlying Lie algebra, which was previously absent. Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their limited ability to reason complex relationships between paper sections. Developing effective Question Answering tools necessitates large datasets that capture the challenging nature of this task, including interpreting claims from multiple parts of a document. Unlike traditional information-seeking datasets that typically consist of fact-based questions, the proposed QASPER dataset contains a diverse range of questions over 1,585 NLP research papers. These 5,049 questions were posed by NLP specialists who relied only on paper titles and abstracts, requiring answers that would appear in the full paper, accompanied by supportive evidence from separate NLP practitioners. We observed significant performance disparities between existing models that excel in other Question Answering tasks and human capabilities, with models struggling to surpass a random search baseline. We hope this new dataset will accelerate progress in this area. Further details are available at https://qasper dataset.github.io/. We would be grateful if researchers could share their results, as we believe shared knowledge leads to greater advancement. To access the QASPER dataset, please register at https://hugocarpool.github.io/qasper-registration/. We kindly request that all registered users adhere to our dataset usage agreement. Donor agreements can be viewed at https://github.com/qrates-dataset/agreements. We are eager to collaborate with researchers, as we believe collective efforts lead to greater breakthroughs. To get in touch, please email [hugo.carpool@cornell.edu](hugo.carpool@cornell.edu). We are committed to continuing to support this new benchmark, and we look forward to witnessing significant progress over time. To facilitate this evolution, we propose the development of an open competition, the CQASPER challenge, where researchers can showcase their results, as well as an updated dataset release schedule, as described in our upcoming research. Specifically, we suggest re-releasing the dataset every 6 months to allow existing and new approaches to be evaluated, and we propose the development of an online demo to showcase the potential of the most recent models. We envision this new benchmark to be a driving force for significant advancements in the area of question answering. In order to understand fast neutrino flavor instability in supernova events, two advanced simulations were conducted, one involving a massive 9 solar mass star explosion and the other, a 20 solar mass non-explosion. These studies revealed neutrino instabilities primarily occur within regions where neutrinos separate and near the shockwave barrier. Notably, only the explosive model exhibited instability behind the shockwave due to the interaction between particles and neutrinos. This could be attributed to the density of the matter which influences the direction and rate of neutrino distribution. Our results show that the success of a supernova explosion and properties of the collapsing star greatly affect neutrino instability. Therefore, it is essential to conduct more accurate and diverse stellar collapse simulations to predict how neutrino flavor conversion behaves. These predictions can later be used to interpret future neutrino detector observations. ADHD is a widely prevalent psychiatric condition that has been challenging to diagnose accurately. The advancement in computational capabilities and machine learning methods has enabled researchers to investigate the use of resting-state fMRI imaging data for classifying ADHD. In contrast to prior studies, which often relied on the entire brain, this study focused on pinpointing the essential regions for utilizing a deep learning model. By using rsfMRI data from the ADHD 200 global competition, the researchers discovered that using strategically selected regions of interest for training and testing yielded an impressive 90.3% accuracy without any supplementary information. Notably, the top-performing model achieved a remarkable 91.5% accuracy when incorporating an ensemble of models derived from different training datasets. To ensure generalizability of the findings, the researchers tested the model on an independent dataset of fused rsfMRI-behavioral data from Singapore, which demonstrated a high cross-challenge accuracy of 88.1%. Furthermore, the model successfully identified and localized the key brain areas associated with ADHD, as well as provided correlations between functional weightings and anatomical locations. The model's predictions were also compared to those from clinical scales, revealing substantial agreements. To facilitate reproducibility, the code, data, and figures are available for public access at https://github.com/AlyxRESAD/Selected_ROIs_for_ADHD_diagnosis. In conclusion, this study successfully validated the effectiveness of a deep learning model in diagnosing ADHD using combined rsfMRI data from two datasets, while identifying the critical regions involved. The findings of this research can serve as a foundation for creating more efficient and accurate ADHD detection models. The model can potentially be applied to other neuropsychiatric disorders in the future. In addition, the study's method can be adapted for predicting continuous symptoms scores rather than categorical diagnoses. Lastly, the study's analytical approach can be extended to analyze the inherent biological variations present in brain imaging data. The potential therapeutic implications of targeting the critical regions associated with ADHD are also worth exploring in future research. We illustrate the convergence of trajectories through simulations based on the recent COVID-19 pandemic's average monthly infection rates in the United States. Additionally, our research identifies a critical value of the infection rate above which the trajectory approaches the model's disease-free equilibrium, resulting in nearly all individuals eventually becoming infected. We also derive an inequality indicating a lower bound for the infection rate required for the pandemic to spread widely. Our analysis sheds new light on the pandemic dynamics and provides valuable insights, particularly regarding the critical infection rate threshold beyond which the pandemic spreads rapidly and reaches near-universal infection rates. Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both researchers and software developers are directed at creating systems capable of accurately identifying and interpreting acronyms within various contexts. Unfortunately, existing solutions have failed to present a unified, comprehensive approach applicable to different domains and available for public access. In response, our project offers the first publicly accessible, web-based acronym identification and disambiguation platform capable of processing multiple domains. This system can be accessed via the website https://iq.cs.uoregon.edu:5000/. Furthermore, the source code and data used in this study have been made available for perusal at https://github.com/naverqom/Acronym-ID-Disambiguation. To facilitate reproducibility, additional information can be obtained by contacting the author at naverqom@gmail.com. In terms of future developments, our vision encompasses expanding the system's domain to encompass all areas, incorporating more prominent acronyms such as AI and NASA, and making the platform accessible via APIs to enable seamless integration with existing systems. To achieve this, we propose the establishment of a collaborative, integrated database for acronyms similar to existing databases for words and phrases. If realized, this vision has the potential to greatly enhance how people comprehend complex, written terminology. Until then, our system remains a usable, albeit less comprehensive, alternative. As such, it represents a suitable starting point for addressing the intricate challenges surrounding acronym identification and disambigation. In addition to solving this particular problem, our work also showcases the utility of character-level language models in accurately capturing acronym-specific word meanings and the benefits of combining both character-level and token-level representations in achieving better performance. Last but not least, the experiment results indicate that acronym identification and disambigation necessitate different approaches and require distinct input representations, as demonstrated by the notable performance gaps observed between these two tasks. These findings are particularly significant and may extend to other areas within natural language processing. In conclusion, our developed system contributes to the advancement of acronym identification and disambigation through its effective integration of multiple techniques and a unified, publicly accessible platform, thus facilitating improved comprehension of complex written terminology. Studies have shown that phase-coherent effects become extinct as the system size increases due to the inevitable presence of disorder. Although this notion is widely accepted, a thorough examination of the impact of disorder on quantum coherence is still required. We have developed a time-dependent quantum Monte Carlo method to simulate coherent and incoherent charge and heat transport in small chains with randomized structures. Our experimental setup consists of a chain coupled to two heat baths. Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their realizations in photonic systems. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges associated with both experimental and theoretical investigations of topological nodal lines. Lastly, it highlights potential future prospects for topological nodal lines in artificial materials and discusses their potential applications.

In oscillatory media, regions that oscillate faster than their surroundings can give rise to outgoing waves, which are crucial for synchronization across entire systems and are prevalent in many biological and chemical processes. These waves, typically triggered by pacemaker-generated activity, serve as a means of transmitting information at a constant speed over extended distances. This research utilizes advanced analytical tools to explore the determinants of wave velocity, focusing specifically on singular perturbation and phase reduction techniques applied to two distinct types of oscillators, one representing a simple cell and the other a more complex cell with multiple oscillatory states. The findings demonstrate that wave velocity is largely determined by a specific combination of the cell's oscillation frequency and its relaxation time, but when frequency differences between cells are significant, additional considerations arise, leading to increased synchronization across the system. These results are subsequently validated through numerical simulations, incorporating a three-dimensional network of cells and revealing the intricate dynamics of global synchronization. Ultimately, the analysis provides a framework for making predictions about synchronization capabilities in oscillatory systems of extended scale. The research also highlights the potential for designing new types of wave transmission systems, opening up new avenues for information transmission in biological and chemical oscillatory systems. The analytical methods employed in this research are themselves significant contributions to the field of nonlinear dynamics, as they represent the first application of the singular perturbation method to intercell communication. Additionally, the research extends its findings to a distinct type of oscillator, revealing that wave velocity can still be accurately predicted through modification of the reduced model. This research is the first to thoroughly examine the phenomenon of wave transmission through oscillatory systems using analytical methods, and its findings significantly contribute to our current understanding of the field. Physicians' written assessments and interviews with patients, stored as unstructured clinical text notes (CTNs), have been analyzed by recent studies using machine learning techniques to forecast diagnoses based on CTNs, a task known as International Classification of Diseases (ICD) coding. Annotating medical data can be particularly labor-intensive due to the required level of specialization. This study presents an innovative approach to supplement a sparsely annotated collection of Icelandic CTNs using semi-self-supervised machine-learned imputation. By initially training a neural network on a small number of annotated CTNs, the model extracts clinical characteristics from un-annotated CTNs, generating "pseudo-annotations." These predicted medical codes are then used to train a logit-scale linear model, which serves as the final forecast model. While this method may introduce some noise, the results show significant improvements in the accuracy of ICD coding on newly seen cases without requiring additional manual annotation. Code and data are accessible upon request.

These predicted medical codes were then used to train a logit-scale linear model, which proved to yield high accuracy in ICD coding on previously unseen cases both in controlled and real-world settings. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up visibility queries and cast shadow mapping. By formulating scene illumination and visibility in spherical approximations, we can efficiently derive an explicit, differentiable representation for the spherical approximations, effectively capturing the scene's overall illumination and visibility characteristics. Our approach enables the efficient training of deep models on large datasets, which we subsequently demonstrate by applying it to the problem of monocular depth estimation. Our results reveal the extent to which incorporating the scene geometry's visibility information improves depth estimation accuracy, particularly when compared to previously proposed methods. To facilitate further research, we provide our approach as an open-source implementation on GitHub, accessible at the specified URL. Our approach's efficiency allows us to achieve state-of-the-art results on the KITTI and NYUv2 datasets, surpassing previously proposed methods in terms of testing depth error metrics. To achieve this performance, we take advantage of the benefits described in Section 2, which we discuss in detail below. Our approach's overall efficiency is also highlighted by its more than 100 times improvement over prior research on spherical harmonics approximations, demonstrating significant practical value. To further validate our method, we conduct a series of experiments creating synthetic shadow datasets by varying factors such as the presence of occluding surfaces, illumination intensity, and a novel "clear day" scenario without occluding surfaces or diffuse illumination. We test the generalizability of our approach by applying it to these varied datasets and discovering that it successfully predicts depth information in each case, demonstrating robustness across diverse light source configurations and visibility scenarios. To enable replication of our shadow synthesis process, we provide our approach as an open-source implementation on GitHub, accessible at the specified URL. Our method's efficiency allows us to efficiently utilize computational resources, successfully estimating depth information in each of the varied shadow datasets we created. Recent research on transportation networks has highlighted the need to account for uncertainty and reliability by modeling the probability of origin-destination demand and network flow. Building on long-term traffic data collection, this paper develops a framework to estimate the average and statistical relationship of origin-destination demand while considering the day-to-day variability resulting from travelers' independent route selections. The framework also determines the probability distribution of link and path flow along with their associated costs, with variations stemming from origin-destination demand, route choice, and unforeseen errors. By employing iterative least squares and lasso regularization techniques, the framework can iteratively estimate origin-destination demand while maintaining sparse covariance matrices for enhanced interpretability and computational efficiency. Notably, the probabilistic estimation method demonstrates an equivalent level of precision to the best possible estimators with diminishing errors as the sample size increases. The method was tested on two small-scale networks and two real-world large-scale networks, showing consistent and computationally efficient results with fast convergence. The study further confirms the effectiveness of lasso regularization in maintaining a balanced trade-off between the biases and variances of covariance matrix estimates. This study uncovers a broad class of non-trivial and smooth travelling waves that arise in the vicinity of the Couette flow in 2D Euler equation, at low regularity in vorticity $H^s$ for $s<3/2$. The velocity of these waves is directly proportional to their distance from the Couette flow. This finding significantly deviates from scenarios involving highly regular solutions in Gevrey spaces, where a damping mechanism prevents long-term perturbations. This research is particularly notable given that it contrasts with previous results showing no non-trivial travelling waves in areas immediately surrounding Couette flow with regularity higher than $3/2$. This work is further expanded by the discovery of a new, higher regularity criterion that distinguishes weak solutions of the 2D Euler equation from strong solutions. This distinction is characterized by a value of $\frac{3/2}{1-\epsilon}$ for a given positive $\epsilon$ less than $1$, representing a regularity threshold for weak solutions that doesn't apply to strong solutions. This means that as $\epsilon$ approaches 0, the regularity threshold for distinguishing weak solutions from strong solutions tends towards the previously established regularity threshold of $3/2$. This discovery is significant because it implies that regularity is not the sole determining factor for a solution to be considered strong. Finally, this study investigates the existence of large-time regaining regularity in solutions of the 2D Euler equation under certain conditions. This involves analysing solutions with initially low regularity that experience a significant decrease in regularity over time but eventually regain their original level of regularity when acted upon by an appropriate flow, which may occur before or after experiencing a decrease in regularity. This phenomenon holds true in a vicinity of Couette flow but could also be applied more broadly. This research is further complicated by the discovery of solutions that experience an irreversible drop in regularity. We experimentally control the linear polarization of exciton-polariton condensates using optical traps with elliptical geometries that favor specific polarization modes. Due to anisotropic splitting in the cavity, ground state degeneracy is lifted, yielding fine structure modes along the trap's axis and orthogonal to it. These modes are selectively occupied by the condensate. Our results reveal a unique method for polarization control with potential applications in spin-based photonics and research on complex optical systems with adjustable coupling properties. Additionally, we observe a dependence of spin degeneracy on trap shape and magnitude of anisotropic splitting. This behavior could be useful in the design of optical devices for the production of polarized photon streams. Furthermore, our findings promote the concept of using optical traps as adjustable couplers in photonics, enabling the modulation of photon exchange between distant emitters. Lastly, we discuss the possibility of utilizing such anisotropic traps in the research of complex optical systems characterized by non-abelian gauge fields. These systems, which we suggest should be referred to as complex exciton-polariton condensates, exhibit unique properties such as spin degeneracy and optical momentum localization. We illustrate the existence of such localization by calculating the optical momentum distribution of an exciton-polariton condensate trapped by an elliptical beam with a non-circular momentum pattern. This theoretical prediction can be verified by future experiments. By developing optical traps with adjustable anisotropic properties, it is now feasible to manipulate and control the optical momentum of exciton-polariton condensates. This opens up new avenues for research in optical science and technology. Lastly, we briefly review the prospects for future research in optical science and technology.

Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally posits that if subsets A and B, of size k and comprised of integers, share a sumset with a size near 2k, then A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. In this paper, we aim to enhance this by limiting the number of possible summands available from subset B. It's shown that if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every four-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it follows that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. This is a special case of a more general finding applied to non-commutative group settings. Moreover, using this theorem, we're able to derive novel conclusions about various structures of small sumsets, such as sets of integers, polynomial families, and vectors in finite fields. An example demonstrates that our result isn't merely a consequence of Freiman's 3k-4 theorem. Additionally, it's shown that if a subset B, of size k, satisfies a different condition - for every three-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k - then A and B exhibit some, albeit limited, similarity to arithmetic progressions. These conclusions also extend to the settings of cancellative semigroups. Our work is in part inspired by similar findings in a paper by Bourgain and Zeleke. To tackle these challenges, we employ novel applications of combinatorial logic, specifically the compactness theorem, alongside other innovative techniques. These applications enable us to derive significant conclusions about the presence or absence of arithmetic structures within various mathematical systems. Furthermore, by examining the presence of certain arithmetic structures within two distinct systems - the set of integers and the set of powers of two - we're able to derive two distinct versions of the Fibonacci conjecture. These hypotheses appear to be the latest iterations of a longer-standing line of investigation dating back to the early 20th century. In conclusion, the results obtained relate Freiman's 3k-4 theorem's implications on subsets of integers with small sumsets to conditions involving the presence of arithmetic structures within general combinatorial systems. We analyze the transmission eigenvalue problem involving $u$ and $v$ in the Sobolev space $H^1(\Omega)$ associated with $(\Omega, \sigma, \mathbf{n}^2)$. Considering the case where $\Omega$ is a 2 or 3-dimensional ball, and the functions $\sigma$ and $\mathbf{n}$ only depend on the radial distance $r$, we find a sequence of transmission eigenfunctions that tend to concentrate their energies around the boundary of $\Omega$ as the associated wavenumbers $k$ increase without bound. If $\sigma$ and $\mathbf{n}$ are constant, we prove the existence of transmission eigenfunctions that become localized around the boundary of $\Omega$. Our results generalize the recent studies in the mentioned literature and also illustrate the influence of medium parameters $\sigma$ and $\mathbf{n}$ on the geometric patterns of transmission eigenfunctions via numerical experiments. Moreover, we derive a potential application of our study to detecting changes in media properties within complete data inverse problem. Lastly, we present several numerical experiments that verify our theoretical findings. These experiments also showcase the phenomenon of transmission eigenfunction concentration around the boundary of $\Omega$ when $\sigma$ and $\mathbf{n}$ only depend on the radial distance $r$. They further illustrate how these functions geometric patterns can reflect changes in media properties within partial data inverse problem.

To expand a dialogue system's capabilities and facilitate its practical use, discovering new intent categories from user inputs is essential but remains understudied. Current methods are often inefficient, inaccurate, and require extensive labeling. We address two key research questions for this challenge by presenting two new intent discovery approaches. Firstly, we develop a multi-task pre-training framework that leverages a diverse set of data, including both structured and unstructured dialogues. This framework enhances the representation of our model's new intent classification task. Secondly, we present a new unsupervised approach to discovering new intent categories based on clustering. This method groups user inputs that deviate from typical behaviors and could indicate unknown intents. Experimental results show that our multi-task pre-training method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by 10.3% and our clustering method matches the performance of the top unsupervised method without relying on our multi-task model. Notably, our unsupervised method achieves 6.7% better intent classification accuracy compared to the traditional unsupervised approach. Human evaluation confirms that our newly discovered intents correspond to real, previously unrecognized intentions. Our new intent discovery data and implementation have been made publicly available. This marks the first time unsupervised new intent discovery has achieved reasonable accuracy without supplementing the data with semi-supervised information. Moreover, our multi-task pre-training method enhances various downstream tasks by boosting overall system performance by 3.3% in dialogue classification and 4.6% in natural language generation. We observe a 65% reduction in labeling requirements for these tasks after using our method. In contrast, the unsupervised approach to new intent discovery we tested increases labeling requirements by 105%. We attribute this to the unsupervised method's increased false positive rate of 55.1%. In conclusion, our multi-task pre-training method is recommended for enhancing dialogue system effectiveness and efficiency in downstream tasks. While the unsupervised new intent discovery method we presented may be beneficial in low-data scenarios where no semi-supervised information is available, it is less accurate than the multi-task pre-training method and increases labeling requirements. We anticipate our work to be particularly useful in resource-constrained settings where the cost of manual data labelling is prohibitive. In such scenarios, our unsupervised new intent discovery method could facilitate a more thorough understanding of the data distribution at minimal financial cost, paving the way for more resource-intensive data curation efforts. In our analysis, we demonstrate that a finite group of order $r$ possesses no more than $$7.3722\cdot r^{\frac{\log_2r}{4}+1.5315}$$ subgroups. This outcome holds based on the classification of two subclasses of solvable groups, specifically non-abelian metacyclic groups and abelian groups comprising high-power elements, as defined by the definitions of prime-power thickness and oligosubclasses. Consequently, we deduce that a finite group of order $r$ contains no more than $$7.3722\cdot r^{\frac{\log_2r}{4}+1.5315}$$ normal subgroups. This result is particularly notable in abelian groups, yielding a more straightforward expression: a finite abelian group of order $r$ possesses no more than $r^{1+\frac{\log_2r}{2}+0.5315}\lessapprox r^{1.6594\log_2r}$ subgroups. This theorem can be useful in resolving the Nilpotent Maximal Subgroup Problem, and our analysis partially solves this problem for prime-power orders, except for orders of the form $p^{2\alpha+1}$ or $2^{2\alpha+2}$, where $\alpha$ is a non-negative integer. Furthermore, our analysis allows us to derive a simplified estimate for non-abelian solvable groups, yielding a $r^{\log_2r+1.5315}$ upper bound. This finding is closely related to the Zorn's Lemma applied to the set of subgroups of a given order, where the existing literature provides a $r^{\log_2r+1}$ upper bound, as proved by the researchers Fulman and Gelbmann. Lastly, our analysis offers insights into the Nilpotent Thickness Problem by showing that a nilpotent group of thickness $p^2$ or $2p$ does not exist, where $p$ is a prime number. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA by introducing a novel spatial gate mechanism. This innovative gate enables low-frequency proposals with ambiguous spatial information to be given more significance. Consequently, the proposed SABRA framework significantly reduces false positives and achieves superior results compared to the existing VRD state-of-the-art methods. Our code will be publicly available at https://github.com/IndigoPurple/SABRA.

A new measure, referred to as quantum correlation cost (QCC), quantifies the amount of quantum correlation employed in weak measurement procedures utilizing the trace norm. It's demonstrated that the QCC is directly linked to the trace-norm-based quantum discord (TQD) by a factor dependent on weak measurement strength. However, this measure only captures a portion of a quantum system's quantum nature in contrast to the TQD. Furthermore, our results reveal that remaining quantum features can be extracted not only via further von Neumann measurements but also through a series of infinitesimally weak measurements. We exemplify these outcomes using a Bell-diagonal state. Our work establishes a connection between the QCC and TQD and offers insight into the fundamental properties of quantum measurement. It's also shown that the QCC can serve as an effective tool for identifying quantum systems that are least affected by weak measurements. We develop an algorithm to efficiently calculate the QCC for arbitrary density matrices. Additionally, our study explores the relationship between the QCC and the conditional quantum entropy (cqent), revealing that the QCC is lower bounded by a function of the cqent. Our work includes a thorough examination of the properties of the cqent and proposes it as a valuable measure of quantum information. Moreover, our results are used to investigate the relationship between the QCC, the TQD, the information plane, and the hyperplane. Our work is also utilized to identify minimal quantum systems that are least affected by weak measurements. We demonstrate that these systems are referenced to an optimal probe state. Our work is accompanied by the publication of open-source quantum software that can calculate the QCC, the TQD, the information plane, and the hyperplane. This paper introduces a graph neural network specifically designed for long-range dependency modeling in semi-supervised classification tasks. The proposed dynamic graph message passing network adaptively establishes connections between nodes in the graph, enabling effective communication of message passers. The framework commences by selecting key nodes for message passing, followed by message exchange, with operations like message aggregation adjusted accordingly. The approach is applied to two semi-supervised classification tasks - Stanford Artificial Dataset and Clustering - yielding superior results compared to existing methods. Optimized hardware is often required in embedded systems, leading to a common operation called Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM) over integers. One efficient way to achieve this optimization is by replacing expensive generic multiplication with bit-shifts and additions in a multiplierless circuit. Our approach uses a novel method in designing MCM circuits, starting from arbitrary constant polynomials instead of the more common approach of using coefficients. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. We examine differential forms on an algebraic compactification of the metric graph moduli space, derived by mapping invariant differential forms from the tropical Torelli map. It's known that these invariant forms give rise to the stable real cohomology of the general linear group, a finding by Borel. We compute period integrals by integrating such forms across graph metrics and find them to be always finite and expressible as generalised Feynman integrals. Our integrals have further application in identifying non-zero homology classes in the graph complex, providing novel perspectives on the cohomology structure and forging links between graph theory, motivic Galois groups and quantum field theory. By exploiting these new perspectives, we prove the non-triviality of specific graph cohomology classes, which are then used to establish the non-triviality of others through suitable transformations and comparisons with known results. Our approach also enables the computation of integrals either as functions of variables that arise in quantum field theory or as constants. Notably, our findings align with prior observations in quantum field theory. Lastly, our research reveals novel relationships between the graph theory, motivic Galois groups and quantum field theory. We demonstrate the existence of an isomorphism between the general linear group's cohomology and the graph complex's cohomology in a limit scenario, bringing insights from both fields closer together. Our computations may also be useful in studying the critical behaviour of a $\phi^3$ field theory in four dimensions. Our general theory applies to any type of differential form whose restrictions to non-singular graphs are rational functions. This encompasses many examples, including those related to the moduli space of smooth curves, their extended versions, and the moduli space of hypermaps. Our research provides precise formulas for the period integrals of forms associated with curves and hypermaps, which may be useful in studying quantum field theory. Moreover, our integrals provide a valuable connection between the moduli space of smooth curves and the moduli space of hypermaps. We show that the period integrals of forms associated with curves can be expressed as special cases of the period integrals of forms associated with hypermaps. Our general theory applies to any type of graph, and our results provide precise formulas for the period integrals of forms associated with graphs that have a special property called hyperlinearity. This hyperlinearity means that for any given edge in the graph, there exists a form that is non-zero only on edges that are equivalent to that edge under the graph's symmetries

In various object categorization tasks, particularly in visually complex conditions, it has been demonstrated that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can outperform feedforward models.  This research aimed to uncover the specific role of RNN recurrence in aiding object categorization.  We trained RNNs on an object categorization task and discovered through linear diagnostic analysis that auxiliary variables such as object position, orientation, and size are communicated through recurrence and contribute significantly to performance improvement.  This evidence confirms our hypothesis that auxiliary variables are utilized to optimize object categorization in cluttered environments.  This finding is further validated by the observation that recurrent units were primarily engaged when auxiliary variables were dynamically updated.  We speculate that one possible explanation for this phenomenon is the protection of information related to auxiliary variables within the recurrent system.  This speculation is supported by the fact that incorporating additional information regarding auxiliary variables within the input layer did not yield the same level of performance as seen with recurrent systems, albeit possibly due to nonlinear interaction patterns between variables.  This research highlights the significance of communication among auxiliary variables during object categorization and provides further understanding of how recurrent systems contribute to improved performance in object categorization tasks. Given an algebraic variety X that has a transitive action from the group Aut(X), the highest degree of transitivity of this action is called the transitivity degree. This degree is denoted by the maximum value of m for which Aut(X) acts transitively m times on X. In cases where Aut(X) is m-transitive for any positive value of m, we define the transitivity degree to be infinite. This study involves determining the transitivity degree for specific varieties, such as quasi-affine toric varieties, and homogeneous spaces, while exploring related open problems and conjectures. It has been found that the transitivity degree for these varieties and homogeneous spaces is generally finite, with exceptions only for some specific low-dimensional cases. This research further extends by identifying a new class of varieties for which the transitivity degree is known to be infinite. These varieties include those that are not projective and have a positive dimension, as well as those that are projective but have a non-abelian automorphism group. This class includes many of the studied varieties, such as certain homogeneous spaces and quasi-affine toric varieties. By developing an axiomatic description of infinite transitivity degrees, this study presents a new, powerful tool for detecting infinite transitivity degrees in a wide range of geometric structures. This tool enables us to conclude that many projective varieties also have a transitivity degree of infinity. This research complements a previous study by D. Elift, D. Herrero, A. Nemanja, and V. Pavese, which established that many quasi-affine toric varieties have a transitivity degree of infinity. This work expands their results by showing that the transitivity degree of homogeneous spaces can also be infinite. Furthermore, two new conjectures have been stated for two specific classes of varieties, with the aim of providing a theoretical explanation for the finite nature of the transitivity degree in these two categories. This research specifically concerns smooth projective toric varieties and toric varieties that are not projective. By addressing these two groups separately, the transitivity degree for many other varieties, including Segre varieties, Veronese varieties, and homogeneous spaces, has been determined to be finite. However, it is known to be infinite for some low-dimensional variety classes, with potential applications in combinatorial problems. This research further reveals that the transitivity degree for toric varieties that are not projective can be represented by a fundamental combinatorial object called the invariant ring, which has strong connections to group theory. To capture the essence of non-terminating processes in PCF, we employ the lifting monad from topos theory, which has been adapted for univalent type theory by Escard\'o and Knapp. Our work confirms that using the lifting monad provides a viable way to handle partiality within univalent type theory, and we also demonstrate that a predicative and constructive Scott model is achievable. Notably, we avoid reliance on choice or quotient inductive-inductive types, unlike other approaches to dealing with partiality. We represent the Scott model as a type within a specific well-ordering topos, and our definition of numerical functions aligns with the Scott definition, utilizing the powerplus class and lifting monad. To validate that Scott values accurately represent the notion of approximation, we establish that any Scott value can be approximated by a sequence of finite Scott values. Additionally, we prove that PCF's fixed-point principle for partial functions is equivalent to a corresponding principle within our Ported Scott model. Notably, we can derive the fundamental properties of the fixed-point principle without using transfinite induction. This implementation allows us to automate proof generation for a wide range of theorems, leveraging univalent type theory's strong normalisation and the lifting monad's strong normalisation properties. Designing effective collision avoidance systems for mobile robots remains a key challenge, particularly when accounting for the robot's spatial structure.
In this paper, we develop a novel control approach that leverages Control Barrier Functions and Quadratic Programming to enable safe navigation for mobile robotic arms around obstacles, factoring in their unique geometry.
Our proposed method successfully incorporates geometric constraints by converting them into control constraints, allowing for seamless integration with the robot's spatial structure.
Simulation results for both a simple rod and a modeled robotic arm validate the method's efficiency and scalability, demonstrating its ability to adapt to varying levels of complexity without excessive computation time. Additionally, the method's ability to balance performance and safety is demonstrated through trade-off analysis. While the current implementation is confined to planar movements, the proposed methodology can be extended to three-dimensional environments with additional modifications. Overall, this method provides a versatile solution for mobile robotic arms navigating complex environments while accounting for their distinct geometry. 
The related kernel code for this research is available at https://github.com/CIMelino/CCBFGeometricCAF.

To address the complexity involved in identifying the optimum edit distance, the work presents two innovative approaches: (1) establishing a graph to represent sentences as nodes, linked by edges representing similarity metrics, and (2) applying a graph walk to identify highly similar sentences. Furthermore, the work proposes a graph-based methodology that treats text as a network, where sentences are represented as nodes, connected by edges reflecting similarity metrics, and editors (manually or through supervised learning) that delete unnecessary sentences to achieve optimal abstraction. Experimental findings on the Reuters-21578 dataset demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach in enhancing abstracts by deleting redundant sentences. The work also highlights the potential of incorporating these methods into real-time news summarizers. To automate this process, the work employs a graph-based depth-limited search algorithm informed by the edit distance metric. The work concludes with an evaluation of two renowned news articles using the proposed approach, showcasing its feasibility of being utilized in real-time news summarization systems. Polynomial system solving plays a crucial role in various applications to capture nonlinear geometric attributes. To obtain a solution set devoid of degeneration, which end-users seek to avoid, the nondegenerate locus of a polynomial system needs to be computed. The nondegenerate locus comprises points where the codimension of the solution set matches the number of equations in the system. Historically, the nondegenerate locus has been obtained using ideal-theoretic techniques like saturation ideals and equidimensional decompositions. We propose an algorithm leveraging signature-based features of Gröbner basis algorithms to directly calculate the Gröbner basis for the nondegenerate locus closure without initially solving the entire polynomial system through Gröbner basis computation. The method applies to finite-dimensional algebraic systems, with a demonstrated codimension 1 case having a near linear computational complexity. The proposed method represents a significant shift from current approaches, as it directly calculates the Gröbner basis for a specific complementary ideal related to the nondegenerate locus closure, bypassing the requirements of equidimensional decompositions. The algorithm significantly simplifies computations for various fundamental attributes of the nondegenerate locus, allowing for more efficient exploration and parameterization of this geometric shape. The presented results provide a foundation for further developments in Gröbner basis algorithms centered on the concept of dimension. The Gröbner basis algorithm for the nondegenerate locus closure can be viewed as a special case of a more comprehensive problem, where the proposed method can be extended to systems with codimension greater than 1 by analyzing the Gröbner basis structure of specific complementary ideals related to Hilbert zeros. The study offers an innovative dimension-specific Gröbner basis algorithm, which holds promising implications for parameterization and sampling techniques on algebraic systems. To demonstrate the computational efficiency of the proposed method, the study showcases Gröbner basis calculations for two real-world nonlinear algebraic systems. The results show comparable computational performance to other currently used methods. The study concludes with suggested avenues for further research, including analyzing the computational complexity of the proposed method and its potential applications in learning algebraic systems. The accompanying code can be accessed at https://github.com/alexeyev/nondegenerate-locus.

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the weakly nonlinear approximation scheme, we adapt this approach to create an interpolation operator using the hyperbolic tangent multiquadric, which converges at a rate proportional to $s^{-2}$, where $s$ represents the normalized distance. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this new interpolation method is approximately equivalent to a Gaussian function, while also maintaining higher precision in local approximation tasks. To evaluate the efficiency of this algorithm, we perform numerical experiments on randomly generated functions and present some striking results. Additionally, we apply this interpolation method to solve two classical partial differential equations—Laplace's equation and the heat equation—achieving notable success. All computational tests were performed using the MATLAB software. Moreover, we provide open-source code for the implementation of this interpolation method and its associated gradient operator. Lastly, we outline future research directions based on these findings.

Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for safe and predictable transportation navigation.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather conditions, which require a dataset tailored to their detection.
We introduce the RFS Dataset, created with the purpose of detecting four types of adverse weather: rain, snow, fog, and haze.
Featuring  DEMO videos lasting up to 10 seconds and subsequent labels indicating the presence of one or more weather conditions, this dataset caters to the needs of a robust weather detection system.
We utilize the RFS Dataset to develop a robust fusion approach for combining individual vehicle and network sensor data to enhance weather condition detection accuracy. 
The proposed technique surpasses state-of-the-art competitors in accuracy, successfully identifying weather conditions in each given video sequence. 
With the RFS Dataset and this new method, we aim to boost the effectiveness of weather condition detection systems. 
The source code for our project, as well as the RFS Dataset, can be accessed at https://github.com/arkhshvds/RFS..fhir. For dataset download requests, please email [rfsdataset@rfsdataset.com](mailto:rfsdataset@rfsdataset.com).

Our analysis examines how climate change interest shifts among diverse groups and how their individual interests interconnect. Initially, we track the individual trends, followed by developing a cross-influence model that we then validate using a VAR model. Our results indicate significant fluctuations in the general public's climate change interest, as evident from our creation of a Climate Change Index for Europe and the US based on media mentions, whereas economists show relatively little interest as measured by prominent journal publications. Interestingly, science journals and policymakers display a more stable interest in the subject, albeit with policymakers typically becoming interested somewhat later. Moreover, our findings suggest that media mentions influence policymakers' interest, but we find no such relationship between media mentions on policymakers' interest and scientists', and nor do we find any cross-influence between economists' interest and that of the other groups. It is crucial to note the differences between our measure of interest and other forms of engagement, such as donations to environmental charities or voting in elections. Therefore, our research does not seek to establish causal relationships between climate change interest and actual actions but instead provides a thorough exploration of the subject. Lastly, our research does not attempt to identify the direction of cross-influence by other groups' interests on a particular group but rather examines the overall effect of their individual interests on one another. Hence, our research does not imply that one group is interested in another's interests but rather highlights the dynamic and interconnected nature of climate change interest among the groups in study. It is also worth noting at the onset that our research primarily focuses on the time period from 1988 to 2009, although we sometimes extend it to 2014 in the case of our index. A novel approach combining machine learning is introduced, enabling the accurate reconstruction of high-redshift cosmological density perturbations through observed quasar spectra analysis. By leveraging sophisticated simulations of cosmic structure formation, a substantial synthetic dataset of absorption spectra and associated 1D matter densities is generated. With this dataset, a series of machine learning models are constructed to predict matter density power spectra. We achieve reconstruction accuracy of approximately 1% for certain wavelengths while noting a corresponding error increase at higher wavelengths. Furthermore, we investigate the size of datasets required to attain a specified error rate, highlighting the data requirements for a desired level of accuracy. This work lays the groundwork for analyzing the forthcoming large-scale datasets anticipated with future observational facilities. It will allow us to analyze quasar data and set limitations on matter density error rates, thereby informing hypotheses about cosmology. We suggest that future research should focus on utilizing supervised learning to derive direct measurements of cosmological parameters from quasar data, thereby eliminating the need for intermediate assumptions about the matter density's statistical behavior. Moreover, we propose an original strategy to utilize the small residual errors in our reconstruction for a statistical analysis of the matter density fluctuations, which could provide valuable constraints on the cosmological parameters. This approach might be particularly beneficial when analyzing the forthcoming extremely large-scale spectrographic surveys. In the end, we briefly explore the potential applications of this method to the reconstruction of higher-dimensional cosmological fluctuations and the separation of gravitational waves from the cosmic density perturbations. We then outline future research directions, where localized volume data could be used to analyze the cosmic homogeneity on a large scale. Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints to open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to consistently
maintain assigned roles during human conversations. Achieving this involves
defining a role specification with specific criteria for stated features and
policies on allowed types of utterances. To build this system efficiently, we
propose a framework for collecting data that leverages few-shot learning from
large language models, thereby enabling the creation of role-compliant dialogue
datasets quickly. We recognize that relying solely on pre-trained models may
yield subpar results and therefore support the use of role-compliant data
training for enhanced performance. Experimental findings demonstrate that our
approach successfully imposes role constraints on generated conversations, and

This research explores various spectral characteristics of the Seidel matrix associated with a connected chain graph, demonstrating that $-1$ is always an eigenvalue, while other eigenvalues may have a multiplicity of at most two. We derive the multiplicity of the eigenvalue $-1$, the minimum number of unique eigenvalues, eigenvalue limits, the characteristic polynomial, and bounds for the Seidel energy of a chain graph, which outperform previously proposed energy bounds by Haemers. We also obtain the minimum Seidel energy for specific chain graphs of order $n$, along with presenting several unresolved questions. Our study complements and extends earlier work on the spectral properties of Seidel matrices by Makhnev and Makhnev. In our investigation, we focus on a mean-field optimal control issue for stochastic differential equations featuring time-delay, which are influenced by fractional Brownian motion with a Hurst parameter exceeding 0.5. Given the fractional Brownian motion's nature, which defies the criteria for being a Markov process or semi-martingale, we resort to the fractional White noise calculus and specialized tools for differentiating functions of measures to establish necessary and sufficient stochastic maximum principles. This approach is further exemplified by two applications, including solving a delayed consumption optimization problem from a cash flow and a linear-quadratic problem under delay constraints. These applications demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed maximum principle in deriving explicit solutions and recovering the classic results for fractional diffusion processes. Moreover, when the Hurst parameter equals 0.5, we establish the equivalence between the necessary and sufficient conditions derived in this study and those derived by the Backward Stochastic Differential Equation method. This is rare instance where the connection between the fractional and the classical stochastic maximum principle is achieved. Keywords - Fractional Brownian motion, mean-field delay stochastic control, state feedback, necessary and sufficient stochastic maximum principle, fractional White noise calculus. We've developed a unique, detailed two-parameter set of finite-band Jacobi elliptic potentials that correspond to the non-self-adjoint Dirac operator, seamlessly linking two well-known limit cases, each associated with the absence or presence of elliptic parameters. To thoroughly analyze the Dirac operator's spectrum, we've made connections between periodic/antiperiodic eigenvalue problems for the operator, equivalent tridiagonal operator actions in weighted Hilbert spaces and relevant Heun equation connection issues. This, in turn, ties into four related non-self-adjoint, unbounded tridiagonal operator eigenvalue problems which surprisingly possess real eigenvalues. These problems originate from eigenvalue problems of the Heun equation's associated discrete Schrödinger operator and its first derivative counterpart. We've proven that our eigenvalue problems are uniquely defined, relative to symmetry type, and made connections to self-adjoint problems, including periodic/antiperiodic eigenvalue problems for the standard Dirac operator. We've also found that solutions to eigenvalue problems for the operator and its counterpart relate to connections in elliptic potentials, missing in the standard case. To validate our findings, we provided explicit examples and noted potential applications in mathematical physics and related fields. Our work laid the groundwork for a broader, related research project.
