RSUs are a vital component in V2X, facilitating communication with users; however, congestion areas are often poorly served due to high data traffic, weak signals, and interference, which can be addressed through the use of vehicle relays. To enhance the network in these situations, this research utilizes stochastic geometry to develop an innovative analytical framework for the performance evaluation of vehicular networks incorporating RSUs, vehicle relays, and mobile vehicle users. Our two-dimensional analytical model effectively considers the spatial interdependence of RSUs, vehicle relays, vehicle users, and road infrastructure using a Cox point process. By assuming relay backhaul to RSUs over reserved wireless channels and user association with the closest RSU or relay, we calculate the probability that a typical user is linked to either an RSU or a relay, determine the SIR coverage probability of a typical user, and subsequently, calculate the average effective transmission rate of a typical user within the network. This method enables the quantification of the increase in average effective transmission rate resulting from the deployment of relays. Our analytical findings are validated through simulations and tractable numerical evaluations. This work's success paves the way for the strategic deployment of RSUs and vehicle relays in vehicular networks, enabling improved coverage for users in congested areas. Our numerical results show the efficacy of this approach in enhancing network performance, with the instance that the increase in average effective transmission rate is maximum when the density of relays is less than half the density of RSUs. Moreover, higher densities of relays result in an increase in the area where the network's coverage probability remains above a minimum threshold, but this phenomenon reaches a limit at high relay densities before stabilizing. Our analytical model is versatile and may be applied to a variety of scenarios, such as evaluating the enhanced coverage probability resulting from the addition of relays at locations with high data traffic but few RSUs. Our work's goals are aligned with those of recent initiatives, such as M2M and vehicle-to-grid communication, in the context of V2X. Additionally, our stochastic geometry model may be applied to other complex networks, such as M2M networks with vehicle users, vehicle-to-grid communication, and vehicle networks with the assistance of road-side units and device-free models. Our method's efficiency is demonstrated through its ability to accurately calculate the average effective transmission rate with just two numerical integrals, in contrast to geometric models that require more complex evaluations. Furthermore, our model's efficiency enables the computation of network performance metrics with greater precision, without compromising computational intensity

Wikipedia's ultimate goal is to be an authoritative reference on various topics.  However, due to a limited number of editors and a vast amount of articles, only 0.6% are considered of high quality according to their established criteria. To enhance article quality through machine learning, we must first label individual sentences as high or low quality, yet this process relies on human annotations that are time-consuming and often yield inaccuracies. To resolve this, we developed an automated system that examines semantic modifications in Wikipedia edits to create labels, considering the pre-edit version as an example requiring improvement, and high-quality sentences as instances that need no improvement. By employing our labels in machine learning models, we found that performance improves over relying on existing, manually generated labels. Furthermore, we discovered that Wikipedia editors often express approval or disapproval of sentence revisions in comments, providing valuable, unseen labels. When combined with the existing data, these comments enable us to achieve state-of-the-art performance on the task and open up new avenues for research. We anticipate this work to inspire further investigation into the complexities of human assessment, editor behavior, and the effective utilization of annotated data. Moreover, our study demonstrates the practical value of incorporating natural language explanations found in human interactions with automated systems to improve their performance. Knowledge distillation has emerged as a key method for compressing deep neural networks. Traditionally, its application has been limited to model post-training. This study delves into the capabilities of knowledge distillation as a layer-wise regularization technique during model training. Although the concept may seem intuitive, early experiments reveal that simply applying it to all model layers yields underpar performance compared to conventional methods. To address this challenge, this study introduces two novel approaches: utilizing knowledge distillation for the linear layers of a model, and combining its effects with data augmentation. These techniques successfully improve the model's performance, with the former achieving this gain particularly by reducing the biases of model weights. When combined with post-training knowledge distillation, they also enable the efficient scaling of pre-trained models. This study presents DistDeep, a multi-stage workflow for deep neural network training that incorporates these techniques. Empirical evidence confirms its efficacy in improving model performance. Notably, this study discovers that knowledge distillation has a contrasting effect on the biases of model weights, which is significant for deep learning researchers. Overall, the findings highlight the promise of in-training knowledge distillation, which may serve as a more effective means of deep neural network regularization compared to post-training knowledge distillation. This study also shows the potential of model pruning as a means of further compressing deep neural networks. When applied to model weights, this technique may serve as an effective means of further compressing deep neural networks. This study confirms its efficacy in improving model performance, especially when employed in conjunction with in-training knowledge distillation. Furthermore, the study finds that in-training knowledge distillation may serve as a more effective means of deep neural network regularization compared to post-training knowledge distillation. To facilitate the reproduction of this study's findings, the implementation details and demo code are provided on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/SingleStep/DistDeep. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically classify and prepare samples for precise pose estimation, particularly effective for devices with inconsistent optical centers. A cutting-edge pose estimation network achieves high accuracy and efficiency, with the capability to process one sample per iteration at a rate of 10 frames per second. Experimental results on various real-world datasets display comparable or even superior performance relative to leading fiducial-based methods, alongside significant time and computational efficiency gains. Moreover, our markerless system is adaptable across diverse environments, demonstrating robust performance on new objects after successful training on a single object with adjustable optical centers. The advantages of this approach include reduced dependency on laboratory setup for marker placement, increased flexibility in unknown scenes, and simplified deployment on new devices with minimal requirements. With the rise of deep learning, our markerless system signifies a significant progression towards automated, efficient, and robust extrinsic calibration both in research and industry settings. The proposed method is expected to have a lasting impact, as it eliminates the limitations associated with fiducial markers and enables seamless transfer of learning to new objects, lights, and devices. A new model is introduced to describe treatment interference in units, 
where the response is influenced solely by its treatment status and neighboring units within a defined radius of influence (K-neighborhood). Traditional approaches for identifying interference involve controlled randomized trials and statistical tests focused on specific, selected units (focal units). We provide criteria to select these pivotal units under the given interference framework and conduct a simulation to assess existing methods for detecting interference in networks. By implementing this selection process, highly effective tests of treatment interference are achieved, surpassing the efficacy of standard experimental methods. Moreover, the strategy enables the partial identification of interference effects by analyzing the pivotal units in relation to their untreated counterparts. By applying a novel nonparametric instrument, we derive efficient estimates of the interference effects. These findings provide a valuable framework for conducting experiments more efficiently and gaining greater insight into treatment interference in real-world applications. For instance, in our study on the adoption of health behaviors, highly influential central units receive an uncontrolled treatment effect, while peripheral units, though influenced by treatments, do not receive an effect. We use treatment interference models to investigate health behaviors' interdependence and demonstrate the novel potential for leveraging these dependencies to promote healthier central unit behaviors through their influence on peripheral units. The properties of thin films made from metallic transition-metal oxides can be significantly different from their bulk counterparts. In this study, we simulate a monolayer of strontium vanadate grown on a substrate to investigate the thickness-induced metal-to-insulator transition. We found that two different terminations lead to the same insulating behavior at equilibrium but exhibit distinct behavior when doped or subjected to a gate voltage. Through many-body calculations, we revealed various nonlocal fluctuations resulting from antiferromagnetic, ferromagnetic, stripe, and checkerboard orbital ordering instabilities. By considering the role of orbital degrees of freedom, we explain how these instabilities emerge and demonstrate how ultra-thin film reconstruction and changes to coordination polyhedra result in unique material properties. Our findings provide a framework to interpret recent experiments and encourage further investigation into the associated phenoena to explore potential new materials with similar properties.  Our results are relevant to various ultra-thin film materials such as LNO/LSMO and it is expected that similar physics can be observed in these materials as well. Our research presents a novel convolutional neural network called HEAT, designed to improve upon existing methods, with a focus on efficiency for high-volume testing environments.  We also investigate the effectiveness of combining teacher-student learning to enhance automated grading performance.  Our findings demonstrate that HEAT surpasses state-of-the-art performance in the TOEFL IRT dataset, both with and without teacher-student guidance.  Additionally, we find that teacher-student learning is particularly beneficial for low-resource datasets, where labeled data are scarce. We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT. This innovation enables the creation of RingCT outputs within the consensus mechanism, causing transactions to occur within the regular blockchain channel. Furthermore, this integration facilitates the formation of RingCT outputs within a batch channel. An additional advantage of Delegated RingCT is its capacity to enhance the efficiency of batch processing by reducing the size of associated data blocks. Moreover, the use of Delegated RingCT enables the implementation of more robust and efficient sidechains. To validate the practical applicability of Delegated RingCT, we conducted a test using the Qtum blockchain and successfully demonstrated the creation of RingCT outputs both directly and through batch transactions. The full source code of our test implementation is available on GitHub, accompanied by live demos showcasing the test results. As a result, Delegated RingCT is now fully functional and ready for use in Qtum. In addition to its potential to accelerate the adoption of RingCT, the framework provides a versatile toolkit for the seamless integration of various sidechains with Qtum, thereby promoting greater interoperability among different cryptocurrencies. We intend for Delegated RingCT to serve as a benchmark or reference point for similar cryptographic innovations, facilitating an exchange of ideas among developers. Ultimately, the primary goal of this research is to accelerate the advancement of RingCT and sidechains, thereby promoting greater usability and versatility of cryptocurrencies. In conclusion, the integration of Delegated RingCT not only enhances the capabilities of Qtum but also positions it as a more attractive and versatile cryptocurrency compared to its competitors. As such, this innovation has significant practical implications for the long-term success and expansion of Qtum in the cryptocurrency market. To that effect, we are exploring opportunities for collaboration with other prominent cryptocurrencies, with a view to promoting a unified, interoperable cryptocurrency ecosystem that benefits the entire community. In line with this objective, the full source code of Delegated RingCT is freely accessible under the permissive MIT license, thereby encouraging the seamless replication of our results across other cryptocurrencies. In the spirit of promoting harmony among cryptocurrency developers, we welcome any inquiries, suggestions, or code contributions from the community, which can be shared on our GitHub repository, specifically at https://github.com/QtumProject/DelegatedRingCT. In the longer term, we plan to expand the scope of Delegated RingCT by incorporating additional supporting protocols that facilitate the secure and efficient transmission of transactions and sidechains.

Previous foundational Hebrew NLP tasks have heavily relied on the 30-year-old Hebrew Treebank. This outdated single-source corpus lacks the diversity of modern Hebrew, found primarily on the web. The newly created Hebrew Web Treebank (HWTB) breaks this barrier, offering a significant improvement. HWTB is an open-source, free corpus consisting of 28,465 tokens, taken from various online articles. This paper details the corpus's creation, showcasing the challenges of annotating Hebrew web text. To assess HWTB's value, we compared it to the existing Hebrew Treebank using two NLP tasks: part-of-speech tagging and named entity recognition. Two distinct sets of machine learning models were developed, one for each corpus, to demonstrate HWTB's enhanced performance, particularly in correcting previous annotator mistakes. Both task results were further validated by conducting a user study. This study involved giving Hebrew NLP researchers access to our HWTB dataset and allowing them to work with it before conducting a survey. This was done to explore how the newly created corpus could affect the daily work of these professionals. All data and study results can be found on our project website: https://hebrew-web-treebank.github.io. HWTB will be updated periodically with additional annotations. Anyone interested in contributing to this project can contact the authors. Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated the growth of data-driven modeling in mechanics, making cooperative modeling more feasible. As research advances, diverse teams can create new models and data, leading to shared knowledge and collaboration opportunities. Nevertheless, a challenge persists in neural networks' tendency to 'forget' previous tasks after training on new ones. This drawback restricts cooperative learning, since adjusting an existing model to address a new problem can negatively affect performance on earlier tasks handled by other teams. To address this issue, the authors developed a groundbreaking 'continual learning' method and successfully implemented it in solid mechanics for the first time. They utilized recurrent neural networks to predict the behavior of materials undergoing plasticity. Notably, the developed method can be adapted for use in a wide range of network architectures and to predict multiple phenomena. This study's purpose is to stimulate innovative applications of continual learning, facilitating collaborative strategies among the mechanics community in addressing increasingly complex problems. Results demonstrate that the employed method can enable sequential learning of multiple constitutive laws without memory loss and often with reduced data requirements, matching or exceeding the accuracy achieved through standard training of separate models for each law. Current studies examining the performance of randomly assembled low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume the independence of degree distributions from edge endpoints. In contrast, our research extends this understanding by investigating LDPC ensembles that incorporate degree-degree correlations. We propose novel techniques for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles, derive density evolution equations applicable to binary erasure channels, and employ numerical simulations to illustrate how degree-degree correlations impact LDPC code performance. Interestingly, our findings indicate that negative degree-degree correlations can enhance the maximum error tolerance of LDPC codes, with further increases potentially yielding superior unequal error protection designs. We also observe that positive correlations impede the existence of finite error thresholds and demonstrate the capability of negative correlations to circumvent this limitation. Moreover, our research reveals the existence of two distinct regimes within the parity-check matrix of degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles, characterized by densely connected vertices and more isolated nodes, which we hypothesize can be independently tuned. Notably, the density of the more isolated set of vertices appears to be the determining factor for LDPC performance, which holds true regardless of the degree-degree correlations. We thereby propose modifying the density evolution equation for LDPC ensembles to solely account for the parameters of the isolated vertices to accurately predict the maximum error tolerance and thereby expand the scope of degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles. Our innovative approaches yield superior unequal error protection designs alongside extensive validation of our proposed ideas. Moreover, our research may offer novel insights into the structure and performance of parity-check matrices in degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles. We provide an intuitive explanation for the observed performance outcomes by analyzing the properties of extrinsic interference relative to the degree of the associated vertices. Moreover, we successfully develop a set of LDPC ensembles featuring negative degree-degree correlations with error thresholds closely matching those of independently assembled LDPC ensembles. A critical flaw exists in the current application of quantum key distribution (QKD) systems due to their vulnerability to quantum hacking. Our novel approach incorporates a hybrid measurement attack, achievable only when the source is not fully controlled (e.g. due to device imperfections), which poses a significant threat to the widely adopted vacuum+four decoy state QKD system even when the source is considered non-ideal. Our research provides a significant improvement in the expected secure key rate of the system when the source is not fully controlled, offering a useful margin against potential quantum hacking attacks under real-world conditions. This advancement makes our research more relevant to practical QKD applications, given that fully controlled sources are rarely achieved in real-world settings. Our results are further validated through both theoretical analysis and experimentally measured data from a standard commercial QKD system, demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed attack. Our findings suggest that the widely adopted positive implementation theory may not be sufficient to provide the required security against quantum hacking attacks, especially under real-world conditions. Our research may open new avenues for research and development in the theoretical and experimental aspects of QKD systems. The objective of zero-speech synthesis is to create a system that converts a single acoustic unit into all possible phoneme-based units while maintaining natural speech characteristics. Current approaches rely on the suppression of non-target acoustic units using acoustic models and cost functions. However, the quality of the generated speech is largely dependent on the specific model used. In this study, a framework called Informed Acoustic Unit Removal (IAUR) is proposed, incorporating prior knowledge of the target units' distribution in the form of a directed graph. This prior knowledge is applied as a regularization term during the cost function calculation. The effectiveness of the proposed method has been tested on the CMU USARSIP dataset, where it outperforms the existing baseline method in terms of speech quality and perceptual similarity. Moreover, the quality of the IAUR-generated speech is less dependent on the specific acoustic model used. As a result, IAUR's speech quality remains consistent across speech styles, whereas the baseline method's speech quality degrades significantly when different acoustic models are used. Therefore, IAUR offers more flexible and generalizable zero-speech synthesis capabilities. Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion under posture and force constraints poses a challenging nonlinear optimization issue, often accompanied by extensive computation times. We've developed a multi-step optimization method incorporating data-driven linkages between stages to tackle these nonlinearities efficiently. Both cluster analysis and evolutionary strategies are applied to determine the specific parameters of McCormick envelope relaxations, allowing us to leverage learned constraints across preceding stages, thus yielding better performance, faster solution times, and more interpretable outcomes. Our planner was thoroughly tested and validated through a variety of walking and climbing experiments on a 10 kg hexapod robot. Videos and data are available at https://whenmtl.github.io/mmlro/.

We have developed two overarching methods to quantify the manipulation of quantum states using probabilistic protocols constrained by specific quantum resource limitations.
Initially, we formulated a fundamental criterion for achieving a physical transformation between quantum states using a previously introduced resource theory framework. Grounded in this criterion, we created a comprehensive approach for determining the achievable region in multiple objective functions used to describe quantum resource limitations.
Alternatively, we employed a valuable econometric technique known as dual convexity to analyze the underlying trade-offs in quantum resource manipulation, which provides a useful framework for optimizing achievable regions and identifying essential resource quantities.
These techniques were successfully applied to the scenarios of quantum correlation and legibility using the tools of matrix inequalities and permutohedra. For example, we derived explicit formulas for the bounds of quantum correlation reuse, established a connection between the trade-offs in quantum correlation and the properties of local inequality, and constrained the trade-offs in the precision of quantum states, which led us to the concept of classical advantage as a key resource property. Moreover, we discovered the structure of the permutohedron that emerges when maximizing the classical advantage in qubit systems. Our work is expected to contribute significantly to the broad field of quantum resource theory. Dual visibility, belonging to a broad class of resource theory called promotion, offers an intriguing candidate for yielding a valuable resource property that can be obtained through manipulation of quantum states using probabilistic protocols. Finally, our study reveals the relationship between the trade-offs in quantum resource manipulation and the geometric properties of a statistical state space, which provides a valuable insight into the structure of quantum resource theories. This model was subject to two types of excitation - parametric in the vertical plane and a combination of parametric and direct in the horizontal plane. The position of the pivot changed over time, inducing these excitations. In the scenario of vertical excitation, the averaging method helped to establish stability boundaries for two steady-state solutions, whereas vertical and horizontal excitations led to system resonances identified through multiple scale methods, with results validated using exact numerical integration techniques. Analysis showed that in the presence of horizontal excitation, the equilibrium position became unstable, and a period and amplitude variation phenomenon emerged, accompanied by the creation of a smoke-like capchoid orbit. Additionally, our study revealed the occurrence of a horseshoe embedding associated with a primary resonance in the primary suspension system. Given that our model was validated for daily carrying activities, our research did not yield any circumstances that could lead to catastrophe. In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we analytically prove that our algorithm achieves a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT} + K/T\right)$. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of DR-DSGD, yielding an improvement of up to $10\%$ in test accuracy over various data distributions. DR-DSGD exhibits greater communication efficiency, with reduced communication rounds by up to $20$, compared to traditional DSGD, while also ensuring fairness across decentralized devices. We introduce a general, flexible framework called Partial Registration Network (PRNet), designed specifically for aligning partial point cloud views. Building on learning-based registration methods, PRNet employs deep networks to overcome complex alignment and correspondence issues. Unlike existing methods that require a fully observable shape, PRNet is suited for partial-to-partial registration tasks, surpassing traditional and deep learning-based approaches on synthetic datasets. Our approach features self-supervised learning of a suitable geometric representation and a keypoint detector for common point identification. Experimental results demonstrate PRNet's ability to consistently predict key points across different views and perform accurate shape alignment. Furthermore, PRNet's geometric representation serves as a suitable basis for predicting keypoint correspondences and facilitating shape alignment. We also evaluate PRNet's performance on real camera data, showcasing its potential for outdoor scene and object recognition. Additionally, our code and data are publicly available for reproduction and extension. PRNet has potential applications in 3D object recognition, outdoor scene analysis, and object manipulation tasks. Our approach is versatile and can be adapted for registering multiple views in each step (online) or utilizing a database to find correspondences for challenging pose cases (off-line). Our keypoint-based method is akin to SIFT, but uses learnable and differentiable keypoint representations for correspondence prediction. PRNet employs a flexible and efficient online method for registering multiple views, demonstrating superior performance over the off-line approach on difficult pose cases. Our research also involved adapting PRNet to recognize objects using image data, showcasing promising results and opening up new avenues for research. Our work may be useful for analyzing complex outdoor scenes and objects, presenting a novel approach to point cloud registration. Current techniques typically address a novel modality either by fine-tuning a pre-trained model or by dividing the tasks into independent image translation and segmentation steps, which often result in sub-optimal performance. In this study, a multi-modal instance segmentation framework is proposed, which simultaneously performs image translation and segmentation on unseen modalities in a fully unified manner. The framework achieves this goal by optimizing a combination of cycle consistency loss, cross-cyclic loss, and multi-scale object loss for accurate segmentation of the target modality. The results show that the proposed method outperforms pre-trained and multi-task models in segmenting the target CT scans, with performance comparable to that achieved on directly labeled CT scans. In particular, the Pearson correlation coefficient between the predicted labels and actual labels on CT scans was 0.940, with mean absolute errors of 0.734 cm and 0.822 cm for the left atrium and aorta respectively. Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening for hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum flux of $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  in a well-studied superflare from AD Leo during its peak phases. This prediction model utilizes semi-empirical combinations of radiative electron beam flux spectra consisting of two electron beam models: a high-flux simulation with a high energy cutoff and a lower-flux simulation with a lower energy cutoff. This two-component approach effectively explains the Balmer line broadening, the optical color temperature, the Balmer jump strength, and the far-ultraviolet continuum in the peak phases of this flare. Notably, the lower energy electron beam in the lower-flux simulation is found to significantly influence the far-ultraviolet continuum at $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  with an optical depth of $\tau_{\rm LyC} \approx 0.8$. This leads to an enhanced Lyman-continuum flux that accounts for the observed excess at $\lambda \approx 1650$ Å\  in the flare spectra. This finding is crucial for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures in low-mass stars' UV environments. As such, a comprehensive examination is conducted to evaluate the efficacy of the two-electron beam model in replicating the far-ultraviolet continuum of stellar flares in three low-mass stars, which includes AD Leo, EQ Aguilarae and DX Ceti, with the model showing an excellent match for two of these stars but requiring modifications to replicate the far-ultraviolet continuum of the third star. This implies the possibility of employing low-energy electron beams to account for the far-ultraviolet continuum in rare high-flux flares. As such, a critical limitation in assessing exoplanetary biosignatures in low-mass stars' UV environments is partially addressed. Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Additionally, we design unique validation protocols tailored to a variety of specific transformation scenarios. Experimental results on multiple frequent three-dimensional transformations validate the exceptional performance of TPC. As an example, our research shows that extending the traditional 50% stretching threshold for shearable transformations from 1.15 to 1.25 compensates for adversarial stretching up to 1.5 times the original value. Similarly, our study finds that raising the traditional 50% rotating threshold from 10degre to 20degre accommodates adversarial rotating up to 35degre. These findings indicate a significant enhancement in the safety of frequent three-dimensional transformations. Our research also demonstrates the significant efficiency gains of our two design innovations for validation protocols. Firstly, our frequency analysis indicates that most shearable and compositional transformations have minimal impact and can be omitted, cutting costs. Secondly, we show that incorporating numerical rather than categorical transformation classification significantly reduces computational costs without affecting accuracy. To promote research in this area, our code, data, and models are publicly available for reproduction at https://github.com/Qianhewu/Point-Cloud-Security. In addition, our project has been live-demonstrated on https://3d-security-guarantee.github.io/Point-Cloud-Security-Gurantee/. In conclusion, our research in TPC provides robust security guarantees with efficient performance gains for the most common three-dimensional transformations, setting a new benchmark in the field. Ultimately, we hope this research will lead to the development of novel and creative validation strategies with the potential to cover all types of three-dimensional transformations. Our research in point cloud security also has the potential to inspire the exploration of similar approaches in other areas such as image and video security. With continued advancements, we anticipate that deep learning-based point cloud models will achieve widespread adoption in manufacturing, healthcare, and transportation. To facilitate research, our project has been live-demonstrated on https://3d-security-guarantee.github

In the field of rigid-body impact sound synthesis, the sound produced by the ground is often overlooked. However, in this study, an idealized ground sound model, rooted in elastodynamic theory, is used to determine under which conditions ground sound is perceivable, rather than being masked by the sound produced by the impacting object or its transient vibrations. An analytical model derived from this theory allows for the calculation of the acceleration of the ground surface in a precise and mathematically closed form, which can then be applied in various simulation methods to generate the sound waves. It is found that ground sound can be audible under certain circumstances when the sound produced by the impacting object is inaudible, specifically when a heavy object strikes a soft surface and when the point of impact is positioned at a shallow angle relative to the listener's location. Computational efficiency is also a crucial factor in sound synthesis; therefore, three practical simulation techniques based on the proposed model are developed to facilitate the efficient computation of ground sound. These simulation methods, which incorporate a frequency-domain approach, a waveform envelope-based method, and a correlation-based technique, can be utilized in various acoustic environments to accurately predict the perceptibility of ground sound. The effectiveness of these simulation methods is evaluated through a series of statistical analyses, which demonstrate their compatibility with real-world spectra and their ability to replicate the dynamic characteristics of impact sounds through their application of proper amplitude modulation factors. The suitability of these simulation methods for use in double impulse synthesis is then assessed and compared to the performance of alternative convolution-based approaches. Ultimately, the results of these comparisons confirm that the waveform envelope-based method is a highly effective tool for the efficient synthesis of ground sound in impact sounds. The research findings presented in this thesis contribute to the development of more realistic sound synthesis techniques in the field of impact sound synthesis, thereby enabling precise auditory reconstructions of actual impact sounds and facilitating improved detection and identification techniques for sound events. Additionally, the analysis presented in this study provides a useful reference for designing and positioning microphones in acoustic environments to detect subtle sounds produced by the ground. Knowledge gained from this research can be applied in fields like material science, where the non-destructive testing of rigid targets on soft surfaces can be aided by the accurate simulation of sound produced by the ground. With the current technological limitations of generating realistic sound produced by the ground, a fully accurate auditory reconstruction of actual impact sounds would likely require the integration of computer processing power from multiple sources, including CPU, GPU, and other parallel processing devices. Therefore, future research could focus on developing efficient ground sound synthesis

A newly created hydrogen boride monolayer, existing in the Cmmm phase, exhibits potential as a superconductor due to similarities with MgB2 and an abundance of hydrogen within its structure. Utilizing density functional theory, we've used first-principles calculations to investigate its electronic, vibrational, and superconducting properties. Contrary to expectations, however, the hydrogen boride system fails to possess a notable superconducting critical temperature. Hydrogen in this compound impairs the bonding between boron atoms, thereby reducing the effectiveness of electron-phonon interaction. Further analysis into potential improvements reveals that doping this system with electrons or holes yields unsatisfactory results. Ultimately, the critical temperature's limitations stem from the vanishing hydrogen influence on the Fermi level states, predominantly controlled by boron's p states. Consequently, substantial amounts of hydrogen-like states near the Fermi level are essential for attaining significant superconducting critical temperatures in such hydrogenated monolayers. Despite this disappointment, the study reveals the hydrogen boride monolayer holds promise as an exceptional thermal conductor, with a calculated Kapitza length greater than that of graphene. Therefore, targeting materials with enhanced electronic or phonon properties could serve as an alternative strategy for superconductor design. Moreover, our research provides a unified expression for Kapitza length in terms of phonon properties, applicable for both monolayer and bulk materials. In a similar vein, the phonon-related Kapitza length is observed to be significantly lower than electron-related counterparts for the materials involved, namely hydrogen boride and graphene. Thus, phonons may be more influential in governing thermal transport than electrons. This revelation is consistent with the observed thermal conductivity in graphene, where phonons dominate, potentially offering an explanation for the insulating behavior of hydrogen boride despite its high electron mobility. In a broader sense, this research highlights the significant impact of phonons on thermal transport, emphasizing the need to target phonon properties to enhance thermal conductivity in solid materials. Ultimately, the effective management of phonons could serve as a key strategy for the design of higher-performance thermal conductors. In a related context, the observed variation in Kapitza lengths among the materials suggests the potential for creating better thermal interfaces using two-dimensional materials by tuning interfacial bonding to maximize thermal conductivity. Therefore, targeting phonon properties presents an appealing avenue for enhancing thermal transport in solid materials. We categorize and understand a certain aspect of attractors in groups under study, specifically when the dynamics remains unchanged. It's observed that a particular aspect of these groups, often denoted by $\Gamma$, is represented by sequences of increasing complexity over time, denoted as $\mathscr{P}$. This pattern shows no change over time can be broken down into two cases: one where the sequences themselves don't change and the dynamics is unaltered, and another where the sequences increase in complexity but converge, potentially exhibiting variability. For the second case, a certain measure of rigidity in the group dynamics is quantified through the use of a parameter, denoted by $\rho$, which represents the expectation of the squared magnitude of the sequences. We find that if the sequences exhibit excessive growth in their magnitude, the parameter $\rho$ is fixed. Additionally, when the group dynamics is largely unpredictable and thus close to being completely random, the parameter $\rho$ is found to be at its maximum, equal to the magnitude of the reciprocal of the group size. A transition is seen at points where $\rho$ suddenly changes and where the group dynamics may suddenly become or cease being completely random. A comparison is also made with another related concept, often denoted by $\tau$, which represents the average sequence length over time, providing further insight into the two concepts. A series of tests, referred to as decision problems, are then introduced, questioning whether given elements of the group lie within this transition zone, and an extensive classification is undertaken, grouping these decision problems into defined categories, each with distinct properties. The outcomes of our case study underscore the need for formalization and the benefits it extends to safety-critical system development and testing. To facilitate the replication of our results, we provide an open-source implementation of our method, complemented by an illustrative example involving a steering system. A unified analytical equation of state for the equilibrium gas phase of pure alkali metals has been derived. This concise equation encompasses the perfect gas model, is applicable to all alkali metals, and accurately predicts their behavior across a broad pressure range (up to $\sim 10^5$~Pa) and temperature range (up to $\sim 3 \cdot 10^3$~K). Based on this equation of state, mathematical expressions for key thermodynamic properties and characteristics have been obtained, thereby substantiating the principle of corresponding states within the group of alkali elements. Additionally, the derived equations predict the isothermal compressibility factor ($\beta_{\text{P,T}}$), speed of sound ($\mathcal{C}_{\text{P,T}}$), thermal wavelength ($\lambda_{\text{P,T}}$), and Skalupski number ($\mathcal{S}_{\text{P,T}}$) for each alkali gas with satisfactory precision. The proposed equation and derived properties may serve as a useful reference for evaluating theoretical and experimental data on alkali element gas properties. As a demonstration of its utility, the accuracy of the predicted speed of sound in potassium and cesium gases in relation to experimental measurements has been verified. Specifically, the relative deviations of the predicted speed of sound from experimental values from this work are as low as $6.6 \times 10^{-3}$% and $4.1 \times 10^{-3}$%, respectively. These relative deviations are notably lower than those reported in the measurements themselves, namely $2.1 \times 10^{-2$% and $1.3 \times 10^{-2}$%, respectively. Furthermore, the relative deviation of the predicted speed of sound in potassium and cesium gases from the values calculated using Sasaki's equation of state is $8.8 \times 10^{-3$% and $5.9 \times 10^{-3}$%, respectively.}

Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. Our findings underscore the method's versatility and its potential to facilitate simulations with various matter configurations, including those that fail conventional approaches due to issues with solution generation. The main objective of the JUNO experiment involves identifying the neutrino mass ordering by utilizing a large, 20-kt liquid-scintillator detector equipped with photomultiplier tubes. Over four years, starting from 2017, a rigorous testing program for nearly 20,000 20-inch PMTs was carried out by the JUNO team. By examining these PMTs and implementing a series of stringent requirements, the experiment's investigators were able to verify the high quality of the selected instruments. This study outlines the thorough testing procedures used, the specifically designed testing equipment, and the statistical analysis of the 20-inch PMTs chosen for the experiment, covering over 15 performance indicators, including the uniformity of the PMTs' sensitivity to light. As a result, the largest batch of detailed-tested 20-inch PMTs ever produced, totaling 20,000 units from Northern Night Vision Technology Co. and Hamamatsu Photonics, was analyzed in the experiment. Moreover, by comparing the performance of the PMTs using various testing methods, the investigators were able to select the most suitable options for the experiment. Ultimately, the large-scale testing program validated the high quality of the chosen PMTs, which will be utilized in the experiment's underground detector, and provided valuable insights for the selection and procurement of photo-detectors in future large-scale neutrino experiments. This testing program has set a benchmark for large-scale neutrino detector experiments, which might require similar or more stringent requirements in the future. In practical scenarios like power consumption forecasting and air quality analysis, long sequence time-series forecasting (LSTF) is indispensable. The complexity of multidimensional time series data presents significant model demands, necessitating precise representation of long-term input-output relationships and relationships across multiple dimensions. Recent work employing the Informer model based on the Transformer architecture has yielded impressive results for long-term forecasting, yet it falls short in addressing dimensional interactions. Our enhancement of the Informer addresses these limitations in multidimensional forecasting through several key approaches. Firstly, we incorporate an adaptive graph neural network to identify dimensional connections often hidden in time series data. Secondly, we incorporate adaptive graph convolutional networks into spatio-temporal prediction models, enabling these models to recognize dimensional interactions. Our empirical evaluations with diverse datasets have revealed that the integration significantly boosts model accuracy by around 10%. The source code is available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/APFBai/LSTF_for_MDT.

This paper explores the recovery of one-dimensional Radon measures on a torus from their low-frequency Fourier components up to a given cutoff frequency, denoted as Kc. The proposed method involves minimizing the total variation among all compatible Radon measures through the problem of basis pursuit in the continuum (BPC). A characterization of BPC's solution set, including uniqueness and sparse solutions, is established in terms of a Toeplitz matrix. The matrix's inherent positive semidefinite property leads to a unique, sparse solution within the convex cone of BPC's solution set when it has a non-trivial existence. The BPC solution is shown to be the minimum total variation measure among all compatible Radon measures, and its Fourier coefficients up to Kc are the exact negatives of the lowest Kc+1 eigenvalues of the matrix, when it exists. The study also yields novel results in the field of functional Jacobi operators and a new formula for the spectral measures of these operators. The findings are supported by numerical examples and the analysis of periodic sinc functions, as well as a related convergence theorem for approximation problems. In numerical simulations involving fluid dynamics, the Raviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables like velocity or momentum. Nevertheless, the standard finite element methods that employ the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements tend to have low spatial accuracy in the vector transport equation. This paper explores two methods that elevate the accuracy of transporting such vector-valued fields across curved surfaces in two-dimensional environments. The proposed methods utilize a higher-order function space to refine the transported field, which is a crucial component in advection-diffusion equations. By utilizing the "build-down" approach, we decompose the transport equation into successive quadrature error corrections, ultimately achieving a high-order approximation of the transported field. Similarly, the "build-up" approach integrates the finite element and transport stability analyses to reach the same outcome. Through rigorous numerical testing, the efficacy of these methods is confirmed, and their potential applications are demonstrated. Lastly, the study highlights a novel connection between the "build-up" approach and the finite element formulation of the vector transport equation. This connection proves critical in developing stable finite element approximations for advection-diffusion equations, particularly when nonlinear relationships between variables are involved. In such cases, a careful selection of numerical time-stepping methods is essential to ensure robustness. By extending the finite element formulation, the paper provides a framework for solving a broad class of nonlinear advection-diffusion equations within quadrilateral meshes. This includes equations governing fluid dynamics, such as the Navier-Stokes equations, as well as momentum transport and scalar advection-diffusion reactions. The method's stability and accuracy are verified through various 2D numerical simulations. Interestingly, the study finds that the highest-order approximation of the transported field is a crucial factor in achieving robust and accurate results, even when the spatial accuracy of the involved variables is lower. This is particularly observed during the "build-up" approach for vector transport. In contrast, the most challenging scenarios for convergence are related to the "build-down" approach, specifically when attempting to correct the quadrature errors at a high order. In such cases, the method's rate of convergence is largely determined by the rate of decay of the error terms. In the last few years, the creation of accurate numerical solutions for problems with Hamiltonian dynamics led to the establishment of a specific class of energy-preserving Runge-Kutta methods known as Hamiltonian Boundary Value Methods (HBVMs). These methods can be interpreted as a continuous, multi-step approach, similar to Runge-Kutta methods but with continuous stages, and are explored here in the context of more general differential problems. This study reveals their underlying structure as interpolation techniques to solve differential problems, and further develops new classes of energy-preserving methods for first-order problems that subsume existing HBVMs and introduce new variants. Our research also demonstrates that these methods can be effectively applied to problems with singularities, and a range of numerical examples confirms their ability to conserve energy and preserve stability with high precision. Additionally, our work provides guidance on how to select method parameters, including order, stage number, and interpolation points, through a systematic approach based on theoretical criteria. This approach leads to a method constructor that allows users to generate specific energy-preserving methods tailored to problem requirements. Our method constructor is accompanied by three illustrative examples that demonstrate its utility. Lastly, our research delves into the potential for extending this framework to problems with second-order dynamics, and identifies key challenges and opportunities for future investigation. This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing specialized networks to refine neural network updates. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and applying error gradients from corresponding critic modules, the learning process is efficiently decoupled for both CNNs and RNNs. We demonstrate that this method not only converges to an optimal solution, but also facilitates structural optimization. The proposed method also significantly reduces training time and decreases the memory usage per machine. The code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/hjdw2/Local-critic-training. We expect this work to enhance the model-parallel training of neural networks. Nevertheless, our current implementation still relies on a centralized parameter control, which might limit its broad applications; thus, a future goal is to implement a fully decentralized method. Experimental results are presented for vision tasks using the top three backbones, and the compounding gains of efficiency, memory, and time are clearly shown. Moreover, the topological robustness of local critic training is empirically verified on various datasets, including ImageNet, CIFAR-10/100, and Tiny ImageNet. Given its robust performance, local critic training is deemed suitable for numerous real-world applications. We strongly believe that the thesis of local critic training can serve as a foundation for future research in neural network training. Accordingly, multiple potential avenues for further exploration are provided. To this end, a new research direction is introduced, which we refer to as the 'neural network segmentation theory.' We anticipate that future research on this direction will offer more refined and precise guidelines. Specifically, the challenges associated with selecting suitable layer groups, which critically impact the efficiency of local critic training, need to be addressed. Moreover, the issue of controlling the update magnitude for each layer, which might lead to sub-optimal solutions, necessitates further inquiry. To resolve these problems, we propose an innovative method of growth, which is demonstrated to be effective in selecting suitable layer groups. Moreover, the variance backpropagation can be utilized to control the update magnitude. These techniques not only enhance the performance of local critic training but also facilitate its application to various transfer learning scenarios. By employing the growth method, the topological robustness of local critic training is verified on all the mentioned datasets, which shows its capability in performing task-aggressive fine-tuning. We re-examine a widely accepted model for complex semiconductor production lines and analyze it in the context of states, inflows, and outflows being represented by measures on Borel spaces. This investigation arises from the lack of optimal solutions for transitioning from a smaller to a larger equilibrium state with zero inventory levels in the standard L1 framework. Novel contributions involve addressing the issue of non-differentiable velocities with discrete objects and a bounded domain subject to inflows and outflows. Employing a Lagrangian perspective, we establish that solutions exist and are unique and define a notion of weak solutions. Furthermore, we prove that the flow is continuous with respect to time, and also with respect to the initial condition. However, due to generally non-differentiable velocities, these refined regularity results only hold under carefully constructed semi-norms adapted from the standard norm. In general, the solution is not continuous with respect to any standard norm on the space of measures. To verify the regularity of the flow, we introduce a novel approach based on constructing and using a specially tailored Lagrangian solution that outcomes in a distinctively optimized solution with desired regularity properties. We demonstrate that this optimized solution is in fact a weak solution. As a by-product of our methods, we also establish that solutions are continuous with respect to changes in the inflows and outflows. To the best of our knowledge, the regularity results obtained here represent the most comprehensive to date for solutions of this important class of complex manufacturing systems with a focus on optimal control applications.

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological entities as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and oscillatory motion. By leveraging this trait, our approach uses a novel combination of optical flow and frequency domain analysis to detect biolocomotion, with the assistance of a comprehensive dataset consisting of moveless and biolocomoting videos taken in real-world settings. The proposed technique achieves impressive results, with our classifier achieving 90.5% accurate identifications across multiple context conditions. The proposed method undergoes extensive testing across various biological and robotic locomotives in controlled lab environments as well as real-world field recordings. The study demonstrates that our classifier generalizes effectively across various cameras with different resolutions. The proposed method undergoes successful applications on unfamiliar datasets consisting of insects, robots and vehicles. Modern artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methods are now employed to automatically identify physics principles and governing equations directly from measurement data. Nevertheless, formulating a universal physical law using data exclusively proves to be difficult without proposing a corresponding discrepancy model to account for the theoretical-measurement discrepancies that inevitably arise. By reexamining the long-standing problem of simulating the falling motions of objects with diverse size and mass, this work highlights several critical issues that need to be resolved by data-driven methods of automated physics discovery. It's particularly demonstrated that noise from measurements and secondary physical mechanisms such as complex drag forces, can mask the primary gravitational acceleration and yield inaccurate conclusions. Development of intelligent data sampling and regression algorithms, referred to as the predictive flux quotient (PFX), is presented to mitigate noise and obtain more accurate velocity measurements. The PFX technique is shown to accurately recover the known relationship between gravity and mass without accounting for drag forces. However, when the size of objects is reversed and only the velocity of the object near ground is known, the PFX technique still fails to yield an accurate conclusion regarding the role of gravity. This work underscores the significance of incorporating physical intuition when data-driven methods are used for automatic identification of physical laws and underlying governing equations. It also emphasizes the necessity of designing novel sensors that are more suitable for data-driven modeling of motion. The proposed approach presents a simple and effective solution to uncover the dominant role of gravity from complex motion data, thereby providing a practical solution for similar challenges in predictive physics. This work was done in collaboration with predictive science researchers at Harvard University, UC Berkeley, and MIT. The code for the project is publicly available. \\ \\

The Stable Roommates problem concerns pairing a set of agents according to their individual preference lists with specific hierarchical rankings. Variants of the Stable Roommates problem, including those involving larger groups of agents and distinct valuation methods, offer alternative scenarios for exploring agent matchings. A more complex form of the Stable Roommates problem, incorporating additively separable valuations and three-dimensional groupings, was explored, revealing instances where no stable matches exist and a direct approach is NP-complete. However, under the condition of symmetric valuations, we found that a stable matching will always exist and can be found within polynomial time using a new algorithm. Additionally, we identified the conditions under which the valuation method does not affect the existence of a stable matching. We examine the class of all metric spaces with their distances measured by Gromov--Hausdorff distance. The subsets of spaces with bounded distances are called clouds, representing maximal subclasses within this group. Scaling the distances of a space by a positive factor yields a transformed metric space, belonging to the same Gromov--Hausdorff class. This type of transformation can cause some clouds to jump into others, as noted in our previous study. To explain this phenomenon, we investigated the stability of these space transformations. This paper demonstrates that any cloud having a stabilizer with nontrivial action will contain a unique central metric space, such that transformations from the stabilizer all converge to this space, thereby indicating that it is zero distance away from all others within that group. The key proof for this lies within our previously established cloud completeness theorem. The presented work also introduces the concept of cloud isometries, which generate the stabilizers of these spaces, as shown by our chain of implications leading to this result. Additionally, we provide examples of clouds with non-trivial stabilizers, featuring spaces that are not isometric to one another within that group, but are closely positioned to each other. The outcome of this study implies the existence of clouds with infinitely many elements. Lastly, we explore the relationship between cloud completeness and the convergence of metric spaces, as dictated by the Gromov--Hausdorff distance. The example of spaces that are not closely related, yet converge under the Gromov--Hausdorff distance, along with the existence of clouds with infinitely many elements, raises questions about the structure of these spaces and their distances. This raises the primary question of whether all elements within a cloud must be isometric to each other. The answer to this question remains unknown. To resolve this, it is necessary to find an example of a cloud that has spaces that are not closely related, yet converge under the Gromov--Hausdorff distance with non-trivial action. The outcome of this study also raises the secondary question of whether all clouds with action that can be amplified by a constant factor must have spaces that are isometric to each other within that group. A microstrip-fed patch antenna designed to operate at mm-waves with broad bandwidth and low gain has been created for use in planar arrays. The design, which operates between 34.1 GHz and 36.3 GHz with a 1.2 GHz bandwidth, is suited for applications in 5G communication technology. The antenna's simple microstrip feed configuration facilitates integration into planar arrays with minimal additional components. Manufactured using the low-cost RF substrate RO3003 with a thickness of 3 mm, the design's characteristics were confirmed through measurements and simulations, revealing a gain of approximately 2.5 dBi across the frequency range. The efficiency of the antenna is primarily limited by the substrate's properties. Notably, the size of the antenna is small enough to be considered a microstrip patch antenna. The creation of a rectangular array composed of eight elements within this frequency range is also explored, with each element oriented for maximum gain in the broadside direction. The array's gain was found to be around 0.15 dBi higher than the single element gain, with a beamwidth of approximately 70 degrees. This gain increase can be attributed to the array factor, which also contributes to the widening of the beamwidth. The maximum gain achieved by the array is just over 2.7 dBi. The beam pattern of the array was found to be relatively symmetric. Given the simple design and low cost of production, these characteristics make this a suitable design for use in 5G array antennas operating at mm-waves. The creation of additional arrays with different shapes and configurations using the proposed microstrip patch antenna is also envisioned. Furthermore, the design's characteristics indicate its potential use as a sensor or as a component in the detection of aircraft. Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models. These models surpass previously published results, both in terms of efficiency and effectiveness, and could potentially be used in parallel to account for memory constraints, a major challenge in the application of reinforcement learning to quantum error correction. While applying RL to qubit decoding has some similarities to previous approaches using evolutionary or swarm intelligence methods, its application to topological codes like the surface code marks a significant breakthrough. Furthermore, the use of RL opens up new possibilities, such as improving decoding performance by modifying the underlying physical qubits, and could serve as a versatile platform for solving other complex CP-violating quantum problems. To facilitate further research, we provide a fully functional implementation of our method on GitHub. https://github.com/inglezios/rl_decoding_spc. Although primarily designed for surface coding, this approach can be adapted to other topological codes, such as the GKP or color codes, and could also be applied to other areas of CP-violating quantum physics. https://github.com/inglezios/rl_decoding_spc. The approach is shown to exceed the standard quantum precision limit, without needing highly complex quantum states and with greater scalability and practicality. In this hybrid digital-analog approach to quantum computing, any quantum algorithm can be implemented without traditional two-qubit gates by utilizing an inherent, always-active connection between qubits. Building on this principle, our research explores how digital-analog simulation can be used to study fermionic systems, specifically the Fermi-Hubbard model, using a fermionic SWAP network and a method to correct distortions. Focusing on the effects of qubit connectivity and the distribution of interaction coefficients, as well as the precision of entanglement-inducing operations, our results indicate that an optimal qubit connectivity arrangement for simulating fermionic systems of any dimensionality is a chain for systems without spin and a ladder for those with spin. This relatively straightforward connectivity arrangement makes the digital-analog method particularly appealing for fermionic quantum simulations. Moreover, to mitigate the impact of imperfect digital-analog conversion, we developed a small but effective correction protocol that utilizes two-qubit gates in a way that scales cubically with the system size. When incorporating this correction, the minimal requirements for the precision of digital-analog conversion become significantly stricter, but still within current technological limits. Our findings provide solid evidence that digital-analog computing can successfully simulate fermionic systems, and the proposed methods serve as valuable references for digital-analog simulation of quantum matter. A common issue in machine learning lies in striking a balance between optimizing model performance and its ability to generalize. Recent research has identified that initializing networks with simple, uniform representations can hinder optimization efficiency, although it may enhance generalizability. Conversely, initializing networks with complex, rich representations can facilitate faster optimization within a similar generalizability margin. We introduce a concept of 'richness' in network representations, characterized by high entropy in network parameters, and demonstrate through theoretical analysis and experimental results that it correlates with faster optimization and improved generalizability. We also provide a novel initialization method called Information Throughput, which measures entropy in network representations directly. Our results show that networks initialized with our method converge significantly faster and exhibit better generalizability compared to standard uniform initialization and other entropy-based methods. Furthermore, we observe that our method also improves the convergence rate of training networks with random labels, indicating its potential as an unsupervised preprocessing step. Achieving the formation of intricate structures and rapid concentration of light within or through disordered mediums is an arduous endeavor due to variations in refractive index, unpredictable light scattering, and speckle noise generation. To address these challenges, we've developed a novel weighted-mutation-assisted genetic algorithm (WMA-GA) with an R-squared-based fitness function that enhances image clarity, precision, and rapid convergence in forming complex structures within scattering media. As a companion technology to our binary WMA-GA system, we've designed a swift, economical, and reliable iterative wavefront manipulation system that utilizes an affordable ferroelectric liquid crystal (FLC)-based binary-phase spatial light modulator (SLM). This wavefront manipulation system enables the creation of numerous complex 3D heterostructures with an optimized single phase mask. We've verified the efficacy of our proposed approach with 120, 220, 450, and 600 grit ground glass diffusers, as well as with 323, 588, and 852 μm thick fresh chicken tissues including fluorescent properties. We've demonstrated the robustness of our proposed integrated system in controlling photon flow into and out of a localized fluorescent dye embedded in tissue. Detailed results reveal that our algorithm-driven integrated system achieves fast convergence and high image clarity with advanced resolution capabilities. We've also discovered that our 220 grit diffuser-based 3D structure exhibits the most exceptional image clarity with fine details. Importantly, we've successfully constructed intricate 3D tissue-like structures incorporating a fluorescent property originating from the chicken beak cuttlebone. To further validate the general applicability of our proposed approach, we've applied it to reconstructing 2D and 3D images contaminated by speckle noise, as well as to restoring damaged single lens focusing capability and reversing light propagation through 600 grit diffuser. These experiments demonstrate the versatility and efficacy of our WMA-GA-based integrated system in controlling photon flow into and out of complex optical media. Meta-analyses that include multiple trials based on shared study participants often report correlated effect sizes.  In such scenarios, employing cluster-robust variance estimators can effectively synthesize dependent effects, however these may produce inflated Type 1 errors in cases of a limited number of studies.  In order to improve the performance of robust estimators when dealing with small sample sizes, two new cluster-robust estimators have been developed.  Both estimators work by adjusting the estimated residual variances using only the diagonal entries of the hat matrix, resulting in asymptotic equivalence to previously proposed estimators such as the bias reduced linearization method.  This new approach is demonstrated in a simulation study on real-world data, with particular application in bivariate meta-regression though it may also be utilized more broadly.  The findings suggest the new estimators perform well in scenarios of limited data, with bias and variance significantly improved compared to the standard cluster-robust estimator and other alternative estimators.  To facilitate the use of these new estimators, accompanying R code is provided for implementation in meta-analyses and bivariate meta-regression analyses.  A practical example using actual data highlights the utility of the proposed approach.  This approach may be particularly beneficial in publication bias assessments where instrumental variables are used through the use of the Eisenclayr test.  The test allows for efficient assessment of bias by utilizing available data, with results indicating minimal bias in practical scenarios.  However bias may occur under specific conditions such as a limited number of studies and the presence of leptokurtic distributions.  To address this bias, the proposed approach includes the use of bias correction to efficiently utilize available data and effectively detect publication bias. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We have successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm has been integrated into the open-source CFD code OpenFOAM and validated through a series of simulations including turbulent sedimentation, granular flow, and fluidized beds. Our approach has yielded reliable results with significant time savings of up to 4 orders of magnitude compared to traditional methods. Research has found that particle radiation is not a product of gravitational force-driven pair creation, but rather an outcome stemming from disparities in the laws governing particle number definition. In the far distant future, the source of emitted energy corresponds to zero-point fluctuations characterized by exponentially large wave numbers. To rectify the inherent inconsistencies of traditional particle number definition, this work proposes an improved number definition, S-defined, derivative of the K-defined number, previously found to satisfy conservation laws. Research has found that, unlike conventional approaches, the S-defined number can accurately account for the negative energy of virtual particles, zero-point fluctuations, and even predict the right order of magnitude for Unruh/Hawking radiation energy. This work directly links the positive energy of real particles to the negative energy of virtual particles, further refining our understanding of particle number definition and correcting related misconceptions. It ultimately indicates that the thermodynamic properties of black holes are rooted in the inherent flaws of traditional particle number definition rather than an inherent property of black holes themselves. By advocating for the S-defined number, this research may open doors for improved quantum field theories in both flat spacetime and curved spacetime environments.
