Finally, the theoretical framework of quantum gravity could be the ultimate beneficiary of correcting the traditional particle number definition. In particular, the concept of fiducial state may serve as a valuable tool for detecting the prediction of quantum gravity - the gravitational pair creation of particles. It potentially offers an innovative method for the non-perturbative analysis of quantum gravity. This sheath plays a significant role in the dynamic behavior of the jet and its penetration into the stream. Additionally, we examine the instability effects that develop on the liquid jet and the consequences of these effects on its behavior in the context of fluid dynamics. These findings have significant implications for our understanding of various hydrodynamic phenomena. This analysis holds important insights for researchers working in the field of material science, engineering, and physics. This model helps us understand the steady-state condition of the jet and the stability of its configuration through a series of numerical calculations and analytical expressions. High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault tolerance to prevent data loss and ensure system reliability. Recent advances in non-volatile memory have made it feasible to achieve fault tolerance using check-pointing with minimal performance overhead. However, the frequent check-pointing required to cover all possible failure scenarios leads to a high number of data movements, which can be problematic when combined with poor network architecture. In this paper, a new model called NVM-FLV is presented, focusing on the effects of network congestion during check-pointing. NVM-FLV evaluates different network congestion awareness strategies at two distinct levels: network device and software application. The model underlies a comprehensive empirical study which compares the performance of three different network congestion awareness strategies, including network-based and software-based approaches, in relation to various network congestion scenarios. The study examines NVM-FLV under two different communication patterns, serial and parallel, and assesses the impact of network congestion on system performance. The results show that even minor network congestion can compromise the effectiveness of NVM-FLV, but network-based awareness strategies perform better than their software-based counterparts. Furthermore, the benefits of check-pointing are largely dependent on the network configuration and specific application. A significant gap in performance was observed between different network congestion cases, ranging from minimal to severe. The research offers valuable insights for developers of high-performance computing applications, suggesting that a hybrid approach to awareness strategies could provide a better balance between cost and effectiveness. The model underlying NVM-FLV can be utilized as a benchmark to evaluate the performance of future network devices, devices under development, and novel hardware technologies. The research provides novel insights into the behavior of checkpointing operations, revealing an unexpected correlation between network congestion and system performance, as well as a surprising relationship between the cost of check-pointing and system reliability. The results can be utilized to inform decisions regarding system design, network architecture, and application development. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. This approach reveals the underlying structure of a network, allowing for the grouping of related documents and words within cohesive topics and subtopics, and as such, it holds significant potential for the classification and summarization of large networks. You can apply this model to your own data by downloading our implementation from https://github.com/jvpts/hdtm. In addition to the implementation, we provide a detailed documentation on how to train and evaluate HDTM. As a testament to its effectiveness, our model performs comparably with more advanced approaches when used on standard benchmark datasets. At the time of writing, HDTM is one of the few hierarchical topic modeling methods capable of operating at large data scales. You can find more information and updated material on our project homepage at http://jvpts.github.io/hdtm. We are confident that HDTM will be a valuable tool for the discovery of information networks and the detailed study of large corpora. In the near future, we plan to expand upon this work by incorporating graphical models and utilizing this framework to tackle more challenging information discovery problems. Ultimately, we aim to utilize this framework for the detailed analysis of Wikipedia's full content and the discovery of its underlying structure. With the continued growth of Wikipedia and the increasing accessibility of computational power, we believe that this problem presents an opportunity for significant contributions to the fields of computer science and Wikipedia research. By running and analyzing one million simulations for diverse initial conditions, both with and without equal masses in three-body systems, we were able to achieve precise statistical accuracy. Four key measures were used to characterize the distribution of ergodic disintegrations: the probability of escape for individual bodies, the exponent representing narrow escapes, the predicted absorption rates, and the distribution of binary system eccentricities. Our results showed that escape probabilities matched theoretical predictions with high precision, marking a significant improvement over previous statistical theories. Furthermore, the measured values of the exponent representing narrow escapes were in line with a previously proposed value of 1/2. Our findings on absorption rates aligned closely with existing data, and the shape of the binary system eccentricity distribution was found to be dependent on the distribution of initial velocities and consistent with existing knowledge. These results provide comprehensive support for statistical models of star-disintegrating three-body systems, offering valuable insights into the dynamics of such systems and their implications for the detection of gravitational waves. We propose an arrangement of predicates in continuous logic such that the
logical framework's meaning can be structured within a hyperdoctrine framework.
This hyperdoctrine can be incorporated into a hyperdoctrine representing subobjects within a suitable category of topological structures. 
To achieve this incorporation, we first simplify the hyperdoctrine framework for continuous logic and establish an equivalence between its category of equivalence relations and that of complete metric spaces under uniform mappings. 
Next, we introduce a suitable notion of subobject in this context and incorporate the resulting hyperdoctrine of continuous logic within the hyperdoctrine of subobjects within the category of complete metric spaces. 
This incorporation is facilitated by the representation of predicates as subobjects, which in turn enables the representation of sentences as appropriate equalizers of subobjects. 
This approach allows for the first-order part of continuous logic to be represented within a suitable category of algebraic fractions, where the representability of sentences is akin to that in first-order logic with ordered algebraic fields. 
This result generalizes and combines previously introduced notions of representability in first-order and continuous logic. 
In addition, we show that any predicate class in continuous logic is necessarily homogeneous and that the representability of a sentence is unchanged under uniform mappings.

A new technique is proposed to forecast suicidal ideation based on the integration of Electronic Health Records and Ecological Momentary Assessment data utilizing advanced deep sequential models. These datasets consist of asynchronous, variable-length, randomly sampled sequences which are modelled separately using Recurrent Neural Networks and combined through the alignment of hidden states, along with attention and pre-training schemes to handle differing sequence lengths. Experimental outcomes using 1023 patients' data from the University of Pennsylvania Patient Self-Report Surveillance system, reveal that the incorporation of EMA records increases the recall and precision of predictions of suicidal ideation from Electronic Health Records, with a 6% improvement in F1-score. Furthermore, clinical evaluation indicates that individualized risk assessments from our method and EHR-based machine learning models exhibit strong correlation, with a 0.78 correlation coefficient observed. These findings underscore the potential of Deep Sequential Models in the coordinated forecasting of suicidal ideation from disparate healthcare data streams. Our research reports a significant $\sim 5\sigma$ discovery of polarized X-ray emission within a range of 3-6 keV originating from Cassiopeia A with the IXPE. Our findings reveal a combined polarization level of $1.8 \pm 0.3$%, obtained after summing the polarization vectors from a large region, under the assumption of circular symmetry. Analysis of the synchrotron radiation suggests an average polarization level of $\sim 2.5$%, while the forward shock region indicates a nearly 5% polarization. Our model considers both thermal and non-thermal radiation contributions using detailed Chandra data for a spatial-spectral analysis. Our individual pixel analysis reveals numerous polarization detections above a $3\sigma$ confidence level and indicates a significant non-thermal radiation component in the mixed non-thermal emission band. Our analysis reveals a total non-thermal energy of $\sim 3.3 \times 10^{51}$ erg within this band, which suggests that the shock wave's energy loss is predominately caused by the synchrotron radiation. In this work, we employ a technique called skeletonization to extract the fundamental information needed to represent their geometry. By applying a modified version of a previous approach that efficiently captures the dynamics of multi-component flows with distinct interfaces, we successfully simplify the complex geometry of a droplet undergoing splashing. Our findings demonstrate that the resulting framework is versatile and capable of general application to various gas-liquid interfaces, including those influenced by gravity and buoyancy. In addition, we have implemented a novel method to evaluate the effectiveness of our simplified models, which we used to study a droplet passing through a fluid stream and accurately compare its behavior with real-world observations. In contrast to previous numerical simulations, our approach has the added benefit of allowing us to determine the extent to which the resulting interface is influenced by the presence of the skeleton. This enables the option to adjust the model to better represent situations where the interface is in close proximity to the skeleton. In one such instance, we observed a droplet that was successfully passed through a narrow conduit without interacting with the surrounding skeleton, which we hypothesize could be applied to targeting medications within cells. In another example, we found that a droplet was successfully merged with a nearby fluid stream through the interaction with our simplified model. These experiments not only validate the efficacy of our approach but also provide new insights into the various applications of fluid dynamics. Researchers discovered that certain influenza viruses exhibit active movement on surfaces with carbohydrate layers by rolling along them, as shown in recent studies. This phenomenon was previously proposed to be an example of viral surface metabolism, where the collection of spike proteins interacts with the carbohydrates, generating mechanical movement through a self-organizing process. This research aims to investigate in greater detail the physical aspects underlying this rolling motion, developing a theory that explains the motor's behavior, as well as validating the results using simulations to analyze the impact of various factors. The outcomes of this study strongly indicate that viral movement on surfaces is statistically certain to occur when the virus exhibits enzymatic activity. Additionally, the research found that viral parameters are sensitive to the physical characteristics of the surrounding environment, including factors like viscosity and surface stiffness. This information could be exploited to disable viral movement by modifying external conditions, offering a promising new approach to combating infectious diseases caused by influenza and potentially other viruses. We examined over 8,000 massive, edge-on disk galaxies from the SDSS dataset, focusing on two types: S and U galaxies. Our analysis revealed that U galaxies have distinct characteristics, including bluer optical colors and higher star formation rates, compared to S galaxies. U galaxies, particularly those with more extreme warping, exhibited higher star formation rates. Contrary to expectations, U galaxies in groups and clusters do not show a correlation with the tidal force exerted by their nearest neighbor. However, U galaxies are more common in groups and clusters and share similarities with 'jellyfish' galaxies formed through ram-pressure stripping (RPS). This led us to suggest that RPS could be a potential mechanism explaining the presence of U galaxies in groups and clusters. Their star formation properties, however, differ significantly, with U galaxies exhibiting lower star formation rates compared to jellyfish galaxies. Our findings imply that star formation is slowed in U galaxies soon after they become warped, possibly due to an internal mechanism. If RPS is responsible for their warping, it is ineffective in enhancing star formation in these galaxies. Our research also highlights the importance of observing U galaxies form through new star formations, which could provide insights into their origin. Our analysis further showed that U galaxies with bar features tend to have inner disk features, which could be influenced by a bar. Our findings, however, do not suggest that a bar causes warping in U galaxies. Our study, for the first instance, compared U galaxies with jellyfish galaxies and revealed distinct differences in their color and star formation characteristics. Our research also explored the relationship between U galaxies and the large-scale structure of the universe, focusing specifically on clusters, groups, and the field regions. Our data indicates that U galaxies are more common in groups and clusters but not as common as expected. Our findings, however, suggest that U galaxies found in these regions could be affected by a stripping process. Our research, for the first time, thoroughly analyzed U galaxies found in the field regions, where they were found to have lower star formation rates and bluer colors. Our data suggests that U galaxies in these regions could be different from S galaxies with similar characteristics. Our research, however, is still unsure if these U galaxies in these regions could be affected by a stripping process. Our study, for the first time, compared S and U galaxies in different environments, focusing on their mass, which suggested that U galaxies could be more common in high-mass environments. Our research, however, needs more data to confirm these results.

By adapting established techniques to reason about high-level probabilistic code, this study achieves a breakthrough in linking operational and denotational views with a proven adequacy theorem, thereby closing a key outstanding issue identified in earlier work (Bacci et al., 2018). Our results are further generalized to cover a range of higher-order probabilistic programming languages through the application of final coalgebras, as well as by utilizing a cut-free relational proof system based on the Curry-Howard correspondence. As a practical outcome, this investigation yields a clear, effective method for proving adequacy of compiler targets for such languages. Specifically, we define a stochastic compiler for the higher-order probabilistic pushdown automata studied in Caires et al. (2019) and demonstrate its compiler target is adequately represented by a while-language with random access to a stack. As an additional application, we use our framework to establish adequacy of a compiler for an imperative probabilistic tail-recursion marker, as initially proposed in Harlow (2019). While the latter part of this study does not rely on the stochastic lambda calculus, it benefits significantly from our previous results, as it leverages our established definitions and proof techniques to tackle an imperative version of the noted paper's key problem. In turn, solving this problem allows us to extend the main result of Caires et al. (2019), as it concerns the probabilistic analysis of higher-order pushdown automata, by demonstrating that the high-level probabilistic code can be effectively translated into a low-level probabilistic assembly code. Hence, alternative and potentially more efficient design choices for compiler targets and their respective time and space bounds are advocated for specific measurable probabilistic programming languages, as exemplified by the MSVC. Discussions among developers encompass a variety of interactions, including in-person conversations and online comments.  They are an invaluable source of information about software development, containing insights from experts who may not otherwise be documented.  Design mining is an emerging approach that involves analyzing discussions to better understand designers' thoughts and plans.  While design mining has been applied to various domains, its potential for improving software design is largely unexplored.  This paper outlines a design mining framework tailored to software design, with a specific focus on how requirements are shaped through discussions.  We also present initial findings from a study of this nature, involving the analysis of over 2000 online comments related to software requirements.  So far, our results indicate that design mining can be a useful tool for discovering new requirements, gaining insights into designers' thoughts, and providing references for future design work.  However, our analysis also reveals that online comments often lack essential context, leading to difficulty in fully understanding the resulting requirements.  Future work could focus on addressing this issue by incorporating more contextual information or using more sophisticated analytical techniques.  Ultimately, our goal is to establish design mining as a valuable method for enhancing software design, whether used independently or in conjunction with other design approaches. A major uncertainty in determining the initial mass function of the first (Population III) stars hinges on the ultimate fate of secondary protostars that form in the accretion disk - whether they will merge or remain separate. We focus on how the initial star formation was influenced by magnetic effects in a cosmological setting with existing magnetic fields. We conducted a series of simulations of magnetohydrodynamics, running up to 1000 years following the initial protostar formation. To represent the protostars and their magnetic field structures, we utilized a stiff equation of state approach instead of the conventional sink particle technique. Ten years after the initial protostar formation, we observed an amplification in magnetic field strength from picogauss to kilogauss in the region around protostars, matching that of contemporary stars. Due to the rapid orbital rotations in the vicinity of protostars, their magnetic field becomes increasingly wound up over the initial decade of protostar formation. As mass accretion proceeds, the area where the magnetic field plays a crucial role in determining protostar formation's outcome shrinks. In our simulations, we see that when we include early cosmic reionization, which causes ionization to occur before the initial decade, fragmentation of the disk develops under certain conditions, leading to separate protostars. However, when we consider late cosmic reionization, the magnetic field's effect on protostar formation is minimal. Our findings, though, are contingent on a high amplification of the magnetic field from early cosmic structures, which we verify through separate cosmological simulations. In contrast, if early cosmic structures do not significantly amplify magnetic field strength, our results suggest that separate protostar formation is unlikely to occur. Thus, we maintain that Population III binary formation is unlikely. In a series of subsequent simulations, we observed that as protostars' mass accretion continues, their magnetic field further amplifies, eventually reaching a point where it prevents the merger of secondary protostars within their accretion disk. Consequently, we see the emergence of low-mass Population II binary stars in a high-mass ratio. In a series of cosmological simulations, we saw that this trend applies to many (but not all) instances of early cosmic reionization. Our analysis is accompanied by several numerical simulations to gauge the performance of these estimators. Achieving dependable data privacy while ensuring data utility is an intricate problem in various real-world applications. To address this issue, a novel framework known as One-Sided Differential Privacy (OSDP) has been developed. OSDP enhances data utility by recognizing that not every data record contains sensitive information. The main challenge hindering the advancement of integrated gallium nitride electronics lies in its low hole mobility. In our investigation, we consider whether the mobility of gallium nitride can be enhanced through epitaxial strain from a template material. We performed detailed computations utilizing the ab initio Boltzmann transport equation to calculate the hole mobility of bulk gallium nitride under various strains. Our results indicate that applying uniaxial compressive strain to gallium nitride significantly alters its hole energy bands, increasing its mobility by a factor of two when compared to unbiased material. However, only strain-matched growth with certain nitride materials applies such strain to gallium nitride, resulting in acceptable but not exceptional transport properties. Nonetheless, combining strain with other mobility-modifying mechanisms could potentially enhance gallium nitride's transport properties for use in high-electron-mobility field-effect transistors. Finally, our study includes a discussion of the underlying physics governing the strain-induced changes in gallium nitride's transport properties.

This note enhances and reinforces Bates' theorem which indicates that for row-finite graphs classified as strong shift equivalent, their associated graph C*-algebras are also Morita equivalent. This discovery opens up possibilities to investigate if the stronger notion of Morita equivalence effectively describes strong shift equivalence. This line of inquiry will likely hold significant value for ongoing research regarding infinite graphs and their associated C*-algebras. Moreover, this note specifically explores insplits and outsplits as key examples of strong shift equivalences, demonstrating that these equivalences lead to Morita equivalences that maintain consistency across various weighted gauge actions. Consequently, a question is raised about whether strong shift equivalence can be expressed as a product of insplits and outsplits. Finally, the note briefly discusses K-theory's behavior under strong shift equivalence, incorporating graphs with $K_0$-algebra of $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{5}]\oplus\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{5}]$ as a primary case focus. This investigation promotes the hypothesis that strong shift equivalence effectively describes Morita equivalence, provided that the graphs in question possess a weight-rigid property. If proven, this hypothesis would significantly impact the relationship between strong shift equivalence and Morita equivalence, thereby simplifying the process of establishing Morita equivalences from weaker notions like topological Morita equivalence and ordered Morita equivalence. Moreover, the hypothesis raises additional speculation that perhaps the only underlying cause of Morita equivalence in graph C*-algebras is the presence of a weighted gauge action, thereby promoting gauge equivalence as a primary means of comparing these graph C*-algebras. Ultimately, the hope is that the relationships identified in this note will contribute meaningfully to ongoing research in graph C*-algebras and their associated weighted actions. Moreover, the focus on K-theory behavior under strong shift equivalence positions this research to potentially benefit from future discoveries in both graph theory and algebraic topology. As a concrete example, the C*-algebras generated from the graphs K_0 and K_1 exhibit identical K_0-algebra properties but differ in their 1-dimensional Hilbert space projections, demonstrating the necessity of additional technical considerations beyond gauge equivalence to define Morita equivalence. In this research, we have examined the complex aspect of the Heavy Quark potential, focusing on its dissociation at high temperatures and strong magnetic fields. Our work builds upon previous studies by introducing three distinct features: comprehensive calculations of Landau levels, a novel gauge boson propagator in a magnetized plasma, and an intricate, direction-dependent heavy quark potential. To showcase our advancements, we have generated detailed visualizations, such as heavy quark potential tomography and dissociation probability diagrams, at various temperature and magnetic field conditions. Interestingly, in a high magnetic field environment, the heavy quark potential exhibits unique anisotropic spacing characteristics. Moreover, the heavy quark potential exhibits a complex, entwined structure in isothermal conditions. Furthermore, the heavy quark dissociation probability displays a complex, multi-faceted structure as well. These groundbreaking findings provide profound insights into the intricate nature of heavy quark potential, thereby encouraging further research in related topics. Our study's methods and results provide a reference point for the Platini process, where the Platini quark is a composite of a top quark and antiquark, present in a magnetized plasma. Our findings suggest the possible appearance of a momentum-dependent mass for the Platini quark. Moreover, the dissociation probability calculations for the $t\bar{t}$ and $\psi(2S)$ states in a magnetized plasma at various temperature and magnetic field conditions have been determined, demonstrating the significant influence of the magnetic field on such processes. Our study's results provides reference data for future theoretical and experimental research in related topics. Additionally, the heavy quark potential and dissociation probability results for the $b\bar{b}$ state in a magnetized plasma at the conformal phase transition temperature have been determined, suggesting the heavy quark quark regime may not be reachable in a magnetized plasma. Our study's results provides fundamental advancements in the understanding of heavy quark physics in a magnetized plasma at finite temperature. Our work is expected to encourage further theoretical and experimental research in related topics. To facilitate such research, the associated numerical data has been made accessible on GitHub. Moreover, the heavy quark potential and dissociation probability results for the $c\bar{c}$ state in a magnetized plasma at the QCD phase transition temperature has been determined, suggesting the heavy quark quark regime may not be reachable in a magnetized plasma. To effectively answer complex questions, large language models need information about specific entities, but can't store all necessary knowledge themselves. To compensate, they rely on external sources of information, like knowledge graphs, which provide a framework for organizing and connecting data. In this research, we explore ways to incorporate knowledge graph information into language models, with a specific focus on open-domain question answering. By using embeddings based on graph structures, we can highlight important node connections that are relevant to both question and answer, but may not be immediately apparent. By integrating these embeddings with language models, we can enhance their ability to find accurate answers. We conducted experiments using multiple datasets and found that this new approach leads to better results, which can serve as a foundation for future improvements. Additionally, we can use this method to identify key parts of the knowledge graph that are particularly important for solving particular questions, which can help to reduce the size and complexity of the graph without compromising its usefulness. This ability to filter and refine the knowledge graph based on actual performance makes it a valuable tool for improving how language models use and rely on external knowledge sources. In this research, we examined the relationship between language models and their sources of information, and explored ways to more effectively utilize those sources, which may also have implications for how language models use and rely on other external sources of information, like databases and sensors. In the future, we plan to incorporate sensory data into our knowledge graph embeddings as well, in order to further improve language model performance and capabilities. In addition to improving language model performance, this research also demonstrates the potential of incorporating knowledge graph structures into language models, which could have a range of other benefits, including the ability to explain model choices and decisions, identify and mitigate bias, and improve communication about model limitations and capabilities. In particular, we suggest that one useful way to improve model explanations is to use the embeddings to identify the key parts of the knowledge graph that are most relevant to the model's choices and decisions, which can serve as a foundation for developing new, graph-based methods for explaining model behavior. In addition to our primary results, we also conducted a range of additional experiments and analyses to better understand how language models use and rely on external knowledge sources, including a detailed ablation study of our novel approach, as well as a more in-depth examination of its key components and variations. These additional studies and analyses allow us to better understand and explore the complex relationship between language models and their sources of information, which will likely continue to be an important and promising area of research in the future

We have developed a novel method of constructing high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of simplicial complexes. Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a vital role in theoretical computer science but unfortunately, there are only a few constructions available that offer arbitrarily small local spectral expansion.

Our research involves presenting a probabilistic algorithm that takes an input high dimensional expander X and generates a sub-complex Y, also a high dimensional expander with infinite covers of bounded-degree simplicial complexes. The generated Y preserves Y's graph structure, spectral properties, and geometric properties with a high degree of accuracy. The program also accepts parameters that control for deviations from these properties. 

Our program is inspired by the Lipton-Solovay uniformization principle and resembles a quantum algorithm described in [Arora et al.'22]. Though our algorithm randomly selects Y from all possible high dimensional expanders with 4 vertices, it can also be modified to work deterministically with specific properties. 

We apply our program to the hypergrah H_3 and show it can be transformed into a high dimensional expander with a geometric property known as quasi-embeddability, assuming H_3 does not have a certain extension. Lastly, we provide a novel proof that shows a quasi-embeddability of H_3 would imply a negative solution to a long-standing open problem in quantum logic known as the dichotomy conjecture. 

Our method reveals connections between the field of operator algebras and the study of high dimensional expanders, offering new insights and perspectives. Specifically, we apply our program to the finite coherent logic CoherentMatch, reveal a hidden relationship between its semantic spaces and the covers of high dimensional expanders, and demonstrate that a quasi-embeddability of CoherentMatch would imply a negative solution to a hard open problem in finite proof theory known as the dichotomy conjecture.

We have computed the Benois $\mathscr{L}$-invariants for weight one cuspforms and their corresponding adjoint representations. Furthermore, our calculations extend Gross' $p$-adic regulator to non-critical Artin motives, which aligns with Deligne's framework. The construction proposed by Benois hinges on the selection of a regular submodule. When the representation is $p$-regular, choosing such a submodule is analogous to selecting a'motivic' $p$-refinement, making the process fairly intuitive. However, when the representation is $p$-irregular, things become more intricate as regular submodules are categorized by a flag variety, resulting in an abundance of choices that involve continuous parameters. Despite these complications, our analysis in select examples highlights how Hida theory and eigencurve geometry can facilitate the identification of a limited set of choices that possess notable arithmetic and'mixed-motivic' significance. Our work is made more coherent by the observation that the $\mathscr{L}$-invariants of degree $p$-irregular representations can be related to the $p$-adic height of an algebraic curve, which is itself an example of an algebraic motive. This connection to algebraic geometry provides further support for the'arithmetic'motivic perspective suggested by Deligne. Finally, as part of our work, we found and proved a novel theorem describing the relationship between the weights of certain cuspforms on eigencurves and their distribution, which may hold independent arithmetical significance. This theorem could be seen as a minor precursor to more substantial results that might be derived from the principles of'motivic Galois representations.' Consequently, our work could be viewed as an instance of'motivic influence in arithmetic context,' which in turn reflects the'motivic influence in Galois context' described by Serre. As a byproduct of our research, we gained further insight into the architecture of certain eigencurves, which are characterized by cuspforms whose weights become arbitrarily negative. This gain in understanding makes our work relevant to questions initially posed by Serre and later addressed by Fakhruddin and Harpaz. Our analysis in this matter reveals that for nearly all cases, cuspforms whose levels become arbitrarily low still possess a limited number of possible $p$-refinements, which are determined solely by their weight. UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparison with four other spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. Instead, the extreme star formation is primarily a result of the smooth distribution of stars in the galaxy's outer rim. The relatively low surface density in this region enables the formation of gas clouds with minimal potential energy, promoting the onset of star formation. Compared to other spiral galaxies, the HII region in UGC 8839 is distinguished by its lower surface density and proximity to the galaxy's center, highlighting a correlation between stable dark matter halos and the appearance of young stars near galaxy centers. Possibly, the HII region in UGC 8839 is an example of a "nurse cloud" that's feeding the broader star formation in the galaxy. The relatively high gas fraction in the HII region might also be the source of its young stars' extreme off-axis location, provided the stars formed farther inward and then diffused to their current position through dynamical forces. UGC 8839 offers an uncommon opportunity to observe a "fossil record" of galaxy evolution, suggesting that stable, dark matter-dominated disks can persist for extended periods and perhaps even protect the stars within them. If proven to be representative, this finding could challenge current theories of galaxy evolution, potentially linking low-surface-brightness galaxies to those with galactic fountains or other mechanisms promoting the continuous circulation of gas within the disks. Conversely, UGC 8839 could be an isolated example, requiring further observation of similar galaxies to confirm its status as a high-risk precursor to major star formation in the broader BSB population. Recent breakthroughs in audio generation through visual stimulation involve selecting short, low-quality sounds and using sampling-based methods. However, current models using top-notch graphics processing units can still take several minutes to sample one second of audio. Our approach presents a unified model able to produce visually relevant high-fidelity sounds and generate these in under the time it takes for audio playback on a high-end graphics processing unit. We train a transformer that draws upon a codebook obtained from a variant of VQGAN optimized to produce compact spectral samples and utilizes a novel spectrogram-based quality measure. These spectral samples are transformed into waveforms using a window-based generator, which significantly enhances the generation speed. Since there are limited tools for automatically assessing the quality of synthesized soundscapes, we introduce FID and MKL, a family of metrics relying on Melception, a novel audio classification model designed to evaluate the authenticity and relevance of synthesized soundscapes. Our results showcase the efficacy of this new method in both small-scale and large-scale datasets and reveal a notable enhancement in audio quality, file size, and processing time. A demo, the codebase, and generated samples are available at v-iashin.github.io/SpecVQGAN. Our approach presents a versatile technique for visual audio synthesis that can serve as a robust alternative to VQGAN and inspire future research in audio generation. Moreover, our method facilitates unsupervised soundtrack creation from graphic novels, as well as audio effects that are conditional upon transcribed speech. Moreover, its spectrally conditioned context allows it to be used in audio remixing and synthesis. The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue: understanding the influence of data quality on training. The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples serves as a theoretical framework, however current methods are primarily limited to non-interactive machine learning models. The absence of a scalable solution for interactive models like Transformer-based models and graph neural networks has hindered the practical implementation of Shapley value computation. We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks are more effectively modeled as hypergraphs, yet their associated datasets are often presented as projected graphs. To better comprehend this phenomenon, we establish a theoretical framework to examine its underlying principles and worst-case scenarios. This framework informs our proposal of supervised hypergraph reconstruction, a novel task aimed at recovering a real-world hypergraph from its graph projection using domain-specific knowledge. To achieve this, we develop a method that involves two components: first, a sampling strategy is employed to significantly reduce the large number of potential hyperedges; second, a hyperedge classifier with two optimized variants is designed to identify candidate hyperedges based on their structural properties in the graph projection. Our experiments validate the efficacy of our approach and its extensions, with impressive results that outperform baseline methods by a significant margin in accuracy, particularly on difficult datasets. Our implementation and data are freely available for download. Furthermore, we release a benchmark dataset consisting of 7 real-world hypergraphs and their graph projections, which can be used as a reference point for future research. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time such a dataset has been published. Our research is the first to tackle the problem of supervised hypergraph reconstruction, with promising results that indicate the effectiveness of our approach. While there is room for improvement, we aim to address the currently prevalent challenge of analyzing real-world hypergraphs and provide a valuable resource for future researchers in this field. We propose an advanced concept for measuring directional emission in microcavity lasers. Initially, entropy in the polar far-field profile effectively gauges the degree of unidirectional light release, outperforming previous methods which struggle with variation. Secondly, we introduce a phenomenological angle for measuring emission directionality, but its practical application is limited to straightforward cases due to the inability to handle complex structures. Conversely, entropy based on semi-marginal probability in the Cartesian coordinate achieves comparable results and is also adaptable to emissions with complex structures. Using these measures, we calculate the threshold behavior of unidirectional emission and demonstrate that our entropy based on semi-marginal probability can be mathematically derived from the traditional method. We apply these concepts to study emission directionality in a planar structure microcavity and investigate the impact of introducing a waveguide. The outcomes reveal a feasible approach for designing microcavity lasers which not only achieve high beam quality but also are compatible with integrated photonic systems. Moreover, our work may inspire new research into calculating emission directionality based on probability distribution and its potential applications in photonic engineering. The associated source code can be accessed at: https://github.com/Linlinpeng/QD-MC-Laser-Emission-Directionality. The simulation data for emission directionality versus photon density for our proposed entropy angle approach and semi-marginal probability approach are provided in the reference file. Our findings provide concrete evidence for the stability of cryptocurrencies as a medium of exchange. Between 2016 and 2020, the prices of major cryptocurrencies remained steady when compared to other significant financial assets. After isolating shorter price fluctuations lasting less than a month, we analyzed the daily returns in US dollars of leading cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Ripple, alongside their respective counterparts – the Euro and Japanese yen, and major stock indexes, the S&P 500 and MSCI World Index. To evaluate the stability of filtered daily returns, we applied three distinct measures. Firstly, the Pearson correlation coefficients between the analyzed periods showed a notable increase in later years of our study. Secondly, the results of our dynamic time-warping analysis, which permits both leads and lags in relation analysis, demonstrated the existence of similarities in daily returns among cryptocurrencies and their comparators as far back as 2016. Finally, our investigation involved assessing whether cumulative errors in predicting cryptocurrency prices would fall within the predicted bounds as dictated by the Black-Scholes model when considering stable relationships with comparators' daily returns, resulting in a significant surplus – our data shows a 4.35% surplus in 2020, equivalent to a 14.65% premium in predicted error margins for cryptocurrencies compared to their comparators. To rule out potential biases stemming from differing stability measures, we repeated our analysis using alternative models including the GARCH, Bollinger Bands, and a general linear model, yielding consistent outcomes. Furthermore, we utilized the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test to verify the normality of daily returns in cryptocurrencies and their comparators – our data shows normal distribution for leading cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin and Ethereum. Our research identifies the weekly price fluctuation cycle, lasting around a week, in cryptocurrencies as consistent with similar patterns observed in their comparators. By integrating analytical methods including field theory, probability and integrability, we resolve the large deviation issue of the KPZ equation at early time periods. Expanding the existing weak noise theory, which reformulates large deviations into a nonlinear hydrodynamics problem, we reveal its complete solvability through a link with the integrability of the Zakharov-Shabat system. Employing the inverse scattering technique and a newly developed Fredholm determinant framework, we arrive at exact solutions that depend on the specific initial conditions of the KPZ equation, allowing for further generalization to other initial conditions. This framework is further applied to the random energy model and the directed polymer with a KPZ equation to obtain exact large deviation results, solvable via the same integrability methods. We then demonstrate that these results match well with existing numerical simulations and theoretical analyses. Additionally, we explore the scaling behavior of the underlying solutions and other associated zero-level set solutions, which corresponds with the scaling hypothesis for the KPZ equation. As a byproduct of our analysis, we derive exact solutions to a time-dependent nonlinear hydrodynamics problem, which may also be relevant to other physical models such as the CPFP model and the BESRP model. We then establish that the large deviation behavior of the random energy model and the directed polymer with a KPZ equation differ only by a specific reparameterization of time, which reflects a longstanding observational analogy between these two models. Our study thus far has only addressed large deviations related to the height of the growing interface, but we extend our results to derive large deviation solutions for growing interface velocities and relate them to solutions of a modified nonlinear hydrodynamics problem. Finally, we reflect on the significant implications of our findings, which involve connections between mathematical methods and physical models, as well as the potential for our large deviation solutions to influence future research in the field of statistical mechanics. Moreover, our analysis highlights the inherent relationships in statistical mechanics between thermodynamic zero-level set solutions, which are solvable via the same integrability methods, as well as the potential for large deviation solutions to provide new insights into critical scaling behaviors of the KPZ equation and other related models. Due to space constraints, many of the supporting mathematical proofs and additional analytical details are presented in two companion papers. We hope that our study may serve as a blueprint for future research in the field of statistical mechanics, which can be adapted to address analogous statistical mechanics issues in biophysical models of membrane curvature and related membrane-related statistical mechanics problems. A mathematical model examining the impact of turbulence on a stratified flow is investigated, incorporating eddy coefficients that influence viscosity but neglect those affecting diffusivity. By combining both vertical and horizontal viscosity factors, a fourth-order Taylor-Goldstein differential equation arises to describe vertical velocity perturbations, reducing to a modified equation when only the latter factor is considered under inviscid conditions. Assuming that key parameters are slowly changing, geometrical and physical approximations are explored for this modified equation using the WKB method near critical levels and singularities, including turning points. These approximations lead to four-type singular junctions with solutions behaving differently near these singularities and critical levels. When comparing numerical solutions with WKB approximations, excellent agreement is found, particularly in determining turning point locations, which in turn calculates the width of phases with opposing fluxes. Numerical outcomes also demonstrate that as Rayleigh numbers increase, phase widths decrease and eventually vanish. However, for a given Rayleigh number, larger parameters result in narrower phases; this behavior is independently confirmed by WKB approximations. These findings suggest that phases may emerge only under a specific criterion defined by the parameter relationship. This research provides a mathematical framework and analytical solutions to understand non-oscillatory phases in a visco-oscillatory stratified fluid. It notably illustrates a perfect agreement between numerical and analytical outcomes for a difficult problem, as well as shows the ability to determine key parameters without numerical solutions, saving computational time and effort. This study also provides new analytical solutions for a modified equation and applies the WKB method near critical levels and singularities for both this and the original equations. Furthermore, it confirms that the modified equation can accurately predict turning point locations and phase widths with equivalent precision to numerical solutions, indicating its value in modeling buoyancy-driven flows. These outcomes have significant implications for studying similar problems involving both stratified fluids and modified buoyancy-driven flows. It is worth noting that this research would be suitable for advanced undergraduate or graduate students familiar with assemblage and series methods, but may require additional background study in this and related topics for a thorough comprehension. The direction-aware GHOG descriptor weights importance equally or unevenly across 8 equally spaced direction bins. It utilizes a direction-oriented descriptor, derived from Harris-Laplace corners, to focus on corners or edges by equally or unequally allocating importance to 8 direction bins. The optimized direction-aware GHOG descriptor is used to extract features from both target and reference images. The descriptor's direction orientation parameters are adjusted to best fit the pattern fabric fabric through correlation analysis, following feature extraction. The simplified direction-aware GHOG descriptor is used to classify images as defect or normal. Experimental results show that this method outperforms traditional techniques using incomplete or partial datasets. It also shows potential to automatically identify defect types, but this requires a full dataset of known defect types. Two novel defect type inference algorithms are introduced to overcome the lack of complete dataset. The first type inference algorithm uses a module-based approach to learn and combine multiple classifiers trained on various fabric modules. The second type inference algorithm uses a graph-based approach to infer defect types based on likely relationships between current and target image types. Experimental results show that both algorithms outperformed a baseline approach using a majority vote from multiple classifiers. The proposed method performs comparably to a recently published method on detecting defect types with a complete dataset. However, this method requires modification to use the proposed direction-aware GHOG descriptor. Also, some assumed parameters used in the module-based approach require calibration before use. Nevertheless, our method differs from the existing method in using a direction-aware GHOG descriptor and considering both complete and incomplete dataset scenarios. To enhance the robustness of target-driven visual navigation systems powered by deep reinforcement learning, we introduce an information-theoretic constraint to the learning process. By maximizing the correlation between the agent's navigation actions and the resulting visual transformations, the agent makes more informed decisions, effectively learning a predictive model of the environment. Through a variational generative approach, the agent learns to simulate the impact of its actions, leveraging this understanding to forecast the outcome of different navigational choices. As a result, the agent achieves improved cross-target and cross-scene generalization capabilities, outperforming current state-of-the-art models by at least 10% according to AI2-THOR evaluations. Our method demonstrates real-world efficacy through successful navigation in diverse environments, including unseen indoor spaces and continuous real-world settings. The project code can be found on GitHub at https://github/infotree-qnnav.

We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centres of galaxies and 5-50% of these will merge in nuclear star clusters at high redshifts. These events peak at z=5-7 with a merger rate of 0.4-10 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our predictions also reveal that the most massive of these remnants primarily reside in small, low-mass nuclear star clusters formed in the early universe. These clusters host black holes of masses 40-85 M_\\odot that can produce detections similar to GW190521, specifically in a mass range typically found for pulsational pair-instability supernovae with a merger rate of 0.01-0.09 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Inspired by intermediate Lang conjectures concerning hyperbolicity and rational points, we establish new theorems on the finiteness of non-constant morphism sets from a specific fixed variety to another, also defined over a specific number field, by adapting Faltings's work on the finiteness of maps in moduli spaces. This result implies the finiteness of non-constant morphisms with a specific target when that target's dimension exceeds a certain threshold. Additionally, combining our work with Faltings's findings on hyperbolicity, we prove the finiteness of non-constant morphisms to projective spaces and, consequently, the finiteness of non-constant maps to varieties satisfying a specific non-denseness condition outside a finite set of points. The underlying number field can be chosen arbitrarily large; the upper bound on its size is determined by an explicitly stated formula. This work is a direct consequence of Faltings's results on hyperbolicity and the application of Arakelov theory. In a broader context, this research fits within the scope of questions initially explored by the Woods-Hole conference. The mathematical theories and results discussed here are specifically related to the applications of Faltings's work and the implications of assuming the Riemann hypothesis. We also discuss an alternative approach based on the geometric Arakelov intersection theory, which allows us to obtain similar results without depending on the assumption of the Riemann hypothesis. This approach also enables the creation of a new scheme, modeled after Deligne's scheme for absolute Galois group, which encodes information about the Galois group acting on the finite fields. This scheme's construction is similar to the Deligne model but is based on the arithmetic version of the complex moduli space of curves, which comes from arithmetic hyperbolicity theory. This scheme's formation involves the application of arithmetic hyperbolicity theories to moduli spaces of curves, which enables the relation of its geometric properties to the properties of curves themselves, especially their relation to the finite fields. This scheme's relationship to the finite fields is also reflected in the properties of the curves, especially their relationship to the images of non-constant maps from curves to projective spaces. This scheme's geometric properties can be quantitatively assessed by examining the arithmetic hyperbolicity theories, which enables the determination of the degree of the non-constant map equations. A novel method is introduced for training single-view 3D object pose estimation models, utilizing unstructured, 'in-the-wild' video footage where objects are rotated. These scenes are commonly encountered and can be easily gathered (e.g. cars navigating roundabouts, planes near airfields). The combination of traditional structure-from-motion techniques and cutting-edge object detection and feature matching methods yields surprisingly accurate 3D pose estimations in such video footage. The proposed method, which consists of two stages, initially learns a canonical pose from multiple videos, followed by adjusting to a common object model. In contrast to existing top-down methods that rely on 2D keypoint annotations, this approach provides more accurate results. Additionally, the method can accommodate multiple views, but for our experiments, we focus on a single view to evaluate the performance. Testing this method on a range of objects such as race cars and aircraft demonstrates its effectiveness, and the approach can potentially expedite 3D pose estimation in novel images. The code and data will be made available online. In particular, our method excels at pose estimation in cases where the object's backside is visible. While the method's accuracy may not quite match that of top-down approaches for fully visible objects, it significantly outperforms existing work in two key challenging scenarios: partially occluded objects and harsh lighting conditions. The latter scenario often results in noisy 2D annotations, and the method's ability to bypass this annotation limitation becomes a major advantage. In an effort to validate the method's robustness, our experiments involve a novel form of evaluation that consists of manipulating the model's parameters to mimic real-world variability, and the results confirm its effectiveness across different settings. Furthermore, the method can be combined with traditional top-down approaches to expedite their training and expand their applicability to more scenarios. The proposed method's accuracy is approximately 30 millimeters for predicting 3D pose from a single image. With the rapid growth of available video footage, our approach is poised to expeditiously develop precise 3D pose estimation models for a wide range of objects. The method can potentially accelerate top-down approaches and even leverage them to verify and refine the 3D pose estimations generated by the proposed technique. In particular, we observed notable improvements when combining the proposed with top-down methods trained on 2D keypoint annotations. To our knowledge, this is the first standalone single-view 3D object pose estimation method to bypass traditional 2D keypoint annotations altogether. The code and data will be made available

Despite widespread vaccination, a substantial number of people still harbor doubts due to misconceptions disseminated through social media regarding COVID-19 vaccines. Misinformation spread online does not necessarily lead to the adoption of false information; in fact, a proposed novel framework can discern one's attitude toward this misinformation. This new framework leverages neural networks and attitude consistency to classify stances toward COVID-19 vaccine-related misinformation. A novel neural framework, utilizing knowledge graphs to organize stances, successfully identifies attitudes toward this misinformation with outstanding results, outperforming other current approaches. Experiments were conducted on the recently created CoVaxLies dataset, a comprehensive collection of COVID-19 vaccine-related misinformation gathered from Twitter discussions. This new dataset allows us to distinguish which specific types of misinformation are more commonly accepted and which are more commonly disputed. This framework and dataset can potentially enable designers to create more effective counter-narratives and other interventions to combat the spread of this kind of misinformation. Results show that stances related to health issues are more commonly disputed while stances related to politics are more commonly adopted. A significant discovery was that stances consisting of single sentences are more commonly disputed as opposed to those consisting of multiple sentences. Furthermore, certain words and phrases increase the likelihood of adopting or rejecting misinformation, revealing a complex landscape of attitudes toward this misinformation and highlighting the importance of individual perspective when classifying attitudes. This framework and dataset offer a fresh perspective on understanding how people process and respond to false information, which could lead to the development of more targeted interventions in the future. This could be accomplished by creating customized counter-narratives aimed specifically at reducing the spread of particular types of misinformation, rather than general misinformation. By tailoring these narratives to individual perspectives on specific topics, rather than broad categories, we may be able to effectively reduce the spread of COVID-19 vaccine-related misinformation. This study seeks to enhance the computational efficiency of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) in point cloud learning. We critically examine the conventional graph convolution, comprising a KNN search and a multilayer perceptron. By dissecting its underlying mathematical operations, we arrive at two key insights for GCN optimization. Firstly, the 3D point cloud representation's geometric structure is efficiently propagated across the GCN through KNN search. This insight drives the simplification of multiple KNN searches within GCNs. Secondly, rearranging the sequence of feature aggregation and multilayer perceptron operations yields equivalent results. Based on these findings, we refine the computational procedure for GCNs. Experimental results demonstrate the optimized networks enjoy lower computational complexity, reduced memory usage, and accelerated inference speed while retaining comparable accuracy for point cloud learning. The source code will be publicly available at the GitHub repository: https://github.com/ofsoundof/EfficientGCN.git.

Deep neural networks are fundamentally altering the landscape of how data and physical laws are combined, resolving complex problems in physics and engineering that had proven insurmountable with conventional methods. Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves more complicated than traditional methods. This difficulty arises from the inherent uncertainty inherent in the training process of NN, which can be categorized into model-related and data-related uncertainties. Although some researchers have attempted to address this challenge, their approaches are either overly simplistic or exclusively applicable to specific tasks. This work presents a comprehensive framework for quantifying NN-based inference uncertainty, validating its efficacy on a diverse range of problems, including a high-energy physics experiment and various mechanical engineering tasks. By validating this framework, we can enhance our trust in NN-based predictions and facilitate their adoption in fields where uncertainties were previously a major limitation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed framework provides a viable solution for performing Bayesian optimization of complex systems, a task of significant value in fields like materials science and chemical engineering. This work thereby opens up new avenues for integrating NN and optimization methods in these fields, a combination that could significantly accelerate high-target-design processes. Lastly, we showcase the efficacy of our framework in a simulated fast-eddy correction system, allowing for the development of a novel control system for free-electron lasers that could potentially greatly reduce beam losses. Overall, the proposed framework represents a significant contribution to the integration of deep learning and engineering/physics, promising far-reaching impacts in the related fields. Upon further development, this framework can likely be extended to other fields such as quantum physics and medicine. Here we present the results from relevant studies and present an updated write-up of our work, including a newly developed method for quantifying the efficacy of various inference methods, a crucial tool that did not exist previously. This revised version of the paper provides essential clarity and is significantly improved. Further enhancements to this work have resulted in the development of an open-source package, deepinfer, which is now being utilized in multiple research projects; we anticipate that this resource will continue to be valuable and versatile. Finally, we are exploring the potential for incorporating adversarial training, an additional method for quantifying uncertainty, which we believe holds great promise and may be applied to a wide range of problems. Here we outline the challenges and opportunities associated with this approach, which represents an exciting direction for future research. To facilitate the replication of our results, the code for our research is freely accessible on github, which is where our team actively maintains the deepinfer package, enabling the seamless integration of NN-based inference

Policy iteration comes with computational drawbacks in large-scale Markov decision processes due to a local quadratic contraction rate and the costliness of its iterations for many states. Informed by its relation to the semismooth Newton method and the efficiency of its inner linear systems solving, we propose the application of an interior-point method for fast policy evaluation. This method, known for its $\sqrt{N}$ convergence rate in Newton-type iterations, also enables the efficient calculation of large-scale linear systems resulting from policy iteration. By utilizing a suitable approximation of the interior-point Newton-Karmakar algorithm, we achieve acceleration in policy iteration with $\sqrt{N}$ convergence rate. This leads to two variants of policy iteration, one with the interior-point method and another with an efficient approximation of it, both outperforming the original method and a known variant with $\sqrt{N}$ convergence rate on various benchmark datasets. Additionally, our method resembles the advantage actor-critic algorithm and transforming its policy evaluation into an advantage transformation enables the derivation of a novel proportional-integral-action algorithm with a faster $\sqrt{N}$ convergence rate than existing methods. Experimental results confirm the superiority of our methods over the state-of-the-art techniques in terms of the cumulative regret of the proportional-integral-action algorithm and the mean squared error of the interior-point policy evaluation. Our open-source code can be found at https://github.com/huynhquocam/pipol.

The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. This understanding has led to a theoretical model that uses the axisymmetric Stokes equations to examine the effect of liquid-solid slip on a film coated on a fiber undergoing the Rayleigh-Plateau instability. The new theoretical model reveals that slip leads to a higher rate of instability and longer wavelengths than predicted by previous models. Consequently, larger drops tend to form on fibers with high slip coefficients. The accuracy of the theoretical model is supported by numerical simulations and experimental results from a study conducted by Haefner, et al., published in 2015 in Nature Communications. The study found that certain proteins can induce a significant amount of slip, leading to the formation of larger bubbles on a fiber. This knowledge has potential applications in the development of novel methods for protein detection. Overall, this work provides a comprehensive understanding of the effect of liquid-solid slip on film dynamics and instability, which will contribute to the advancement of research in rheology and biomedicine. The new theoretical model may also be applied to analyze the behavior of liquid films in different geometries and physical systems. Using a line that is less affected by dust at this wavelength, we find that the predictions are accurate within expected measurement errors and are relatively consistent, although the choice of stellar model affects the outcome. Furthermore, even if the predictions for other spectral features are inaccurate, we find that the Prospector-derived star formation rates are generally accurate. Additionally, we consider how observing the $\lambda$2.16 $\mu$m Brackett-$\gamma$ line might be used to constrain the model's parameters and as an indicator of star formation rates in future near-infrared spectroscopy missions like JWST. Despite being less prone to dust effects, this line's measurement is challenging due to being weaker than other Brackett lines; however, we propose that its integration with other features could enhance our understanding of galaxy evolution, particularly in the study of distant and heavily dust-embedded galaxies. For instance, applying this line's indicator in a galaxy at $z\approx3$ helps to match the observed and predicted spectral features more accurately. Therefore, utilizing this line along with other near-infrared recombination lines could help to constrain the Prospector parameters and as an additional tool to study star formation rates in galaxies at high redshifts. Furthermore, we find that the Prospector-derived star formation rates are generally accurate even if the predicted spectral features are less accurate; however, utilizing this line as an indicator helps to validate the choice of stellar models. Lastly, we emphasize the importance of observing multiple near-infrared recombination lines for a precise estimation of star formation rates in galaxies at high redshifts. Conversely, using any single line may introduce a bias in estimating the parameters of the Prospector framework. This is the initial paper in a two-part series aimed at categorizing a substantial number of the type II quantum subgroups within the specified categories $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$. In this particular study, we classify the braided auto-equivalences of the local modules in categories linked to known type I quantum subgroups of $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$. It has been determined that the braided auto-equivalences of each local module are solely defined by four unique orbifold versions, specifically Version 1 related to $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{5},k)$, Version 2 associated with $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{6},k)$, Version 3 linked to $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{7},k)$, and Version 4 connected to $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{8},k)$. Conversely, the braided auto-equivalences of the non-local modules in categories linked to known type I quantum subgroups of $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$ do not follow a similar classification. Instead, their classification will be explored in a future study. It is worth noting that the generated classification of the braided auto-equivalences of the local modules in categories linked to known type I quantum subgroups of $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$ directly corresponds to a previously published classification by Wang and Ye of the local modules in categories linked to known type I quantum subgroups of $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$. The Fisher-KPP equation, a reaction-diffusion equation, was first introduced by Fisher for modelling allele spread within genetic populations, but also gained applications by Kolmogorov for a broader range of scenarios. Applying an innovative approach for tackling non-linear partial differential equations provides a distinctive approximate solution to the Fisher-KPP equation, which, however, defies initial intuition. Although the solution respects the maximum principle, a breakdown occurs once time surpasses zero, leading to an extremely irregular, non-smooth outcome that contradicts conventional travelling wave approximations commonly utilised in the field. Despite the limitations, this new solution has considerable advantages; it can accurately forecast the long-term behaviour of solutions to a variety of spatially homogeneous Fisher-KPP equations. Moreover, by translating the learnt characteristics of Fisher-KPP equation solutions into the context of the heat equation, a new generalised solution framework is formulated. This heat equation solution can anticipate and adjust for the heat kernel's distortions that are prevalent in the long-term heat kernel prediction. To verify the efficacy of the proposed approach, statistical tests were conducted. The new method was compared with conventional approaches, such as semi-Lagrangian finite difference, Galerkin, sparse grid techniques and machine learning algorithms like random forest and neural networks. It demonstrated superior performance in forecasting the long-term behaviour of solutions to the Fisher-KPP equation. Furthermore, the method successfully anticipated the expected spatial homogeneity of solutions to a range of the original equation's variants. Lastly, the method was successfully applied for travelling wave approximation in a cycled periodic domain. This approach holds great potential for a broad range of reaction-diffusion equations, may be extended to fractional diffusion equations and offers a promising framework for predictive modelling in biological, population and genetic dynamics modelling scenarios. The method has considerable practical significance as it can forecast the long-term behaviour of solutions to the original equation and other related equations, and this knowledge can be used to predict and control spatial homogeneity in long-term forecasts, which in turn can be used for predictive modelling in biological, population and genetic dynamics modelling scenarios. The method can potentially be extended to fractional diffusion equations and offers a promising framework for predictive modelling in the mentioned fields. The method can potentially be used for decision-making related to environmental, population and genetic dynamics scenarios where spatial homogeneity can significantly impact predictive models. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and mean durations for synthesis, this new approach can model any distribution on non-negative integers. We explore a median-based output generation strategy, which offers advantages such as being more representative, robust to training data irregularities, and enabling incremental synthesis. This method is in line with a broader goal of concurrently modelling durations and acoustic features at a frame-level. Evaluations show that this approach performs comparably to state-of-the-art methods in predicting the median duration of unseen natural speech. Moreover, it has the potential to significantly reduce the computational complexity of synthesis. Experiments using a shortcut for naturalising outputs reveal improvements of at least 1.5 times in synthesis speed without compromising naturalness or perceptual quality. The model also demonstrates the ability to learn robust phone-unit durations even when given a limited, short context.
