Species distribution analysis can be effectively conducted through occupancy modeling, taking into consideration inaccuracies in species presence data. To address multiple species, states, interactions, false positives, autocorrelation, and data from various sources, various modifications to the single species occupancy model have been introduced. However, creating high-performance software that can analyze large spatial data sets is still a developing field. A newly developed package, spOccupancy for R, is designed to fit single, multiple species, and combined occupancy models that are sensitive to spatial relationships. Utilizing a Bayesian approach with Pólya-Gamma data augmentation and Gaussian Process neighbor techniques, this package enables efficient model computation even for extensive datasets. spOccupancy provides intuitive functionalities for simulating data, testing models, verifying predictions, evaluating model performance, and making predictions on unseen data. Through a case study and a tutorial, this package demonstrates its capabilities by estimating species abundance in two distinct bird habitats: eastern Massachusetts, USA and central Chile. Results include probability maps and species presence probabilities that can be utilized for habitat assessments and predictions for species occupancy. spOccupancy supports the simulation of presence-absence data following the detection function, facilitating the inference of species occupancy and abundance from such data. This package differs from other occupancy model packages by incorporating Pólya-Gamma data augmentation and a flexible Gaussian Process neighbor approach, thus enabling the exploration of spatial relationships in occupancy modeling. spOccupancy is particularly innovative in its ability to model multiple species occupying the same location, competing for habitat. Although primarily created for species occupancy analysis, this package can be applied to the broader field of statistical ecology, extending to the study of infectious diseases and the behavior of herding species. Future plans for this package include expanding to handle multi-state models, false negatives, and data from multiple sources, while developing a user-friendly web interface to streamline model computations. Ultimately, spOccupancy aims to provide a comprehensive and flexible toolbox for the thorough examination of species distribution across diverse habitats and spatial scales. To explore the capabilities of this package, please refer to the included tutorial and case studies. The development of spOccupancy is ongoing, and suggestions for future work can be found in the provided repository. The package is freely available at https://cran.r-project.org/package=spOccupancy. Due to a lack of dermatologists, patients experience long waiting times for dermatologic care. Moreover, studies have shown that general practitioners make fewer accurate diagnoses compared to dermatologists when identifying malignant skin lesions. To address these challenges, we developed an innovative approach called interactive deep learning, combining artificial intelligence and human input. We created a diagnostic system that allows dermatologists to provide input and correct diagnostic errors made by the artificial intelligence model. By doing so, we improved the accuracy of diagnostic results and shortened the diagnosis time. Initially, we gathered a large dataset of skin lesions collected from the Google dermatology community and used it to develop a neural network model. However, the dataset contained many incorrect diagnostic labels, which affected the accuracy of the model. To overcome this issue, we partnered with the CNRS dermatology institute and obtained a smaller, more accurate dataset of skin lesions with corresponding diagnostic labels, as well as expert feedback from dermatologists. We ran two studies to validate our method, one involving 30 dermatologists and another with data from the CNRS dataset. Both experiments demonstrated that incorporating human feedback improved the accuracy of diagnostic results and took less time to complete compared to working with the original AI model. Notably, we found that the number of corrections increased when working with the smaller, more accurate dataset from the CNRS, indicating that the initial AI model had flaws that were addressed through human input. In conclusion, our interactive deep learning method effectively improved the accuracy of diagnostic results, demonstrated the value of incorporating human feedback into AI decision-making, and shortened the diagnosis time. As a result, the frequency of diagnostic errors decreased to zero. With continued progress, we anticipate that AI systems will become essential tools for dermatologists, enhancing their diagnostic capabilities and helping them work more efficiently. Furthermore, the concept of interactive deep learning has broad applications beyond the field of dermatology and can be adapted to other medical image analysis tasks. Ultimately, we aim to integrate our system into the daily routine of dermatologists and provide patients with faster and more accurate diagnostic results. To achieve this goal, we plan to develop mobile applications that make it easy for dermatologists to access the interactive deep learning system and receive diagnostic support. By leveraging advanced technology such as cloud computing, we can create scalable and efficient diagnostic systems that meet the needs of both dermatologists and patients alike. In conclusion, our study demonstrates the value of combining human and artificial intelligence in the field of dermatology, and we believe that the interactive deep learning method presented here can serve as a model for other medical image analysis tasks. The model's two-stage generative architecture can identify a reduced-dimensional representation of SNe Ia, accurately modeling their spectral evolution across wavelength and time directly from data. Introducing a penalty term to address variability correlations and a multi-stage training framework within our physically-parameterized network enabled the separation of intrinsic and extrinsic variability, eliminating the need for magnitude standardization models. The PAE was applied to predict spectral shapes and intrinsic variability patterns, allowing us to generate realistic spectra for arbitrary redshifts and completion rates up to 90%. The PAE's intrinsic variability predictions corresponded closely with observations of high-resolution SNe Ia spectra at low redshifts. We utilized the PAE to estimate the luminosity distribution of SNe Ia at high redshifts, taking into account the inherent variability of these events. The PAE's estimated luminosity distribution matched the data more accurately than a model assuming constant variability. The PAE's ability to predict spectral shapes and variability patterns up to z = 1.3 without direct observations of high-redshift SNe Ia spectra holds great significance. To study the movement of fluid into a swirling, turbulent plume containing heavy particles that sink more slowly than the plume moves, researchers used controlled experiments in a lab setting. The experiments focused on the effects of particle size, density, and the direction in which the plume gains mass, as well as the direction in which the particles move within the plume. The studies showed that when the direction in which the plume gains mass and the direction in which the particles move are opposites, the movement of fluid into the plume increases significantly. The rate of fluid movement increased in direct proportion to the ratio of the particles' gain of mass to the fluid's gain of mass, and this increased rate was greater for smaller particles. In contrast, when the direction in which the plume gains mass and the direction in which the particles move are the same, the movement of fluid into the plume does not increase, and this rate is the same whether or not particles are present. The rate of fluid movement was found to be higher when the direction in which the plume gains mass and the direction in which the particles move are opposites than when these directions are the same, and this difference in rates was greater for smaller particles. The theories used to interpret the lab experiments assumed that the movement of fluid into the plume is the same as a jet of fluid that moves through a medium more dense than water, and the theories also assumed that the movement of the plume is the same as a source of fluid that increases in size as it moves through a medium more dense than water. The assumption that the movement of fluid into the plume is the same as a jet of fluid that moves through a medium more dense than water was found to be accurate for experiments that did not involve particles that move in a direction opposite to the direction in which the plume gains mass. The movement of fluid into the plume that involves particles that move in a direction opposite to the direction in which the plume gains mass could not be explained using the theories based on assumptions that the movement of the plume is the same as a source of fluid that increases in size as it moves through a medium more dense than water. The explanation for this discrepancy is that the movement of fluid into the plume that involves particles that move in a direction opposite to the direction in which the plume gains mass could be due to interactions between the particles that sink more slowly than the plume moves and the turbulence in the plume. Understanding the spread of epidemics within networks, such as contact graphs, reveals patterns of disease transmission. However, assuming only pair-based interactions oversimplifies the complex human interactions seen in everyday life, neglecting the role of group meetings in disease spread. By adopting hyperedges to model these interactions, we create more comprehensive models, allowing the transmission rate to depend on the number of infectious contacts a person has. This approach leads us to develop new spectral conditions and study various types of contagion models, considering both the stochastic individual-level model and the mean-field approximation. Numerical examples and the analysis that follows enable the differentiation between inherent disease characteristics and the impact of individual actions. Ultimately, this framework holds potential for a more precise evaluation of the effectiveness of virus containment interventions. Recent breakthroughs in understanding 2D magnetic semiconductors, exemplified by the study of CrI$_3$, have generated significant enthusiasm due to their intriguing spin-dependent properties and their potential to revolutionize spintronics and magneto-optoelectronics. Through advanced theoretical calculations, researchers investigated the behavior of spin polarization within the prototype ferromagnetic CrI$_3$ bilayer, which has an in-plane magnetization orientation. Their investigation reveals that this ferromagnetic bilayer displays a rich pattern of spin texture within its uppermost valence bands, which arises from two unique spin cants resulting from the interplay of ferromagnetic order with both chirality and electrical polarization. First, a weak cant within the sublattice order creates a near-symmetry spin polarization over the in-plane magnetic layers. Second, a stronger cant emerges along the out-of-plane direction within the valence magnetic layers, which is caused by the presence of electric polarization and chirality factors. To address the uncertainty surrounding spin polarization, researchers suggest the implementation of spin-polarized photoemission spectroscopy as a solution. Their study stresses the significance of considering spin canting effects in comprehensive theories of spin-dependent properties within magnetic semiconductors, as seen in CrI$_3$. Moreover, their findings highlight the versatility of 2D magnetic semiconductors like CrI$_3$, where researchers can engineer spin-dependent properties not only through layer tuning but also through manipulating magnetic order and electric polarization. This research opens up fresh grounds for exploring 2D magnetic semiconductors, which has the potential to provide novel insights and innovative applications in the realm of spin electronics. \textbf{See also SI Abstract}.

Throughout their lives, solar-type stars remain relatively rapidly rotating in their midlatitudes. To explain this, we developed a new version of the differential rotation model that incorporates the effects of angular momentum redistribution within these stars. This revised model applies specifically to midlatitudes and is characterized by a low Rossby number, which signifies substantial tidal interactions due to the stars' orbital environments. We observed that the model's solutions closely match the observed differential rotation patterns of several solar-type stars. Notably, the model requires that angular momentum is predominantly gained at the equator and lost at higher latitudes, which may be attributed to magnetic cycles or other rotational periodic phenomena. To test these findings, we analyzed data from the Kepler mission and discovered evidence supporting latitudinal angular momentum redistribution in several stars. These results support the notion that magnetic cycles contribute to the rotational evolution of solar-type stars. To further validate our model, we studied the rotational history of stars spanning different masses and spectral types, incorporating parameters such as convective region size and core mass. This computational model, known as the evolutionary rotation model, successfully replicates the observed rapid rotation of low-mass stars and the rotational characteristics of T Tauri stars. We discovered that the primary mechanism responsible for the rotational evolution of stars is the early contraction of rotating stars, which influences the rotational properties of stars up to a mass of approximately two solar masses. In high-mass stars, the rotational history is characterized by a period of rapid spin driven by the conservation of angular momentum, which persists until they achieve a stable rotational state. To analyze the rotational properties of star clusters, we applied our evolutionary rotation model to study the population of 10 million stars in the K2 disk population, which spans a mass range from 0.6 to 1.5 solar masses. The model predicts that the distribution of rotational velocities among these stars is primarily influenced by their early thermal expansion, which causes a broad range of rotational velocities, spanning from nearly stationary to around 100 km/s. This method can learn a common representation using contrastive divergence and is applied to classification, information retrieval, and other related tasks. A significant drawback of traditional two-fan deep Boltzmann machine models lies in their inability to handle complex tasks effectively, particularly when multiple input modalities are incomplete or missing. We present a K-fan deep model, featuring a K-branch architecture for handling multi-input, multi-output tasks efficiently. This design outperforms current models, leveraging parallel processing and reduced dependency between model branches to enhance training efficiency. We apply the K-fan model to classification and information retrieval tasks and demonstrate improved results on benchmark datasets. Furthermore, the developed framework exhibits a flexible design, enabling easy adaptation to various machine learning tasks. This enables researchers to explore the effects of different architectures on model performance in a more feasible manner. We conduct an in-depth analysis of model performance and provide a comprehensive guide for future research applications. A related software package is available for reproduction of results. The use of model checking has become increasingly essential in validating the correctness of multi-threaded programs. The McMini model checker, which is based on DPOR, has been expanded with a mechanism that enables the declaration of novel, fundamental thread operations through C code. The mechanism allows end-users to define their own thread activation policies, including the handling of spurious wake-ups triggered by condition variables. By specifying (i) when operations are allowed, (ii) which thread operations are mutually independent, and (iii) when operations can co-occur, users can define their own customized thread activation policies. The McMini model checker's efficiency has been demonstrated through its effective validation of novel, commercially developed multi-threaded programs. We analyze a general branching population where individual lifetimes are independent and identically distributed with arbitrary distributions, and individuals give birth to new ones at random times following a Poisson process independently from each other. Supergravity, an extension of the Standard Model with local supersymmetry, may offer a way to describe new phenomena beyond our current understanding.  Exploring the cosmic applications of supergravity provides a platform to investigate the potential outcomes of this theoretical framework, which could serve as the low-energy effective theory of superstrings-a potential quantum gravity candidate.  Developing inflationary models in supergravity, however, poses significant challenges stemming primarily from the constraints on scalar potentials and complicated interactions within the framework, as well as the excess degrees of freedom.  Addressing these issues requires navigating the constraints on desirable inflationary paths, moduli stabilization to achieve a stable de-Sitter phase, and ensuring the scalars remain heavy during inflation to avoid scalar field-driven inflation.  Additionally, the predictions of gravity waves from the framework need to align with ongoing observations, presenting a growing tension.  This talk overviews the concerns with supergravity inflation, summarizes the current landscape, and introduces novel approaches to tackle the challenges.  Specifically, utilizing the homotopy theory concept to gauge the continuity of symmetries within the scalar potential and examining the non-abelian gauge symmetry properties of the dual magnetic bases may offer the required flexibility to construct refreshing inflationary models, allowing us to more efficiently navigate the issues within the supergravity framework.  A concise review of the applications of homotopy theory in the study of classical singularities, including the use of gauge group reparation to generate monodromy operators, sets the stage for applying this approach to scalar potentials, where distinct topology selections dictate the integration of the gauge field and potentially resolve new scalar potentials, fitting the requirements of cosmic supergravity.  This discussion provides the foundational understanding necessary to construct novel inflationary models, enabling dual magnetic bases to achieve cosmological stability, perhaps offering a path to resolving the cosmological tension.  This research, therefore, presents an innovative method for building dual magnetic inflation, allowing the reconstruction of inflationary models, and providing a novel mechanism for cosmological stability.  The talk also presents specific numerical results, demonstrating the potential for single-field inflation, governed by a single field, with predictions for primordial non-Gaussianity that may be testable.  These models, therefore, present a fresh opportunity for studying the interplay between cosmic inflation and supergravity. Lastly, the work in this study could be modified into a scalable, integrated circuit that integrates nonreciprocity and the study of correlated, directional photons. This development holds promise for the advancement of integrated photonic circuits where the concept of nonreciprocity and correlated photons could be used as new tools for detecting and manipulating light at a quantum level.

Using a computational model that incorporates machine-learned data and density functional theory, we have studied how varying the bonding configuration at the interface impacts the electronic properties. Across the examined configurations, we observed that the energy levels at the interface in InAs are positioned higher than those in EuS. Furthermore, we discovered novel states that arise from the interaction between the two materials, and are localized at the interface due to charge transfer. The arrangement of atoms at the interface significantly influences both the energy position and distribution of these states. While an induced magnetic effect is evident in InAs, the magnetic moment is relatively weak. Conversely, EuS exhibits a magnetic behavior characterized by stronger magnetic moments. The findings of our research could be utilized to develop devices that incorporate the magnetic properties of EuS into the semiconductor material InAs. Moreover, we reveal that the electronic properties at the interface of InAs and EuS are highly sensitive to the atomic configuration, and suggest that quantum devices based on this material pair may demonstrate intriguing phenomena such as spin-polarized conductivity and the presence of topological insulators. Lastly, we highlight the significance of employing efficient computational methods, like our machine-learned approach, to study complex materials systems. Despite significant difficulties in predicting the electronic properties of certain systems, such as the EuS/InAs interface, our research demonstrates the efficacy of using a computational model that combines machine-learned data and density functional theory to resolve such challenges. Our results, therefore, serve as a benchmark for the study of other complex interfaces. The research performed here can be utilized to develop, using the same approach, predictions about the electronic properties of other materials composed of europium sulfide and III-V semiconductors. In addition, the detailed analysis presented in this research, involving the various bonding configurations at the interface, serves as a useful reference for when researching this material pair in the future. A comprehensive classification system for subsets of Baire space, categorized by Borel Wadge classes, has been introduced. This classification system aligns with the hierarchy established by Montalbán and Randall, who demonstrated that every subset of Baire space belongs to a specific class within a particular range of the Borel Wadge hierarchy. Our classification system includes a comprehensive list of subsets corresponding to each class in the hierarchy, as well as additional sets not included in the hierarchy. In particular, we provide examples of sets that belong to classes $\mathcal{X}_\infty$ and $\mathcal{Y}_\infty$, but are not stratified compatible, thereby demonstrating that the hierarchy is indeed exhaustive. Our classification system also reveals that almost all subsets of Baire space belong to projects of Wadge rank 1, and that projects of Wadge rank 0 are in limited supply. In fact, we demonstrate that among projects of Wadge rank 1, only those with positive-negative symmetry correspond to $\mathcal{X}_1$-sets, while those with other symmetry correspond to $\mathcal{Y}_1$-sets. Furthermore, we provide examples of sets that belong to classes $\mathcal{X}_2$ and $\mathcal{Y}_2$, and show that every project of Wadge rank 2 corresponds to a project of Sharpe rank 2. In addition, we introduce the concept of 'downward closed projects' and demonstrate that projects of Wadge rank 1 which are downward closed are in a specific class within the hierarchy. Similarly, we find that projects of Wadge rank 2 which are downward closed correspond to a specific class within the hierarchy. Finally, we tackle the problem of determining whether projects of Wadge rank 1 which have positive-negative symmetry and are downward closed are unique or exist in multiple instances, leaving this question open along with a separate inquiry regarding the existence of projects of Wadge rank 1 which are downward closed and have negative-positive symmetry. In an effort to clarify relationships between projects and sets, we introduce the concept of'masks' which convert projects into sets, and demonstrate that this relationship is one-to-many, and that every set can be expressed as the intersection of a project and a mask. Deep, wide, and complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are emerging due to rising demands for accurate predictions and thorough analyses. However, they necessitate a considerable amount of computational power and time for processing. Previous studies on pruning have focused on enhancing inference efficiency, but there's been limited research on effectively decreasing training costs. Our proposed framework, ClickTrain, efficiently and accurately enables both end-to-end training and model pruning for CNNs, distinguishing itself from previous work with fine-grained architecture preservation through pattern-based pruning, precise weight estimation through linear interpolation, and compiler-optimized calculations. As a result, ClickTrain can deploy high-accuracy and high-throughput pruning models directly on the edge without further processing. Experimental outcomes show that ClickTrain can achieve notable reductions in computational costs, memory requirements, and processing speeds without sacrificing accuracy. Specifically, we observed notable gains in model pruning, accuracy, computational costs, memory requirements, and processing speeds of up to 98%, 6.8%, 2.3x, 99.7%, and 2.5 times respectively. These improvements surpass existing methods by a significant margin. Our proposed technique, ClickTrain, offers notable advancements for resource-constrained deployment of CNNs, distinguishing itself from previous work and opening up new possibilities for more efficient pruning techniques. This research examines the properties of specific modal logics derived from noncommutative lattices by incorporating $\Box$ and $\Diamond$. A new semantics model is introduced, specifically tailored for substructural modal logics. By applying duality principles, we demonstrate that every modal logic derived from the full Lambek calculus has a Kripke model, if it adheres to a specific structural rule. Furthermore, we establish a dual relationship between certain mathematical structures, specifically modal algebras and topological Kripke spaces, utilizing a topological model developed from Priestley spaces. As a result, we obtain equal results for the corresponding categories, thus providing an algebraic-topological duality for certain noncommutative lattices with a specific modal logic. To generalize these findings, we start with a distributive residuated lattice that has a left and right orthogonal set, and derives a new topological model based on a Priestley topology, resulting in the generation of a modal algebra. Ultimately, we apply the modal logic $\Box$ and $\Diamond$ to noncommutative Dedekind numbers, and establish a Stone-Tarski dual relationship for a specific noncommutative Dedekind number with a structural property. These findings can be generalized to any noncommutative Dedekind number with a specific property. Moreover, we observe that every finite noncommutative Dedekind number satisfies this property. Additionally, we provide a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of a canonical extension of a noncommutative Dedekind number with a specific property. Furthermore, we prove that every finite noncommutative Dedekind number has a canonical extension, and provide an example of an infinite noncommutative Dedekind number with a specific property that does not have a canonical extension. The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel results based on a deep learning approach, which employs a convolutional neural network to classify signals from real LIGO data involving neutron star and black hole mergers. The network's effectiveness is showcased in its capacity to differentiate between all types of merging compact binaries, distinguishing them from background noise. With approximately 500,000 training samples, we successfully trained a network that can recover known neutron star and binary neutron star events, and accurately classify a vast majority of candidate black hole binary merger events. These achievements are critical milestones in preparing for the next observing run of the LIGO-Virgo collaboration, particularly in anticipating the potential detection of neutron star events. Given that our approach is adaptable to various datasets, it is likely that similar methodologies will contribute substantially to the analysis of future gravitational wave data. Moreover, the applications of this method extend beyond gravitational waves, and it may be adapted for other areas such as audio classification and the classification of regional characteristics in images. The code used for the research is accessible at https://github.com/gvwillems/CNN-on-GW-data. Specifically, the version that facilitated our analysis may be found at https://github.com/gvwillems/CNN-on-GW-data/tree/LIGORelease. Additionally, the data employed in the research is documented at https://gwdocs.github.io/CNN_on_GW_data. We are in the process of integrating our method into the LIGO Algorithm Library at https://ligo-alleghenygithub.github.io/LIGO.Algorithm/ lib.html. We are committed to sharing our code in a transparent manner, and we welcome contributions from the community towards developing machine learning tools for the analysis of gravitational waves. We are particularly interested in refining our method to enhance its performance in distinguishing neutron star and binary neutron star events from other types of signals. As such, we invite readers to engage with a version of the code that incorporates our findings, and to share their feedback, questions, and new ideas for improving the analysis of gravitational waves. Optimal decision-making in constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs) is vital to operations management, with applications extending to areas like operational risk management and resource allocation. A potential employee may be hired with a promise of a performance-based salary to manage a system with operational risk, but, in this model, we abandon the notion of direct incentives and instead explore a contradictory scenario where we seek to detect and prevent adverse actions by limiting an individual's choices. Adverse actions are actions that diverge from the optimal path defined by a reversible policy in a Markov decision process (MDP). We first establish that detecting adverse actions in CMDPs is a non-trivial task and prove that finding a solution is NP-hard. We then present two heuristic approaches for detecting adverse actions: the First-Order Approximation, which involves reformulating the problem as a classical security problem and utilizing a convex relaxation to identify adverse actions through semi-definite programming, and the Best-Alternative Approximation, which involves finding the closest feasible action using linear programming. We evaluate these methods using a multi-class vehicle routing problem. Our study shows that the Best-Alternative Approximation outperforms the First-Order Approximation in detecting adverse actions but is less effective in identifying all adverse actions within a CMDP. We analyze the performance of these methods and provide guidance on their application. You can access our code here: https://github.com/asarkar/detecting-adverse-actions. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt to detect adverse actions within the context of a constrained Markov decision process. Our research has potential implications in areas such as detecting malicious actions within critical system decision-making and identifying cyber attacks. Our findings show that detecting adverse actions in CMDPs is a complex task and requires significant computational effort. The approach involves segmenting symbols accurately into over 300 categories. Since many complex mathematical symbols require both horizontal and vertical projection to be split, but certain symbols, like the square root symbol, can't be processed this way. What's more, handwritten mathematical symbols can look very similar, for example, handwritten zero and the Greek letter null. Given the numerous mathematical symbols, over 300 in total, a highly effective classifier capable of recognizing such a wide range of symbols must be developed. Initially, this study addressed the challenge of segmentation by applying the Simple Linear Iterative Clustering method. Results showed that the accuracy of the designed kNN classifier was 84% for recognizing mathematical symbols, which involved a total of 28 categories. Additionally, the study successfully combined the segmentation and recognition processes to improve the overall accuracy of the recognition process. The experimental outcomes supported this strategy. Moreover, the method of using the SLIC segmentation approach to segment handwritten mathematical symbols was evaluated and compared with other state-of-the-art methods, including the quick Ilastik and the Maxima document format. The experiments revealed that the integration of the SLIC segmentation approach and the kNN classifier outperformed the competing methods in terms of overall accuracy. Lastly, the study explored the effectiveness of using the SLIC segmentation approach to recognize mathematical symbols written in different scripts. The experiments revealed that the integration of the SLIC segmentation approach and the kNN classifier performed well on both Arabic and Chinese mathematical symbols, achieving an accuracy of 88% for recognizing Arabic mathematical symbols and 67% for recognizing Chinese mathematical symbols. However, the recognition of Chinese mathematical symbols was found to be challenging due to the complexity of the characters and the limited number of training data. Consequently, the overall accuracy of the recognition process was lower than that of the recognition of handwritten Arabic mathematical symbols. In this framework, BPS states can be represented as specific cohomology classes in twisted Dolbeault cohomology on the resolved space. The growth rates of BPS state degeneracies, specifically their indices, are connected to Euler characteristic computations in equivariant sheaf cohomology. A notable instance is when considering the Hilbert scheme of points on a 2D plane; this yields an accurate calculation of exponential BPS state degeneracy growth rates as the number of points goes to infinity. The growth characteristics serve as a theoretical prototype for the duality concept we introduced between a 7D black hole and superconformal quantum mechanics. The duality demonstrates that the duality invariant partition function is equivalent to the Euler characteristic of the symplectic resolution's twisted Dolbeault cohomology. Actor-critic reinforcement learning is commonly employed in robotics due to its versatility in a range of control tasks. However, its practical implementation often results in suboptimal policy outcomes owing to the limitations inherent in the actor-critic model. The HMC actor-critic framework integrates actor-critic reinforcement learning with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, utilizing the latter's capabilities to generate more realistic exploratory actions. The integration of HMC provides several benefits, primarily reducing the need for deterministic noise. As a result, the learned policies become more stable and amenable to faster training. The framework's efficacy has been demonstrated on a set of challenging robotic tasks, including learning a complex control strategy for a 4DoF mobile robot navigating a difficult environment. The experimental outcomes show significant enhancements in both policy quality and training efficiency when using HMC. Capable of operating in harsh environments, the sonar sensors are positionally versatile on the robot, facilitating optimal navigational results through a zoning system. A key feature of this research involves presenting an acoustic flow model, along with a designed controller structure. Diverse sensor configurations were successfully implemented to validate the modularity of the system. Experimental results show that this method yields stable and secure indoor navigation in the presence of moving objects. Moreover, the design of the method respects the principle of sensor redundancy, enabling navigation through adaptation of the flow model parameters as well as the addition of more sensors. Nereid, a satellite of Neptune that holds the distinction of being the largest outer satellite that can be spectroscopically analyzed, exhibits an irregular orbit. Our analysis focuses on Nereid's spectral characterization utilizing its reflectance spectrum between 0.8-2.4 $\mu m$, particularly in the unexplored 0.8-1.4 $\mu m$ range, as we attempt to identify the spectral absorption features that correspond to its icy composition. Our findings indicate the presence of crystalline water ice, coinciding with existing observations. Nonetheless, using simple models consisting of intimate water ice mixtures, we fail to attain a comprehensive match of absorption bands, especially considering the spectral continuum, at the wavelengths of 1.5 and 2.0 $\mu m$. This could be resolved by accounting for both crystalline and amorphous water ice, as well as taking into account the influence of sub-micron grain sizes. Furthermore, combining magnetite with components of the CM2 chondrite Murchison offers a feasible framework for understanding the spectral variations among objects like Nereid, particularly in those with neutral-sloped spectra. It's worth noting that magnetite provides a fitting explanation of Nereid's spectral continuum, eliminating the necessity of incorporating Tholin-like organic substances. Our analysis also reveals that non-ice components of outer solar system bodies may closely resemble those found in carbonaceous chondrites, as proposed by Fraser et al. (2019). Lastly, when compared with the spectra of other TNOs and Uranus satellites, it becomes evident that Nereid's low albedo, profound water ice band depth, and neutral hue are uniquely distinct, yet measurements in infrared wavelengths could offer further insights into this object. These results have significant implications for characterizing the spectroscopic diversity among objects like Nereid, as well as understanding the compositional differences among high-eccentricity satellites. Moreover, their analysis provides a solid foundation for conducting spectral-prospectographic investigations of other TNOs, as proposed by Orton (2008). Lastly, our study underscores the significance of thorough spectroscopic documentation of objects like Nereid, as well as the need for continued and persistent monitoring of its composition, rotation, shear, and collision dynamics. A new pessimism-based approach for Bayesian learning in the offline setting is proposed for creating the optimal dynamic treatment regimes. Traditional offline data solutions often result in sub-optimal policies when the coverage condition isn't met, which frequently occurs with offline data. The pessimism principle resolves this problem by limiting actions with little state-dependent data usage. Although most pessimism-based methods depend on a key hyperparameter for pessimism quantification, their effectiveness significantly depends on this parameter's proper choice. Our approach integrates the pessimism principle with Bayesian machine learning, using Thompson sampling to optimise the pessimism degree without manual adjustment. By developing a credible set with an optimistically bounded Q-function boundary, the need for additional pessimism parameter tuning is eliminated. Our general Bayesian learning method can accommodate a range of action-value function models, including linear models and neural networks. A linear model example is used to demonstrate the performance of our approach. Results show that our method outperforms a baseline pessimism-based learning method and achieves the same performance with reduced pessimism intensity, indicating fewer unnecessary treatments. Additionally, our method performs as well as the optimal dynamic treatment regime, which requires full online data coverage. Our approach is robust to model inaccuracies and accurately identifies optimistic actions even with sub-optimal Q-function estimates. In a flat band superconductor, bosonic modes can freely propagate whereas unpaired electrons are fixed in place. To study this highly interacting system, we developed a family of multi-band Hubbard models exhibiting exact pairing ground states across all symmetries. Through analytical computations, we discovered that many-body excitations are governed by an effective single-particle Hamiltonian based on the non-interacting wave functions of the system. Furthermore, we found a zero-energy excitation characteristic to these bound states with dispersion determined by the minimal quantum metric. Using the framework of topological quantum chemistry, we categorize bound state eigenstates according to their bundle type and provide a visualization of the bound state spectrum via a polarization diagram. Our analytical findings are verified by exact diagonalization calculations. Additionally, we discovered that bound states originate from a subset of nearly degenerate flat bands. Combining these results with a smooth variation of the superconducting symmetry, we construct a family of topological superconductors with a pair of flat bands hosting Majorana zero modes. Our work opens up new avenues for research in flat band superconductors and topological quantum matter. A related code package can be found at https://git.lfdi.de/lfdi/paco_package/-/tree/flatband-superconductor.

The Gaussian distribution is uniquely determined by the distribution of a linear combination and a power function of independent identically distributed random variables. We identify the a-adic solenoids for which this relationship holds, effectively proving a theorem analogous to the generalized Polya theorem. This proof relies on solving a functional equation for a specific class of functions associated with the character group of the a-adic solenoid. Additionally, the properties of the a-adic solenoids are investigated, and it is demonstrated that the solenoids possess topological characteristics akin to compact abelian groups. However, their algebras of continuous functions exhibit a-polynomial relationships, stemming from the inherent properties of a-dimensionality. This work presents a groundbreaking application of a-dimensionality in analyzing continuous probability distributions on solenoids. As a result, the singularly continuous nature of the Gaussian distribution on the real line is re-established, and similar results are obtained for other solenoids based on locally compact abelian groups. Ultimately, the concept of a-dimensionality is shown to pose challenges for the solenoids, including their solenoid groups, as evidenced by the distribution of a random a-dimensionally dependent variable on the solenoid groups. This research provides novel insights into probability distributions on topological groups. Additionally, the topological properties of the solenoids are found to have significant implications for their group structures. A key discovery is that the solenoids are perfect groups, meaning they have perfect subgroups that mirror their underlying group structures. This phenomenon is not unique to the solenoids; similar results can be found in other topological groups possessing a-dimensionality. Ultimately, the characteristics of the a-dimensionally dependent distributions reveal the solenoids to be 'almost' solenoid groups, possessing properties similar to those of compact abelian groups. As a consequence, the solenoids possess a rich structure of subgroups, inclusively a-polynomial groups, and their relationship with probability distributions is deeply connected with their topological properties. Findings from this research may be generalizable to probability distributions on topological groups, which warrants further investigation. To facilitate the analysis, the properties of the topological groups under the influence of a-dimensionality are thoroughly examined. This includes the existence of a-dimensionally dependent subgroups, perfect subgroups, and a-polynomial groups within the topological groups. Presence-absence data is represented as binary vectors or matrices consisting of zeros and ones, typically denoting the presence of something in a specific location. These data types commonly appear in research contexts such as ecological studies, genetic information, and linguistic analyses examining word occurrences in texts. Clustering methods can effectively apply to this data for a range of purposes including the identification of geographically linked species groups, known as biotic elements. Various clustering approaches can be utilized to process such data including the use of latent class mixtures under the assumption of local independence, hierarchical clustering based on the Jaccard distance, or applying continuous data methods to the multi-dimensional scaling representation of distances. These clustering methods vary conceptually and cannot easily be compared theoretically. To address this, we conduct an in-depth comparative analysis through simulation studies grounded in models for species distribution to evaluate their respective performances. 

This study has been accepted for publication in an upcoming publication titled "Innovations in multivariate statistical modelling: navigating theoretical and multidisciplinary domains," part of Springer Emerging Topics in Statistics and Biostatistics, edited by Ferreira, J., Bekker, A., Arashi, M., and Chen, D.

This model allowed for the creation of data sets with distinct cluster structures at different scales of the distance. Through 100 replicates at each of three dataset sizes, we analyzed the effectiveness of the aforementioned clustering methods by assessing the percentage of true positive clusters (TP), percentage of true negative clusters (TN), and average cluster size (ACS). Our results indicate that the use of local log-likelihood ratios based on the latent class model provides the most effective approach for identifying clustered species when the observation units are non-overlapping spatial areas. When the observation units are text documents, we found that the application of local log-likelihood ratios results in an optimal balance between TP and TN rates, compared to the other clustering methods. Conversely, hierarchical clustering based on the Jaccard distance yields the highest TP rates when the observation units are small-sized spatial areas. Moreover, the multi-dimensional scaling representation of distances consistently yields the smallest TP rates compared to the other clustering methods across the three dataset sizes. Finally, the application of continuous data methods to the multi-dimensional scaling representation of distances results in the smallest TN rates compared to the other clustering methods. In recent years, salient object detection using deep neural networks has received significant attention, but dealing with RGB and RGB-D images separately often necessitates the design of specific network architectures. This paper proposes an efficient and unified structure that integrates cross-attention context extraction to effectively tackle both tasks. By effectively fusing two inputs (for RGB images) or three inputs (for RGB-D images) with a cross-attention mechanism, our framework leverages the rich information present in both RGB and depth features. This structure's simplicity and efficacy enable efficient extraction and fusion of contextual information. As shown by experimental results, our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods on various datasets in terms of multiple evaluation metrics. Moreover, it demonstrates robust generalization ability on certain out-of-distribution datasets. The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval OffensEval Task is the subject of this paper. We adopted a dual-strategy to detect and classify hate speech in social media posts. For subtask A, a BERT-based classifier was adapted and achieved a high macro F1 score of 0.8136 in evaluating test data, thereby ranking 3rd among 103 competitors. Meanwhile, in subtasks B and C, a linear support vector machine was used in combination with pre-selected character n-gram features. Our method specifically for subtask C demonstrated effectiveness in identifying the victim of abusive content with a macro F1 score of 0.5243, and ranked 27th out of 65 participants. We present the details of our approach, results, and an analysis of the errors made by our system. Additionally, we share our project's code on GitHub at the address https://github.com/um-iu-ling/semeval-2019-offensEval. \bigskip

Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates, the process of reconstructing images typically involves a reverse ray transformation process. Omitting these variations may result in image distortions such as beam hardening, which poses an additional challenge. In certain settings, the dual effects of radiation and electronic signal degradation caused by devices such as CCD cameras contribute to image degradation. A proposed variational reconstruction model effectively accounts for these two distinct types of noise as well as the polyenergetic X-ray source, and further distinguishes between materials with unique attenuation characteristics. In support of this model, the proposed iterative algorithm has been mathematically justified and verified with numerical reconstructions of data collected from a test setup. The results demonstrate that the image reconstructed by this method exhibits lower mean squared error compared to a simpler model that disregards polyenergetic effects. Moreover, the reconstructed images show improved accuracy in distinguishing between materials with attenuation characteristics. This work makes possible the accurate reconstruction of pure attenuation profiles for various materials. Finally, numerical results confirm that the proposed method is effective in distinguishing between two materials with similar attenuation profiles. This work has potential applications in the accurate identification of mixture materials and the detection of defects within homogeneous materials. Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a complex challenge, largely due to the scarcity of labeled data and limited language knowledge (dictionaries and language models). A specific obstacle is accessing large datasets of modern handwritten text. To overcome this, utilizing naturally handwritten text from historical letters as a training resource has become a common approach. Nonetheless, handwritten text from such sources is often embedded in scanned images contaminated with noise and low quality. To address this problem, a novel method called Supernaova is proposed to cleanly extract pure handwritten text images without text layout or natural language structure constraints. The method is based on a sequential process of background removal, text segmentation, and text generation. Background removal is achieved through adaptive thresholding and morphological processing, while text segmentation is done using a simple yet effective line and word detection module aided by a minimal language model. To generate text images, a range-based post-processing technique is applied to a Generative Adversarial GAN's output, which is trained to create text images based on a minimal dataset of 90 labeled images. When evaluated using the evaluation tools provided by the HTR benchmark, Supernaova demonstrated robust performance in both noise filtering and text extraction, achieving an average accuracy of 67% on WordAccuracy, 52% on CharacterAccuracy, and 57% on LabelPropagation across three varying noise levels (0.1, 0.2, 0.3). The source code for Supernaova is available on GitHub. To our knowledge, Supernaova is the first instance of utilizing GANs for handwritten text segmentation, while its methodological innovations in background removal, line and word detection, and generated text post-processing enhance current solutions to handwritten text segmentation. Moreover, the application of GANs in text segmentation offers an alternative to traditional approaches powered by deep learning and statistical models. This study examines the compactness of composition operators within Bergman spaces associated with certain bounded, convex domains in complex n-dimensional space containing non-trivial analytic circles in the boundary. Consequently, this characterizes compactness of the composition operator with a continuous symbol (limited to its closure) on the Bergman space of the polydisc. Additionally, it's observed that the compactness of a composition operator is equivalent to its weak compactness, and a decisive criterion for weak compactness of composition operators on Bergman spaces of convex domains is formulated. Furthermore, it's discovered that the hypoelliptic property of the $\bar{\partial}$-operator on the zero section of a line bundle over a bounded convex domain, whose fibre is the one-dimensional complex manifold of holomorphic 1-forms on the domain, is necessary for the compactness of a composition operator. High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming.  A major obstacle to overcome is the memory alignment issue when working with objects, which leads to the rule of five memory operations known as the PLOS rule.  The fifth operation refers to the need to perform explicit memory de-alignment to prevent overlap between parallel object threads.  A new approach known as Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO) has emerged as a potential solution, focusing on a single approach to demonstrate feasibility without addressing the general object-oriented scenario.  Applying the SMMO strategy to the Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) algorithm, a significant challenge arises in ensuring the memory alignment requirement is met, and the cause of misalignment can be identified.  A memory alignment tool has been created and tested on NVIDIA GPUs, showing significant speedup under optimal conditions.  Nonetheless, the speedup came at the cost of increased memory usage and reduced memory availability for other applications.  A thorough evaluation across six different algorithms has shown mixed results, highlighting that SMMO can be beneficial for certain algorithms like MCTS, but may not be suitable for others.  A comprehensive assessment of SMMO's effectiveness requires considering not only speedup, but also memory alignment, communication overhead, and performance stability.  Future work should focus on overcoming the speedup limit, and exploring alternative techniques to facilitate high-performance parallelism on object-oriented algorithms.  A new tool has been introduced to provide transparent memory alignment, and the source code is available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/Chen-Hsun-Li/smmo.git. This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by accurately converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, a wide supply voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, and an incredibly compact silicon area of 0.021$mm^2$. Experimental results from 20 test chips revealed outstanding performance characteristics, including a 0.24{\deg}C resolution, a 1.4{\deg}C maximum inaccuracy, a 1.5kHz sampling rate, and an energy per conversion of 1.06nJ. This CMOS temperature sensor boasts one of the lowest power consumption levels among integrated temperature sensors. Furthermore, the design features a trade-off between power and performance, showcasing its potential application as an efficient temperature sensing module in portable devices or as a building block in more sophisticated systems. The design's computer simulation results are available on GitHub at https://github.com/NielsJorritsma/CMOS Temperature Sensor. The technical topic covered here is relevant to the following standards: ISO/IEC/IEEE 802.3az-2018 and ISO/IEC/IEEE 1629-2019. Quantum entanglement serves as a cornerstone for quantum information science and technologies. In optical applications, a common form of entanglement known as polarization entanglement typically arises from postselection methods, which are accompanied by destructive photon detection, limiting their usability in various applications. In this research, a new strategy is proposed to create entangled states of polarized photons without requiring postselection, instead opting for a heralded approach that ensures ready availability of entangled resources. By applying the quantum scissors technique to manipulate a specific type of entanglement known as continuous-variable entanglement, it is possible to create the desired hybrid entangled states, which are a combination of both discrete and continuous variables. We present two methods of implementing this technique, each utilizing a different technique to create the desired polarization entangled states: the first based on single photons and linear optics and the second using a two-mode squeezer. By examining both implementations and discussing the benefits and limitations of each, this research provides an understanding of entanglement preparation and its practical implications, highlighting an interface between diverse types of entangled states and potentially providing an alternative method for generating polarization entanglement through a heralded approach. We predict that this technique could be used in quantum computations utilizing entanglement-swapping protocols by making use of the available entangled resources more efficiently. In specific, it is predicted to boost the efficiency from an current maximum of two entangled resources to potentially multiple hundreds. \textbf{Update:} Since the publication of this work, it has been shown that applying the quantum scissors technique to create polarization entanglement is not feasible using only single photons and linear optics. However, the research remains valuable as it highlights the potential for using other methods to create entangled states of polarized photons, which can be challenging to produce through other means. Furthermore, the work presents alternative implementations of the quantum scissors technique using two-mode squeezer as a means of producing entangled states, which could have significant implications for the production of entangled photons. As research continues to advance in the production of entangled photons, it is likely that multiple methods of entanglement production will be used, each with their unique benefits and limitations. In specific, it is likely that the two-mode squeezer method could be used in space-based quantum communications to produce entangled photons more efficiently. This paper explores the concept of online Euclidean spanners in multiple dimensions. It considers the case where a sequence of points in R^d is given one at a time, and an algorithm must create a geometric t-spanner for each set of points as it arrives. The goal is to minimize the average degree of the resulting graphs while ensuring their distance between any two points is at most t times the actual distance. The paper first establishes a lower bound on the competitive ratio for any such algorithm by showing that a guaranteed factor of at least omega(log n / log log n) cannot be achieved. It also presents more detailed constructions in dimensions d = 1 and d = 2 along with strict competitive ratios for these cases. The study of these problems suggests the need for randomized algorithms. It also examines the related problem of finding the minimum-degree t-spanner for each set of points and establishes lower bounds on the required computational resources. The results are based on a model where the algorithm has access to the entire point sequence before each time step. A companion paper explores the online algorithm model. This research presents a novel and straightforward technique for word-alignment that leverages bilingual information from external sources like machine translation platforms. We demonstrate that a model with limited parameters can achieve performance comparable to GIZA++ when trained on a relatively small dataset. Furthermore, in terms of alignment metrics, such as accuracy or F-score, our approach delivers results equivalent to GIZA++ when trained on a dataset 22 times smaller. Crucially, the method's domain-agnostic training capabilities enable 'on-the-fly' application on any new pair of sentences without requiring extensive retraining. We showcase this capability by successfully using the method to align sentences in datasets from domains where parallel training data does not exist. The code is freely accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/aimenos/hydra. It includes support for training a GIZA++-equivalent model but specifically highlights the benefits of using more efficient models like HYDRA and modern learning methods like fine-tuning language models. Currently, the code does not support alignment using external bilingual information, but we intend to incorporate this feature in future updates. Recently, large text-conditioned generative diffusion models have received considerable attention for their impressive ability to generate detailed images from text input alone, yet achieving high-quality results typically requires multiple iterations. To facilitate text-guided image generation, users must frequently adjust input prompts, but even small modifications can lead to vastly different generated images, restricting artist control. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the Stable Artist, an image editing technique allowing artists to exert precise control over the image generation process. Its key component is semantic guidance (SEGA), enabling the diffusion process to be directed by multiple, varying semantic axes, thereby permitting refined edits to images and changes in style, composition, and artistic vision. Furthermore, SEGA facilitates the exploration of latent spaces, providing insights into the complex relationships between image variables. We illustrate the benefits of SEGA through creative projects demonstrating its capacity to produce high-quality, realistic images and videos from scratch, as well as its ability to make effective use of less accurate initial prompts, and to manipulate difficult aspects of an image while fixing other elements. We also provide a prompt grammar that allows artists to generate multiple, credible explanations for an same image, and one that produces images of famous people engaged in unexpected activities. To achieve these effects, we developed a set of maximally informative prompts, which we found to correspond to key concepts in the diffusion process. We even used SEGA to rotate Latent Diffusion Images, and discovered that our model is capable of detecting and correcting inaccurate prompt definitions with the help of corresponding reference images. We openly share our code and the artist's SEGA prompts to facilitate further research. Additional results can be found on our website. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive modeling that can be achieved using deep neural networks. However, critical inaccuracies persist when dealing with data outside the scope of a model's training and noisy data. To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of uncertainty in predictive models rooted in the theoretical framework of Bayesian deep learning. Bayesian neural networks are essentially intelligent systems that recognize their own shortcomings. To accurately quantify uncertainty, we approximate the posterior predictive distribution by leveraging Monte Carlo sampling combined with stochastic forward passes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that predictive uncertainty can be separated into aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties, both of which can be learned through unsupervised methods. Experimental findings show that the application of Bayesian uncertainty analysis results in improved steganographic performance with regard to capacity-distortion metrics. Moreover, we observe improved image quality and reduced distortion when a limited amount of data is available. To accelerate computational processing, we propose the utilization of a single graph to simultaneously compute both the predictive distribution and the posterior variational approximation. The proposed method is an adaptation of the celebrated KL divergence method, and can be optimized through the gradient descent algorithm. The results show that our method achieves steganographic capacity-distortion results comparable to those of existing methods. The code for our approach is available on GitHub in the repository named steegnography-bdl. Experimental findings show that our method achieves superior performance on discrete steganography when compared to other state-of-the-art algorithms. Additionally, minimal video analysis revealed that human object recognition is spatiotemporally complex, powered by local motion features in lower cortical areas. This work is the first to showcase lower cortical visual functions using a behavioral paradigm, suggesting that local motion features play a crucial role in object recognition through top-down interactions with higher visual areas. This research provides a new metric to evaluate the human-like performance of deep networks in visual recognition, potentially fostering more effective artificial models of human vision. It also offers novel computational evidence supporting the integration theory of visual learning and provides a foundational framework for exploring other aspects of visual perception. In addition to theoretical findings, the developed approach can be used for generating short promotional videos for object categories. These creative videos efficiently convey a quick summary of the object's characteristics, facilitating easier recall and providing a basic blueprint for designing machine learning models capable of producing action videos involving human body parts. Modern motion deblurring methods based on deep learning utilize paired synthetic data for training frameworks, aiming to directly convert blurry inputs to clear outputs. However, the success of these methods heavily relies on high-quality synthetic blurry data available only before training, a constraint that becomes impractical with large datasets. To overcome this limitation, we introduce an on-the-fly data augmentation technique to create blurry inputs dynamically during training and testing. To make the most of this approach, we adopt an unconventional framework incorporating a sequential process of blur removal and subsequent reblurring with the assistance of a module that mimics real-world blur, as well as hand-crafted prior information based on advanced statistical human body models. This module not only enhances the deblurring algorithm's ability to distinguish between human and non-human regions but also improves overall outcomes compared to other recent state-of-the-art methods through adversarial learning. The experimental results show the superiority of our proposed method over other benchmark techniques in terms of performance. However, the computational resources required to evaluate every possible model against a large dataset are excessively expensive, rendering them impractical to execute. As a result, existing benchmarking approaches utilize select, representative datasets, but this limited method restricts extensive analysis and introduces bias towards models that perform well on those chosen datasets, thus overlooking each dataset's distinct features. In response to these challenges, we aim to establish a new framework for a more systematic and dataset-orientated model evaluation, attributing relative weights to diverse datasets according to their compatibility with model outputs and demonstrating the method's efficacy on an evaluation of intrinsic dataset benchmarks. The novel approach we developed reveals that each scientific dataset has unique insights into model capabilities and suggests that dataset-centric benchmarking offers a more comprehensive framework for benchmarking AI models. Additionally, the method allows for an unstructured examination of each dataset's contribution to model selection. Since scientific AI applications often prioritize actionable insights into dataset uniqueness, our method enables researchers to identify and weigh individual scientific datasets based on their relative impacts on model choice. As such, it serves as a more representative method for a more precise model selection. We publicly present our method and results in an open-source framework for other researchers to verify our findings and build upon our work. As such, our work suggests that a more dataset-driven approach is essential for precise model selection while identifying opportunities for enhanced resource allocation across the datasets. This more robust idea has been tested with success for the case of t = 4. Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features. A comprehensive explanation of GCNN operations is provided, breaking down each layer type. Our analysis reveals that GCNNs employ a combination of convolution and global pooling operations to extract features, with the convolution layers acting as matched filters, and the global pooling layers aggregating information and effectively multiplying by an indicator function, effectively selecting specific feature patterns. This understanding leads to the development of a simplified, interpretable GCNN framework. We further explore the fundamental limits of GCNNs in terms of their capacity and generalization ability, providing a framework to evaluate the performance of different GCNN architectures. Our study is accompanied by a collection of code resources, available on GitHub, which includes a variety of GCNN implementations in PyTorch, comprising popular designs such as ChebyNet, GraphUNet, and GAT. These resources comprise a companion code repository and a related paper outlining our findings. Our analysis contributes to the development of new GCNN designs, suggesting the incorporation of Pooling-Matched Filters (PMFs) as a critical component, along with the use of multiple convolutional layers to achieve good performance. It is demonstrated that even with the limitation of only being able to learn geometric transformation parameters, GCNNs can still achieve superior classification accuracy when compared to traditional CNNs on certain datasets. Our study also highlights the significant influence of pool sizes on the performance of GCNNs, effectively serving as a type of data selection mechanism. Ultimately, our goal is to facilitate the creation of more efficient and effective GCNN designs, empowering researchers to develop better models. A recently developed neural dependency parsing method has achieved remarkable results across various languages and domains. However, its high reliance on large, annotated datasets has proven costly and impractical to obtain. This paper proposes a novel self-training technique that mitigates this data annotation constraint by leveraging the parser's own output to improve performance. The proposed self-training method comprises three stages: enhancing the parser with robust features, refining the parser using robust models, and iteratively updating the parser using its own output. Furthermore, a innovative early-stopping technique is introduced to automatically select the most effective parser at each stage. When applied to the UD treebank, our results show substantial improvements of up to 2 stages, with significant gains in macro F scores of 1.49, 1.27, and 1.17 for EN, FR, and DE, respectively. When combined with enhanced evaluation metrics, our approach reached parser performance similar to that achieved using the entire treebank but with data limits similar to those of the WAmbHugeAnn dataset. From a theoretical perspective, the best results were reached at an optimal point where further self-training stages would actually decrease performance. In light of this finding, the proposed early-stopping technique presents a viable solution. The proposed method is open-source and easily reproducible. When applied to other NLP tasks such as neural machine translation, a comparable approach was developed to leverage parser output as an additional source of information. Experimental results confirm the efficacy of this technique, yielding improved performance in sentence-level machine translation. In conclusion, the proposed self-training method offers a practical solution to the annotation cost associated with neural dependency parsing, paving the way for similar advancements in related areas like neural machine translation. In addition, the introduced early-stopping technique presents a useful strategy for automatically selecting the most effective parser at each stage of iteration. From a broader perspective, the proposed method highlights the feasibility of applying self-training and early-stopping techniques across a diverse range of NLP tasks. In terms of model interpretability, the analysis suggests that the robustness of our parser is directly related to its ability to generalize task-specific patterns.
